sources.title: Nvidia says it’s investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy - TechCrunch
passages: Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a Chinese spy operation .

In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers.
As the AI race between the United States and China heats up , chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus .
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said.

Nvidia also published a message that Huang sent to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang added that he’d “fallen short” of his responsibility to the company. “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said. As the AI race between the United States and China heats up , chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus . Huang also seems to have a close relationship with President Donald Trump , who’s been a cheerleader of the AI ( or “superintelligence” ) industry. In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said that it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or company secrets were compromised. It also said that Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that it has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.” The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel. In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers. sources.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang may have been the target of a spy plot through 'Chinese intelligence asset,' report claims — exec from firm under investigation for smuggling banned AI chips to China accused of being a spy, was also feeding information to Beijing - Tom's Hardware
passages: Multiple sources claim that a top executive at a Singapore AI firm suspected of steering Nvidia AI GPUs to China and who has close business ties with Jensen Huang was apparently passing information to Beijing as a Chinese intelligence asset.
According to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence has been aware of her activities for over a year already and has even briefed President Donald Trump on the situation.
However, Trump reportedly chose not to do anything about the information, as he apparently did not want to affect Nvidia sales or antagonize China.
“Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers.

The suspect, Alice Huang or Huang Le, was listed as the managing director of Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed, an Nvidia cloud partner that builds data centers and rents out the compute to Chinese firms like Alibaba.
The investigation into the firm began when the U.S.
Commerce Department visited the firm’s Malaysia data center and found the Nvidia equipment that it ordered still packed in boxes.
This raised suspicion that the machines were either just shipped in or about to be shipped out, instead of being installed on the site.
Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips last year .
The Chinese embassy in Washington denied the allegations, saying that it was merely “groundless smears and slanders” against China.
Nevertheless, it would also make sense for Beijing to keep tabs on senior executives of the top American firms that arguably single-handedly fueled the AI boom.

Huang hasn’t yet been given a defensive briefing — a warning that U.S. counterintelligence agencies would sometimes give to American citizens who have been targeted by foreign intelligence services — even though the surveillance against Alice Huang continues.
The report speculates it is possible this was done to avoid alerting Alice Huang that she was being investigated.
Huang was spotted in public with the Nvidia chief.
She was photographed sitting beside Jensen Huang alongside other executives in an informal event around Computex 2024 in a LinkedIn post by NetThunder, identified as Megaspeed Chairwoman Alice Wong.

Multiple sources claim that a top executive at a Singapore AI firm suspected of steering Nvidia AI GPUs to China and who has close business ties with Jensen Huang was apparently passing information to Beijing as a Chinese intelligence asset. According to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence has been aware of her activities for over a year already and has even briefed President Donald Trump on the situation. However, Trump reportedly chose not to do anything about the information, as he apparently did not want to affect Nvidia sales or antagonize China. The suspect, Alice Huang or Huang Le, was listed as the managing director of Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed, an Nvidia cloud partner that builds data centers and rents out the compute to Chinese firms like Alibaba. The investigation into the firm began when the U.S. Commerce Department visited the firm’s Malaysia data center and found the Nvidia equipment that it ordered still packed in boxes. This raised suspicion that the machines were either just shipped in or about to be shipped out, instead of being installed on the site. However, it remains unclear what made U.S. intelligence agencies investigate Ms. Huang. Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips last year . There have been multiple instances where Ms. Huang was spotted in public with the Nvidia chief. She was photographed sitting beside Jensen Huang alongside other executives in an informal event around Computex 2024 in a LinkedIn post by NetThunder, identified as Megaspeed Chairwoman Alice Wong. About a year later, around the same time as Computex 2025 , she was once again seen with Jensen Huang leaving a restaurant in Taipei alongside other business associates. “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Tom's Hardware . “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security ." Still, the possibility that Chinese intelligence is targeting a senior figure close to President Trump is apparently troubling some U.S. officials. The Chinese embassy in Washington denied the allegations, saying that it was merely “groundless smears and slanders” against China. Nevertheless, it would also make sense for Beijing to keep tabs on senior executives of the top American firms that arguably single-handedly fueled the AI boom. And given Jensen Huang’s status as a celebrity CEO , it’s not surprising that he is surrounded by all kinds of people from both the U.S. and China. Sources cited in the report claimed that Mr. Huang hasn’t yet been given a defensive briefing — a warning that U.S. counterintelligence agencies would sometimes give to American citizens who have been targeted by foreign intelligence services — even though the surveillance against Alice Huang continues. The report speculates it is possible this was done to avoid alerting Alice Huang that she was being investigated. As for Jensen, U.S. officials do not believe that he is aware of Ms. Huang’s intelligence activities. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," Nvidia told Tom’s Hardware . extraction.body: Nvidia has announced that it is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on the company. A statement posted by the board of directors reads: > The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. > The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. > The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate. The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia and is the subject of a Commerce Department investigation into whether it was smuggling AI chips to China. The company’s AI chips are viewed as crucial to the US maintaining technological supremacy. President Trump has loosened those restrictions but still bars sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to Chinese firms, and the Commerce Department must approve individual firms to handle the chips. Just as importantly, Jensen Huang has gotten quite cozy with Donald Trump, and there is concern about what insights into the administration’s deliberations around AI he may have been privy to. And whether any of that information may have been shared with Alice Huang, and eventually found its way to Beijing.

In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers.
As the AI race between the United States and China heats up , chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus .
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said.

Multiple sources claim that a top executive at a Singapore AI firm suspected of steering Nvidia AI GPUs to China and who has close business ties with Jensen Huang was apparently passing information to Beijing as a Chinese intelligence asset.
According to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence has been aware of her activities for over a year already and has even briefed President Donald Trump on the situation.
However, Trump reportedly chose not to do anything about the information, as he apparently did not want to affect Nvidia sales or antagonize China.
“Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers.

The suspect, Alice Huang or Huang Le, was listed as the managing director of Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed, an Nvidia cloud partner that builds data centers and rents out the compute to Chinese firms like Alibaba.
The investigation into the firm began when the U.S.
Commerce Department visited the firm’s Malaysia data center and found the Nvidia equipment that it ordered still packed in boxes.
This raised suspicion that the machines were either just shipped in or about to be shipped out, instead of being installed on the site.
Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips last year .
The Chinese embassy in Washington denied the allegations, saying that it was merely “groundless smears and slanders” against China.
Nevertheless, it would also make sense for Beijing to keep tabs on senior executives of the top American firms that arguably single-handedly fueled the AI boom.

Huang hasn’t yet been given a defensive briefing — a warning that U.S. counterintelligence agencies would sometimes give to American citizens who have been targeted by foreign intelligence services — even though the surveillance against Alice Huang continues.
The report speculates it is possible this was done to avoid alerting Alice Huang that she was being investigated.
Huang was spotted in public with the Nvidia chief.
She was photographed sitting beside Jensen Huang alongside other executives in an informal event around Computex 2024 in a LinkedIn post by NetThunder, identified as Megaspeed Chairwoman Alice Wong.

Some U.S. officials are worried that Beijing may be targeting close allies of President Trump. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Multiple sources claim that a top executive at a Singapore AI firm suspected of steering Nvidia AI GPUs to China and who has close business ties with Jensen Huang was apparently passing information to Beijing as a Chinese intelligence asset. According to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence has been aware of her activities for over a year already and has even briefed President Donald Trump on the situation. However, Trump reportedly chose not to do anything about the information, as he apparently did not want to affect Nvidia sales or antagonize China. The suspect, Alice Huang or Huang Le, was listed as the managing director of Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed, an Nvidia cloud partner that builds data centers and rents out the compute to Chinese firms like Alibaba. The investigation into the firm began when the U.S. Commerce Department visited the firm’s Malaysia data center and found the Nvidia equipment that it ordered still packed in boxes. This raised suspicion that the machines were either just shipped in or about to be shipped out, instead of being installed on the site. However, it remains unclear what made U.S. intelligence agencies investigate Ms. Huang. Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips last year . There have been multiple instances where Ms. Huang was spotted in public with the Nvidia chief. She was photographed sitting beside Jensen Huang alongside other executives in an informal event around Computex 2024 in a LinkedIn post by NetThunder, identified as Megaspeed Chairwoman Alice Wong. About a year later, around the same time as Computex 2025 , she was once again seen with Jensen Huang leaving a restaurant in Taipei alongside other business associates. “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Tom's Hardware . “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security ." Still, the possibility that Chinese intelligence is targeting a senior figure close to President Trump is apparently troubling some U.S. officials. The Chinese embassy in Washington denied the allegations, saying that it was merely “groundless smears and slanders” against China. Nevertheless, it would also make sense for Beijing to keep tabs on senior executives of the top American firms that arguably single-handedly fueled the AI boom. And given Jensen Huang’s status as a celebrity CEO , it’s not surprising that he is surrounded by all kinds of people from both the U.S. and China. Sources cited in the report claimed that Mr. Huang hasn’t yet been given a defensive briefing — a warning that U.S. counterintelligence agencies would sometimes give to American citizens who have been targeted by foreign intelligence services — even though the surveillance against Alice Huang continues. The report speculates it is possible this was done to avoid alerting Alice Huang that she was being investigated. As for Jensen, U.S. officials do not believe that he is aware of Ms. Huang’s intelligence activities. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," Nvidia told Tom’s Hardware . "We often receive updates from the U.S. government regarding parties and entities of concern and always act accordingly." Multiple sources claim that a top executive at a Singapore AI firm suspected of steering Nvidia AI GPUs to China and who has close business ties with Jensen Huang was apparently passing information to Beijing as a Chinese intelligence asset. According to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence has been aware of her activities for over a year already and has even briefed President Donald Trump on the situation. However, Trump reportedly chose not to do anything about the information, as he apparently did not want to affect Nvidia sales or antagonize China.

The suspect, Alice Huang or Huang Le, was listed as the managing director of Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed, an Nvidia cloud partner that builds data centers and rents out the compute to Chinese firms like Alibaba. The investigation into the firm began when the U.S. Commerce Department visited the firm’s Malaysia data center and found the Nvidia equipment that it ordered still packed in boxes. This raised suspicion that the machines were either just shipped in or about to be shipped out, instead of being installed on the site. However, it remains unclear what made U.S. intelligence agencies investigate Ms. Huang. Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips last year .

There have been multiple instances where Ms. Huang was spotted in public with the Nvidia chief. She was photographed sitting beside Jensen Huang alongside other executives in an informal event around Computex 2024 in a LinkedIn post by NetThunder, identified as Megaspeed Chairwoman Alice Wong. About a year later, around the same time as Computex 2025 , she was once again seen with Jensen Huang leaving a restaurant in Taipei alongside other business associates.

“Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Tom's Hardware . “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security ." Still, the possibility that Chinese intelligence is targeting a senior figure close to President Trump is apparently troubling some U.S. officials.

The Chinese embassy in Washington denied the allegations, saying that it was merely “groundless smears and slanders” against China. Nevertheless, it would also make sense for Beijing to keep tabs on senior executives of the top American firms that arguably single-handedly fueled the AI boom. And given Jensen Huang’s status as a celebrity CEO , it’s not surprising that he is surrounded by all kinds of people from both the U.S. and China. Sources cited in the report claimed that Mr. Huang hasn’t yet been given a defensive briefing — a warning that U.S. counterintelligence agencies would sometimes give to American citizens who have been targeted by foreign intelligence services — even though the surveillance against Alice Huang continues. The report speculates it is possible this was done to avoid alerting Alice Huang that she was being investigated.

As for Jensen, U.S. officials do not believe that he is aware of Ms. Huang’s intelligence activities. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," Nvidia told Tom’s Hardware . "We often receive updates from the U.S. government regarding parties and entities of concern and always act accordingly."

A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. > The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders. While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. > The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate. The New York Times reported last month that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with the Megaspeed executive, which he later admitted was romantic in nature in a memo to the company. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia and is the subject of a Commerce Department investigation into whether it was smuggling AI chips to China. The company’s AI chips are viewed as crucial to the US maintaining technological supremacy. President Trump has loosened those restrictions but still bars sales of Nvidia’s most powerful chips to Chinese firms, and the Commerce Department must approve individual firms to handle the chips. Just as importantly, Jensen Huang has gotten quite cozy with Donald Trump, and there is concern about what insights into the administration’s deliberations around AI he may have been privy to. And whether any of that information may have been shared with Alice Huang, and eventually found its way to Beijing.

Huang added that he'd "fallen short' of his responsibility to the company. "To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me," he said. extraction.body: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working for Beijing's intelligence services, according to an email obtained by Axios, prompting an independent investigation into whether the affair compromised U.S. national security or the chipmaker's closely guarded technology. The disclosure has raised concerns about potential foreign influence over one of the world's most powerful technology executives, who has been a prominent advocate in Washington for easing restrictions on exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China amid intensifying competition between the two countries. "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang wrote in a draft email to Nvidia employees obtained by Axios. There is no excuse for what I did." Huang said he took "full responsibility" for his actions, acknowledging that he had fallen short of his obligations to Nvidia employees, the company's board of directors and shareholders. "Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life," he wrote. "I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence." Nvidia announced Sunday that its board had authorized an independent investigation following media reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The inquiry will be conducted by an independent committee with the assistance of outside legal counsel. The company emphasized that it had no reason to believe either U.S. national security or Nvidia's proprietary information had been compromised. The board also expressed confidence in Huang's leadership, saying he fully supported the investigation and had committed to cooperating with it. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," John Rizzo, Nvidia's head of public policy communications, said in a statement. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a separate request for comment on the Axios report. The allegations center on Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman and senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. Despite sharing a surname, she and Jensen Huang are not related. According to people familiar with U.S. intelligence and reports in American and European media, including The New York Times and Britain's Financial Times, Alice Huang was recruited by a Chinese intelligence agency to gather information about Nvidia's advanced AI chips and influence the company's export policies. The alleged intelligence operation reportedly involved cultivating a personal relationship with the Nvidia chief executive that eventually became romantic. U.S. intelligence agencies monitored the relationship for more than a year, according to the reports. In June 2024, Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were reportedly documented together at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan. Around the same period, Megaspeed, which emerged from a little-known Chinese gaming company, began purchasing billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia's advanced chips. The circumstances have drawn scrutiny over whether the relationship could have provided Chinese intelligence with access to sensitive commercial information or opportunities to influence Huang's positions on U.S. export controls. The New York Times reported in October that Huang had maintained a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing. Following that report, senior Republican lawmakers in the U.S. House of Representatives called on Huang to brief Congress this month about the allegations. The controversy comes as Nvidia occupies a central position in the technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing. Its advanced processors are essential to developing and operating powerful AI systems, making restrictions on their export to China a major issue in U.S. national security policy. Huang has been among the most prominent technology executives urging Washington to ease those restrictions. He has argued that maintaining American technology companies' presence in the Chinese market strengthens U.S. competitiveness and helps prevent China from developing domestic alternatives that could eventually surpass American chips. His position has placed him at the center of a debate over whether restricting access to U.S. technology slows China's AI development or instead accelerates Beijing's efforts to achieve technological independence. The allegations involving Alice Huang have added a new dimension to that debate, raising questions about possible attempts by Chinese intelligence to influence a leading advocate for continued technology exports. However, the existence of a romantic relationship does not establish that Huang knowingly assisted a foreign intelligence operation or disclosed sensitive information. Nvidia's board said its investigation would examine all available information, while maintaining that it had found no reason to conclude that national security or company secrets had been compromised. For now, Huang remains at the helm of the chipmaker, with the company's leadership publicly backing him as the independent review proceeds.

extraction.body: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working for Beijing's intelligence services, according to an email obtained by Axios, prompting an independent investigation into whether the affair compromised U.S. national security or the chipmaker's closely guarded technology. The disclosure has raised concerns about potential foreign influence over one of the world's most powerful technology executives, who has been a prominent advocate in Washington for easing restrictions on exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China amid intensifying competition between the two countries. "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang wrote in a draft email to Nvidia employees obtained by Axios. There is no excuse for what I did." Huang said he took "full responsibility" for his actions, acknowledging that he had fallen short of his obligations to Nvidia employees, the company's board of directors and shareholders. "Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life," he wrote. "I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence." Nvidia announced Sunday that its board had authorized an independent investigation following media reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The inquiry will be conducted by an independent committee with the assistance of outside legal counsel. The company emphasized that it had no reason to believe either U.S. national security or Nvidia's proprietary information had been compromised. The board also expressed confidence in Huang's leadership, saying he fully supported the investigation and had committed to cooperating with it. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," John Rizzo, Nvidia's head of public policy communications, said in a statement. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a separate request for comment on the Axios report. The allegations center on Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman and senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. Despite sharing a surname, she and Jensen Huang are not related. According to people familiar with U.S. intelligence and reports in American and European media, including The New York Times and Britain's Financial Times, Alice Huang was recruited by a Chinese intelligence agency to gather information about Nvidia's advanced AI chips and influence the company's export policies. The alleged intelligence operation reportedly involved cultivating a personal relationship with the Nvidia chief executive that eventually became romantic. U.S. intelligence agencies monitored the relationship for more than a year, according to the reports. In June 2024, Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were reportedly documented together at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan. Around the same period, Megaspeed, which emerged from a little-known Chinese gaming company, began purchasing billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia's advanced chips. The circumstances have drawn scrutiny over whether the relationship could have provided Chinese intelligence with access to sensitive commercial information or opportunities to influence Huang's positions on U.S. export controls. The New York Times reported in October that Huang had maintained a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing. Following that report, senior Republican lawmakers in the U.S. House of Representatives called on Huang to brief Congress this month about the allegations. The controversy comes as Nvidia occupies a central position in the technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing. Its advanced processors are essential to developing and operating powerful AI systems, making restrictions on their export to China a major issue in U.S. national security policy. Huang has been among the most prominent technology executives urging Washington to ease those restrictions. He has argued that maintaining American technology companies' presence in the Chinese market strengthens U.S. competitiveness and helps prevent China from developing domestic alternatives that could eventually surpass American chips. His position has placed him at the center of a debate over whether restricting access to U.S. technology slows China's AI development or instead accelerates Beijing's efforts to achieve technological independence. The allegations involving Alice Huang have added a new dimension to that debate, raising questions about possible attempts by Chinese intelligence to influence a leading advocate for continued technology exports. However, the existence of a romantic relationship does not establish that Huang knowingly assisted a foreign intelligence operation or disclosed sensitive information. Nvidia's board said its investigation would examine all available information, while maintaining that it had found no reason to conclude that national security or company secrets had been compromised. For now, Huang remains at the helm of the chipmaker, with the company's leadership publicly backing him as the independent review proceeds.

extraction.body: The latest 13-inch MacBook Air is currently available for $1,099.99, marking the second time we’ve seen this $200 discount following the company’s hefty price increases over the summer. Although the base model — which features Apple’s M5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage — often sold for around $950 to $1,000 shortly after it launched in May, savings have been rare since July, making the current deal worth flagging. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are all honoring the price across all color options. If you’d prefer something with a larger screen, a six-speaker array instead of four, and slightly more power (with two additional GPU cores in the M5), Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air is also on sale for $200 off. It’s an ideal choice if you want faster performance, as it offers double the RAM and a speedier CPU with more cores. Given said differences, it’s easy to see how the Air’s improvements might make it worth the extra cost for some people. coreStoryFacts.text: The 13-inch Apple MacBook Air M5 is now on sale for back-to-school season, with the 13-inch starting at $1,134, or 13% off — the lowest price we’ve seen since Apple’s blanket price increase across its entire MacBook and iPad lineup in June.
It’s still the jack-of-all-trades laptop I recommend to most people, with a thin-and-light build, fantastic battery life, and — compared to the M4 — more memory and faster storage.
Unfortunately, these prices might be as low as they can possibly go for now as companies grapple with the rising cost of device components, memory, and storage.
This means consumers are paying 15% to 25% more now than they would have on the same device a couple of months ago.
While Amazon has changed its prices to match, some of the latest MacBook Air models are still less expensive there than at Apple.
Also: I tried buying a MacBook Air from Apple today – shipping was delayed by over a month
Apple CEO Tim Cook recently warned of an impending price hike in an interview with the Wall Street Journal , admitting that it had reached a point where higher prices were “unavoidable.”

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) launched a new version of Siri just last month, and it's undoubtedly the best version of the personal agent the company has ever released. Siri can now interact like other artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots by answering more in-depth questions; it also has on-screen awareness and more personal context than before because it can search through photos, emails, and texts. But as helpful as all of this is, just a few weeks after its launch, Siri still feels dated. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » With the recent launch of Meta Platforms ' (NASDAQ: META) popular Muse app , which can autonomously complete personal tasks such as booking a flight and shopping online, it's clear that Siri still doesn't measure up. That's a problem for Apple -- and I think it's one the company can solve. But there's a lot at stake if it keeps getting agentic AI wrong. Most of my personal devices are Apple products, and I've been less than enthused by Siri for years now. The latest update was a big leap forward, but it essentially caught Apple up with where OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude were several years ago. Meta's Muse easily helps users with all sorts of tasks, including booking flights, reserving tables at restaurants, ordering groceries, buying clothes online, and more. It's the type of personal AI assistant that many tech companies have talked about for years, finally built into a simple app. Muse has reached the top of Apple's App Store and has more than 3 million weekly users. That rapid adoption is a good sign that consumers want these capabilities, and there are some important reasons Apple should take notice. The bulk of Apple's revenue -- around 50% -- comes from selling its high-margin iPhones. The margins have taken a bit of a hit recently because of soaring memory prices, but management still estimates gross margins will be around 47%. For decades, Apple has paired high-end devices with top-notch software that consumers mostly love. But Muse and other agents could chip away at this sentiment by offering superior capabilities. Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan is concerned about this threat. Mohan said in an investor note last month that Muse could cut into Apple's services revenue by completing online transactions outside of Apple's ecosystem. What's more, if more consumers view Muse as essential to their daily routines, they could shift their smartphone buying habits away from expensive iPhones and toward cheaper Android devices that run Muse just as well. It's still too early to tell whether that will happen, but as users grow more accustomed to highly capable AI agents, paying premium prices for Apple hardware without robust AI built in may not make sense for many smartphone buyers. The biggest hurdle for Muse, and Apple's biggest advantage, is that most users don't trust Meta with their data. A recent Oppenheimer survey found that just 8% of respondents said they trust Meta with their passwords. In contrast, 28% of respondents said they would trust Apple with their passwords. Trust isn't the only factor in winning the agentic AI space, but it's a start. The next step is, of course, for Apple to design Siri to work better within third-party apps to complete autonomous tasks. The real problem for Apple isn't the technical know-how; it may be whether Apple's management believes the company needs to make such a leap with Siri to stay relevant. The latest version of Siri is a step in the right direction, but as an Apple shareholder myself, I wonder how long it will be before Siri catches up to other AI agents. If Apple is in the same place it is now a year from now, after the next iteration of Siri has presumably debuted, Apple's AI software miss could turn into a hardware sales problem. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity. While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. sources.title: Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic
passages: Apple is expected to push Siri to become more agentic and enable features that will allow it to perform ongoing tasks, not just one-offs.

Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI’s Dots or Meta’s Muse.
Two significant improvements are expected to be made to Siri in the coming months.
One will give the assistant fine-grained control over Apple’s first-party apps, allowing it to do things like rotate and crop images in Photos and organize Safari tabs.
That would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable, for example.

sources.title: Apple CEO Pushes Siri Agent Overhaul to Match OpenAI, Meta
passages: Apple CEO John Ternus is putting intense pressure on AI chief Craig Federighi to transform Siri into a full-fledged agentic assistant capable of competing with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.
If third-party apps optimize for OpenAI and Meta agents first, Apple risks becoming a second-class citizen in the AI ecosystem it desperately wants to control.

While Federighi's team managed to ship a working version of Siri AI on what insiders describe as an "incredibly short timeline," Apple executives privately admit they're not keeping pace with rivals who've already deployed AI agents capable of autonomous, multi-step tasks.
Meta, meanwhile, has been aggressively rolling out Muse across its family of apps, giving billions of users access to agentic capabilities.
The company needs Siri to become genuinely useful - not just incrementally better - to keep developers building for Apple Intelligence first.
Users expect agents that anticipate needs, coordinate complex workflows, and actually save time - capabilities that require fundamentally different architectures than what Siri was built on.
Apple's internal urgency around Siri signals a broader shift in how the company views AI competition.
But relying on OpenAI for core assistant functionality undermines Apple's ecosystem lock-in and puts user data in third-party hands - exactly the scenario Cupertino has spent decades avoiding.
Apple is scrambling to catch up in the agentic AI wars.
The pressure from Ternus suggests Apple views agentic AI as existential, not incremental.

For users, the promise of fine-grained app control and deeper automation sounds compelling, but the real question is whether Apple can deliver transformative agentic capabilities while maintaining the privacy and polish that define its brand.

extraction.body: Apple CEO John Ternus is putting intense pressure on AI chief Craig Federighi to transform Siri into a full-fledged agentic assistant capable of competing with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. While Federighi delivered a functional Siri AI on a compressed timeline, the company knows it's falling behind in the race to build powerful AI agents that can autonomously handle complex tasks across apps and services. Apple is scrambling to catch up in the agentic AI wars. CEO John Ternus isn't satisfied with Siri's current trajectory and is leaning hard on software chief Craig Federighi to deliver something that can actually go toe-to-toe with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports. While Federighi's team managed to ship a working version of Siri AI on what insiders describe as an "incredibly short timeline," Apple executives privately admit they're not keeping pace with rivals who've already deployed AI agents capable of autonomous, multi-step tasks. It's a rare admission of vulnerability from a company that typically sets the industry tempo. Two significant capability upgrades are headed to Siri in the coming months, according to Gurman's sources. The first will give the assistant granular control over Apple's native apps - think rotating and cropping images directly in Photos, organizing Safari tabs by topic, or managing complex Mail workflows without constant user prompting. OpenAI just closed an $11 billion funding round that values the ChatGPT maker at $1.25 trillion, cementing its position as the world's most valuable startup. Its Dots agent can already handle sophisticated tasks like booking travel, managing schedules, and coordinating across multiple services with minimal human intervention. Meta, meanwhile, has been aggressively rolling out Muse across its family of apps, giving billions of users access to agentic capabilities. Apple's challenge is architectural as much as it is competitive. The company built its reputation on tightly controlled, privacy-first experiences, but modern AI agents demand access to vast amounts of user data and cross-app coordination to function effectively. Federighi's team is essentially trying to build a competitive agent while maintaining Apple's privacy guardrails - a technical high-wire act that's proving harder than anticipated. The pressure from Ternus suggests Apple views agentic AI as existential, not incremental. The company recently began integrating ChatGPT support into its HomeView smart hub, signaling a willingness to partner with rivals when its own technology lags. But relying on OpenAI for core assistant functionality undermines Apple's ecosystem lock-in and puts user data in third-party hands - exactly the scenario Cupertino has spent decades avoiding. Industry observers note that Apple's historical playbook - wait, watch, then perfect - doesn't work when competitors are shipping transformative capabilities to hundreds of millions of users every quarter. Amazon just launched its own text-to-shop Alexa feature after blocking Meta's Muse from its platform, showing how quickly the agentic landscape is fragmenting. The internal roadmap acceleration also reflects concerns about developer momentum. If third-party apps optimize for OpenAI and Meta agents first, Apple risks becoming a second-class citizen in the AI ecosystem it desperately wants to control. The company needs Siri to become genuinely useful - not just incrementally better - to keep developers building for Apple Intelligence first. What remains unclear is whether Apple can compress its development timeline enough to matter. The company's methodical approach to shipping polished products has served it well in hardware, but software moves faster, and AI moves faster still. Federighi delivered functional Siri AI quickly, but "functional" isn't the bar anymore. Users expect agents that anticipate needs, coordinate complex workflows, and actually save time - capabilities that require fundamentally different architectures than what Siri was built on. The coming months will reveal whether Apple's internal pressure translates to external progress. Ternus isn't just asking for iterative improvements; he's demanding a competitive agent that can stand alongside the industry's best. That's a tall order for a company that's spent the past year playing catch-up while rivals sprint ahead. Apple's internal urgency around Siri signals a broader shift in how the company views AI competition. This isn't about adding features to maintain parity - it's about building an agent capable of genuinely competing with OpenAI and Meta's offerings before the window closes. For users, the promise of fine-grained app control and deeper automation sounds compelling, but the real question is whether Apple can deliver transformative agentic capabilities while maintaining the privacy and polish that define its brand. The pressure from Ternus suggests the company knows it's running out of time to prove it can.

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) launched a new version of Siri just last month, and it's undoubtedly the best version of the personal agent the company has ever released. Siri can now interact like other artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots by answering more in-depth questions; it also has on-screen awareness and more personal context than before because it can search through photos, emails, and texts. But as helpful as all of this is, just a few weeks after its launch, Siri still feels dated. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » With the recent launch of Meta Platforms ' (NASDAQ: META) popular Muse app , which can autonomously complete personal tasks such as booking a flight and shopping online, it's clear that Siri still doesn't measure up. That's a problem for Apple -- and I think it's one the company can solve. But there's a lot at stake if it keeps getting agentic AI wrong. Most of my personal devices are Apple products, and I've been less than enthused by Siri for years now. The latest update was a big leap forward, but it essentially caught Apple up with where OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude were several years ago. Meta's Muse easily helps users with all sorts of tasks, including booking flights, reserving tables at restaurants, ordering groceries, buying clothes online, and more. It's the type of personal AI assistant that many tech companies have talked about for years, finally built into a simple app. Muse has reached the top of Apple's App Store and has more than 3 million weekly users. That rapid adoption is a good sign that consumers want these capabilities, and there are some important reasons Apple should take notice. The bulk of Apple's revenue -- around 50% -- comes from selling its high-margin iPhones. The margins have taken a bit of a hit recently because of soaring memory prices, but management still estimates gross margins will be around 47%. For decades, Apple has paired high-end devices with top-notch software that consumers mostly love. But Muse and other agents could chip away at this sentiment by offering superior capabilities. Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan is concerned about this threat. Mohan said in an investor note last month that Muse could cut into Apple's services revenue by completing online transactions outside of Apple's ecosystem. What's more, if more consumers view Muse as essential to their daily routines, they could shift their smartphone buying habits away from expensive iPhones and toward cheaper Android devices that run Muse just as well. It's still too early to tell whether that will happen, but as users grow more accustomed to highly capable AI agents, paying premium prices for Apple hardware without robust AI built in may not make sense for many smartphone buyers. The biggest hurdle for Muse, and Apple's biggest advantage, is that most users don't trust Meta with their data. A recent Oppenheimer survey found that just 8% of respondents said they trust Meta with their passwords. In contrast, 28% of respondents said they would trust Apple with their passwords. Trust isn't the only factor in winning the agentic AI space, but it's a start. The next step is, of course, for Apple to design Siri to work better within third-party apps to complete autonomous tasks. The real problem for Apple isn't the technical know-how; it may be whether Apple's management believes the company needs to make such a leap with Siri to stay relevant. The latest version of Siri is a step in the right direction, but as an Apple shareholder myself, I wonder how long it will be before Siri catches up to other AI agents. If Apple is in the same place it is now a year from now, after the next iteration of Siri has presumably debuted, Apple's AI software miss could turn into a hardware sales problem. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity. While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook. Bank of America is an advertising partner of Motley Fool Money. Chris Neiger has positions in Apple. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Apple and Meta Platforms. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy . Apple Could Dominate the Agentic AI Market With Siri. If Apple is in the same place it is now a year from now, after the next iteration of Siri has presumably debuted, Apple's AI software miss could turn into a hardware sales problem.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

sources.title: Apple CEO Pushes Siri Agent Overhaul to Match OpenAI, Meta
passages: Apple CEO John Ternus is putting intense pressure on AI chief Craig Federighi to transform Siri into a full-fledged agentic assistant capable of competing with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.
If third-party apps optimize for OpenAI and Meta agents first, Apple risks becoming a second-class citizen in the AI ecosystem it desperately wants to control.

While Federighi's team managed to ship a working version of Siri AI on what insiders describe as an "incredibly short timeline," Apple executives privately admit they're not keeping pace with rivals who've already deployed AI agents capable of autonomous, multi-step tasks.
Meta, meanwhile, has been aggressively rolling out Muse across its family of apps, giving billions of users access to agentic capabilities.
The company needs Siri to become genuinely useful - not just incrementally better - to keep developers building for Apple Intelligence first.
Users expect agents that anticipate needs, coordinate complex workflows, and actually save time - capabilities that require fundamentally different architectures than what Siri was built on.
Apple's internal urgency around Siri signals a broader shift in how the company views AI competition.
But relying on OpenAI for core assistant functionality undermines Apple's ecosystem lock-in and puts user data in third-party hands - exactly the scenario Cupertino has spent decades avoiding.
Apple is scrambling to catch up in the agentic AI wars.
The pressure from Ternus suggests Apple views agentic AI as existential, not incremental.

For users, the promise of fine-grained app control and deeper automation sounds compelling, but the real question is whether Apple can deliver transformative agentic capabilities while maintaining the privacy and polish that define its brand.

extraction.body: Apple CEO John Ternus is putting intense pressure on AI chief Craig Federighi to transform Siri into a full-fledged agentic assistant capable of competing with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. While Federighi delivered a functional Siri AI on a compressed timeline, the company knows it's falling behind in the race to build powerful AI agents that can autonomously handle complex tasks across apps and services. Apple is scrambling to catch up in the agentic AI wars. CEO John Ternus isn't satisfied with Siri's current trajectory and is leaning hard on software chief Craig Federighi to deliver something that can actually go toe-to-toe with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports. While Federighi's team managed to ship a working version of Siri AI on what insiders describe as an "incredibly short timeline," Apple executives privately admit they're not keeping pace with rivals who've already deployed AI agents capable of autonomous, multi-step tasks. It's a rare admission of vulnerability from a company that typically sets the industry tempo. Two significant capability upgrades are headed to Siri in the coming months, according to Gurman's sources. The first will give the assistant granular control over Apple's native apps - think rotating and cropping images directly in Photos, organizing Safari tabs by topic, or managing complex Mail workflows without constant user prompting. OpenAI just closed an $11 billion funding round that values the ChatGPT maker at $1.25 trillion, cementing its position as the world's most valuable startup. Its Dots agent can already handle sophisticated tasks like booking travel, managing schedules, and coordinating across multiple services with minimal human intervention. Meta, meanwhile, has been aggressively rolling out Muse across its family of apps, giving billions of users access to agentic capabilities. Apple's challenge is architectural as much as it is competitive. The company built its reputation on tightly controlled, privacy-first experiences, but modern AI agents demand access to vast amounts of user data and cross-app coordination to function effectively. Federighi's team is essentially trying to build a competitive agent while maintaining Apple's privacy guardrails - a technical high-wire act that's proving harder than anticipated. The pressure from Ternus suggests Apple views agentic AI as existential, not incremental. The company recently began integrating ChatGPT support into its HomeView smart hub, signaling a willingness to partner with rivals when its own technology lags. But relying on OpenAI for core assistant functionality undermines Apple's ecosystem lock-in and puts user data in third-party hands - exactly the scenario Cupertino has spent decades avoiding. Industry observers note that Apple's historical playbook - wait, watch, then perfect - doesn't work when competitors are shipping transformative capabilities to hundreds of millions of users every quarter. Amazon just launched its own text-to-shop Alexa feature after blocking Meta's Muse from its platform, showing how quickly the agentic landscape is fragmenting. The internal roadmap acceleration also reflects concerns about developer momentum. If third-party apps optimize for OpenAI and Meta agents first, Apple risks becoming a second-class citizen in the AI ecosystem it desperately wants to control. The company needs Siri to become genuinely useful - not just incrementally better - to keep developers building for Apple Intelligence first. What remains unclear is whether Apple can compress its development timeline enough to matter. The company's methodical approach to shipping polished products has served it well in hardware, but software moves faster, and AI moves faster still. Federighi delivered functional Siri AI quickly, but "functional" isn't the bar anymore. Users expect agents that anticipate needs, coordinate complex workflows, and actually save time - capabilities that require fundamentally different architectures than what Siri was built on. The coming months will reveal whether Apple's internal pressure translates to external progress. Ternus isn't just asking for iterative improvements; he's demanding a competitive agent that can stand alongside the industry's best. That's a tall order for a company that's spent the past year playing catch-up while rivals sprint ahead. Apple's internal urgency around Siri signals a broader shift in how the company views AI competition. This isn't about adding features to maintain parity - it's about building an agent capable of genuinely competing with OpenAI and Meta's offerings before the window closes. For users, the promise of fine-grained app control and deeper automation sounds compelling, but the real question is whether Apple can deliver transformative agentic capabilities while maintaining the privacy and polish that define its brand. The pressure from Ternus suggests the company knows it's running out of time to prove it can.

The key insight: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported on November 8 that Apple wants to make Siri more agent-like, possibly as early as next year in Gurman’s view, contrasting Siri’s request-based actions with ChatGPT Dots, Meta Muse and Grok, which Gurman said keep working between conversations. Apple also gave engineers six weeks of coding instead of four in the first iOS 28 milestone, which by our arithmetic is 50% more coding time in that stage. Gurman wrote that today’s Siri AI “can properly answer questions, write emails and text messages, set reminders, pull information from the open web, serve up news and take basic actions inside apps”. Gurman described its biggest development this year as the ability to draw context from what is on a user’s display and from private information on Apple devices, such as emails and text messages. The iOS 27.3 beta adds precise control over Apple ’s own apps, Gurman reported, with examples including organising Safari tabs, sorting Files folders, unsending an iMessage and multistep Photos edits. Gurman wrote that support for Apple ’s apps “could come as early as December” and that third-party app support probably won’t arrive until the spring. Our earlier piece reported Apple opening Siri AI to any app . Gurman also posted that Apple is changing how it develops iOS 28, iPadOS 28 and macOS 28, giving engineers more time to explore and build new features before locking them in. The newsletter puts the change at six weeks of coding and two of convergence in the first milestone, instead of four and four. Apple is exploring turning Siri into a background AI agent similar to OpenAI ’s ChatGPT Dots as part of an iOS 28 shake-up, according to Bloomberg. Apple is still delivering the Siri overhaul it promised years ago. Now it is already exploring the architecture that could make that version look obsolete. Choblin29 relayed the Bloomberg report and added a view that Apple is exploring an architecture that could make its promised Siri overhaul look obsolete. That framing is the poster’s own; the newsletter says Apple wants to go in the agent direction and that the in-app actions promised in 2024 are still arriving in iOS 27.3. Apple finally stepping up to compete in AI with a personal AI agent that rivals Meta Muse, grok bot etc. few thoughts: – the new feature would allow 3rd-party apps to integrate siri. which means siri can perform actions, pull context through every app on your phone. that’s pretty sick. – despite being behind in AI, apple has a huge advantage: 3.5 billion devices people love and use everyday – but at the same time siri right now sucks, is incapable of doing even 30% of the things frontier LLMs can do. it can’t even use a computer. – compare this to muse, dots or grok bot that can work autonomously 24/7, self-improving the more you use it AND have access to their own computer. they’re miles ahead. imo apple has to balance delivering quickly (& aggressively) on AI without causing a major security breach. their whole thing is trust and privacy. that’s the challenge ternus will face. An X user posting as cryptopunk7213 (Ejaaz) shared a personal take on Gurman’s report at 17:07 UTC on 8 November. The post describes the reported feature as letting third-party apps integrate with Siri so it can act across apps, and argues that Apple’s installed base of devices is an advantage; that argument and the 3.5 billion devices figure are the poster’s, not Bloomberg’s. Gurman wrote that these features are “nothing close to what you can do with something like ChatGPT ’s Dots, Meta ’s Muse and Elon Musk ’s Grok”. Gurman listed what those agents do: they “can remember projects and preferences over time, monitor connected sources for changes, proactively surface information, and decide when to pause and resume work”. In Gurman’s summary, Siri “can now execute more complicated requests and integrate more deeply with third-party software ”, while Dots, Muse and Grok “can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step”. Apple ultimately wants to go in that direction, Gurman wrote, citing people Gurman spoke to. Apple CEO John Ternus said on the company’s earnings call, as quoted by Bloomberg, that Siri is “primarily request-based today” but “built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand its capabilities over time”. Ternus added that Apple wants agentic features done “in a way that protects security and privacy”. Our earlier piece covered Ternus pressing Federighi on AI , including the separate gap Gurman flagged in computer use. Gurman called a feature Apple showed at WWDC 2026 its “first truly agent-like iOS feature”: software that would analyse passwords saved to a user’s Apple account, identify weak or compromised credentials, and go from website to website changing them. The feature appeared early in the iOS 27 beta cycle before quietly disappearing, and Apple’s iOS marketing site still says it will arrive in the future, Gurman reported. Apple traditionally splits each year’s operating-system work into three milestones, M1, M2 and M3, each running eight weeks of four weeks of coding and four weeks of convergence, Gurman reported. For M1 of this cycle, covering Bell (iOS 28 and iPadOS 28) and Poppy (macOS 28), engineers got six weeks of coding, exploration and feature development and two weeks of convergence, according to the newsletter. Employees say they like the change, which creates more time to come up with ideas before locking them in, Gurman wrote. Development of the M2 milestone kicks off on Monday, and that is the period when Apple will start to finalise what it plans to include, according to the report. Our coverage has also included Anthropic’s Claude ‘Dreams’ memory research and Perplexity’s launch of Teammates . As we read the newsletter, the gap Gurman describes is less about what Siri can do in a single request and more about whether it can hold a goal over time and act without being asked. Apple wants to move Siri toward agent-style work, and Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman wrote in the Power On newsletter on November 8 that Gurman believes the company “could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year”. Gurman contrasted Siri in iOS 27.3, which carries out actions when a user gives a command, with ChatGPT ’s Dots, Meta ’s Muse and Elon Musk ’s Grok, which Gurman said can be handed an ongoing responsibility and continue working between conversations.

The same newsletter reported that Apple changed how it builds its 2027 operating systems. In the first development milestone for iOS 28, iPadOS 28 and macOS 28, engineers got six weeks of coding, exploration and feature development and two weeks of convergence, instead of the usual four and four, according to Bloomberg. By our arithmetic, that is 50% more coding time and half the convergence time in that stage.
An evergreen Business Engineer explainer on AI agents. It teaches the general idea only and does not discuss Siri.

The key insight: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported on November 8 that Apple wants to make Siri more agent-like, possibly as early as next year in Gurman’s view, contrasting Siri’s request-based actions with ChatGPT Dots, Meta Muse and Grok, which Gurman said keep working between conversations. Apple also gave engineers six weeks of coding instead of four in the first iOS 28 milestone, which by our arithmetic is 50% more coding time in that stage.

Gurman wrote that today’s Siri AI “can properly answer questions, write emails and text messages, set reminders, pull information from the open web, serve up news and take basic actions inside apps”. Gurman described its biggest development this year as the ability to draw context from what is on a user’s display and from private information on Apple devices, such as emails and text messages.

The iOS 27.3 beta adds precise control over Apple ’s own apps, Gurman reported, with examples including organising Safari tabs, sorting Files folders, unsending an iMessage and multistep Photos edits. Gurman wrote that support for Apple ’s apps “could come as early as December” and that third-party app support probably won’t arrive until the spring. Our earlier piece reported Apple opening Siri AI to any app .

Gurman also posted that Apple is changing how it develops iOS 28, iPadOS 28 and macOS 28, giving engineers more time to explore and build new features before locking them in. The newsletter puts the change at six weeks of coding and two of convergence in the first milestone, instead of four and four.

Apple is exploring turning Siri into a background AI agent similar to OpenAI ’s ChatGPT Dots as part of an iOS 28 shake-up, according to Bloomberg. Apple is still delivering the Siri overhaul it promised years ago. Now it is already exploring the architecture that could make that version look obsolete.

Choblin29 relayed the Bloomberg report and added a view that Apple is exploring an architecture that could make its promised Siri overhaul look obsolete. That framing is the poster’s own; the newsletter says Apple wants to go in the agent direction and that the in-app actions promised in 2024 are still arriving in iOS 27.3.

Apple finally stepping up to compete in AI with a personal AI agent that rivals Meta Muse, grok bot etc. few thoughts: – the new feature would allow 3rd-party apps to integrate siri. which means siri can perform actions, pull context through every app on your phone. that’s pretty sick. – despite being behind in AI, apple has a huge advantage: 3.5 billion devices people love and use everyday – but at the same time siri right now sucks, is incapable of doing even 30% of the things frontier LLMs can do. it can’t even use a computer. – compare this to muse, dots or grok bot that can work autonomously 24/7, self-improving the more you use it AND have access to their own computer. they’re miles ahead. imo apple has to balance delivering quickly (& aggressively) on AI without causing a major security breach. their whole thing is trust and privacy. that’s the challenge ternus will face.

An X user posting as cryptopunk7213 (Ejaaz) shared a personal take on Gurman’s report at 17:07 UTC on 8 November. The post describes the reported feature as letting third-party apps integrate with Siri so it can act across apps, and argues that Apple’s installed base of devices is an advantage; that argument and the 3.5 billion devices figure are the poster’s, not Bloomberg’s.

Gurman wrote that these features are “nothing close to what you can do with something like ChatGPT ’s Dots, Meta ’s Muse and Elon Musk ’s Grok”. Gurman listed what those agents do: they “can remember projects and preferences over time, monitor connected sources for changes, proactively surface information, and decide when to pause and resume work”.

In Gurman’s summary, Siri “can now execute more complicated requests and integrate more deeply with third-party software ”, while Dots, Muse and Grok “can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step”. Apple ultimately wants to go in that direction, Gurman wrote, citing people Gurman spoke to.

Apple CEO John Ternus said on the company’s earnings call, as quoted by Bloomberg, that Siri is “primarily request-based today” but “built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand its capabilities over time”. Ternus added that Apple wants agentic features done “in a way that protects security and privacy”. Our earlier piece covered Ternus pressing Federighi on AI , including the separate gap Gurman flagged in computer use.

Gurman called a feature Apple showed at WWDC 2026 its “first truly agent-like iOS feature”: software that would analyse passwords saved to a user’s Apple account, identify weak or compromised credentials, and go from website to website changing them. The feature appeared early in the iOS 27 beta cycle before quietly disappearing, and Apple’s iOS marketing site still says it will arrive in the future, Gurman reported.

Apple traditionally splits each year’s operating-system work into three milestones, M1, M2 and M3, each running eight weeks of four weeks of coding and four weeks of convergence, Gurman reported. For M1 of this cycle, covering Bell (iOS 28 and iPadOS 28) and Poppy (macOS 28), engineers got six weeks of coding, exploration and feature development and two weeks of convergence, according to the newsletter.

Employees say they like the change, which creates more time to come up with ideas before locking them in, Gurman wrote. Development of the M2 milestone kicks off on Monday, and that is the period when Apple will start to finalise what it plans to include, according to the report.

sources.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang officially called to Congress due to reports of a Chinese spy plot — officials mention growing concerns over national security - Tom's Hardware
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a man who likely attends numerous meetings, and today one more was added to his busy schedule.
Congress wants to have a closed-door chat with Huang over mounting concerns about national security .
The congressmen bidding for his time say last week's report spurred the move that he may be the target of espionage by a reported Chinese asset: Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (family unrelated).
The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) further claims that she was recruited by Chinese authorities due to her existing relationship with Jensen Huang.

As for Nvidia, the company seemingly reposted today the same comments it offered us last week, stating that "meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The firm adds that "[its] regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security."
According to the WSJ, Singaporean authorities opened their own probe into Megaspeed, and even reportedly questioned Alice Huang directly.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware.

extraction.body: Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation. The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added. The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips. Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said. “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security,” it added. The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against “foreign adversary espionage.” The company said its chief executive had an “outstanding security team” that travels with him. The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity. Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern. The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed. Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter. The company’s supply chain has come under increasing scrutiny as US export controls have prompted increased smuggling of its chips. Earlier this year Wally Liaw, a co-founder of Supermicro, one of Nvidia’s key supply chain partners, was arrested in the US and charged with smuggling Nvidia chips into China. NetThunder, a company that posted this photo on social media, introduced Alice Huang as "Megaspeed Chairperson Alice Wong." The U.S. Congress has summoned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to directly explain his relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. According to Axios on the 5th (local time), Representative Brian Mast, Republican Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Representative John Moolenaar, Chairman of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and Representative Rick Crawford, member of the Intelligence Committee, sent a letter to Jensen Huang that day, requesting his attendance at a joint, closed-door briefing by the three committees. In the letter, they asked Huang to explain Nvidia's security systems designed to protect the company from foreign adversaries, as well as his interactions with Alice Huang. They stated, "Recent reports raise serious national security concerns regarding the possibility of China accessing sensitive U.S. technologies and information," adding, "The issues of Chinese infiltration and access to advanced U.S. technology are core investigative matters for the three committees during this session." They emphasized, "It is crucial for Congress to understand the extent to which U.S. national security has been exposed to risk." This request indicates growing congressional pressure surrounding the investigation into the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who is suspected of Chinese espionage. Alice Huang is a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-headquartered data center company. She was photographed drinking alongside Jensen Huang and other artificial intelligence (AI) company executives at a bar in Taiwan in June 2024, and was spotted with him again in May of last year. Alice Huang herself reportedly flaunted her ties by posting photos with Jensen Huang on social media, which she allegedly used to raise investment funds. Previously, The New York Times (NYT) reported that Alice Huang is suspected of maintaining a close relationship with Jensen Huang and leaking information to China. The NYT also reported that President Donald Trump was briefed on the matter by intelligence agencies but took no action. The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that authorities in at least three countries are concerned that Alice Huang may have leaked sensitive information regarding Nvidia chips to the Chinese government. However, Nvidia has denied the allegations, stating that Jensen Huang's contact with Alice Huang was merely routine business interaction and that no national security-related information was leaked. Nvidia has not released a statement regarding the House's summons. The Chinese government previously dismissed allegations of Chinese espionage targeting Nvidia as "groundless speculation." (Photo: Capture of a NetThunder LinkedIn post, Yonhap News) ※ Please note: This article was translated by AI and may contain errors.
