The backdrop for the situation is that the U.S. has long-standing export controls blocking Nvidia and AMD's most advanced AI accelerator chips from reaching China, among a number of other nations.
The allegations were first published last week in the NYT, and are reportedly sourced from unnamed U.S. intelligence officials.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.
Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.
It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.
Congress has summoned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to directly explain his relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

supportedClaims.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a man who likely attends numerous meetings, and today one more was added to his busy schedule.
Congress wants to have a closed-door chat with Huang over mounting concerns about national security .
The congressmen bidding for his time say last week's report spurred the move that he may be the target of espionage by a reported Chinese asset: Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (family unrelated).
The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) further claims that she was recruited by Chinese authorities due to her existing relationship with Jensen Huang.

As for Nvidia, the company seemingly reposted today the same comments it offered us last week, stating that "meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The firm adds that "[its] regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security."
According to the WSJ, Singaporean authorities opened their own probe into Megaspeed, and even reportedly questioned Alice Huang directly.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a man who likely attends numerous meetings, and today one more was added to his busy schedule. The U.S. Congress wants to have a closed-door chat with Huang over mounting concerns about national security . The congressmen bidding for his time say last week's report spurred the move that he may be the target of espionage by a reported Chinese asset: Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (family unrelated). The meeting was set up by Republican House representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford, respective Chairs of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence. In the House's letter on the matter, the lawmakers say the aforementioned reports "raise significant national security concerns" about China gaining access to U.S. technology and information. The previously reported claim is that Alice Huang is a Chinese plant in Singaporean data center outfit Megaspeed, siphoning information to Beijing. The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) further claims that she was recruited by Chinese authorities due to her existing relationship with Jensen Huang. Megaspeed reportedly bought and continues to buy billions' worth of Nvidia's chips, according to The New York Times (NYT), and stands accused by the Department of Commerce since 2024 of smuggling $2 billion worth of advanced silicon to China. The backdrop for the situation is that the U.S. has long-standing export controls blocking Nvidia and AMD's most advanced AI accelerator chips from reaching China, among a number of other nations. The allegations were first published last week in the NYT, and are reportedly sourced from unnamed U.S. intelligence officials. The House says the purpose of the briefing with Jensen Huang is to discuss "Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and [his] interactions with [...] Alice Huang." According to the NYT, the CEO never got a "defensive briefing," essentially a warning for potential targets of foreign espionage, to acquaint them with signs of such activities. The publication notes that intelligence officials often hesitate to inform potential targets of espionage, as doing so may make the spy aware they're being investigated. The NYT adds that President Trump was briefed on the situation surrounding Megaspeed and Alice Huang a year ago, but chose not to act on it. Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. According to the WSJ, Singaporean authorities opened their own probe into Megaspeed, and even reportedly questioned Alice Huang directly. However, an official response from the country told the WSJ that it "does not implement unilateral export controls imposed by foreign jurisdictions," adding that while it's investigating Megaspeed, it's not targeting Alice Huang herself or inspecting her claimed ties with Jensen Huang or China. The Singaporean does note that the country has "a zero-tolerance stance" on commercial fraud, pointing out that it's charged four companies and four individuals over such wrongdoings, and that they may face up to 20 years in prison. Meanwhile, Taiwan is also seemingly keeping a close eye on Alice Huang, by inspecting her visits to the nation. The WSJ says that the country's authorities are probing her involvement with China and have her under physical surveillance. As for Nvidia, the company seemingly reposted today the same comments it offered us last week, stating that "meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The firm adds that "[its] regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security." Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a man who likely attends numerous meetings, and today one more was added to his busy schedule. The U.S. Congress wants to have a closed-door chat with Huang over mounting concerns about national security . The congressmen bidding for his time say last week's report spurred the move that he may be the target of espionage by a reported Chinese asset: Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (family unrelated).

The meeting was set up by Republican House representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford, respective Chairs of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence. In the House's letter on the matter, the lawmakers say the aforementioned reports "raise significant national security concerns" about China gaining access to U.S. technology and information.

The previously reported claim is that Alice Huang is a Chinese plant in Singaporean data center outfit Megaspeed, siphoning information to Beijing. The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) further claims that she was recruited by Chinese authorities due to her existing relationship with Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed reportedly bought and continues to buy billions' worth of Nvidia's chips, according to The New York Times (NYT), and stands accused by the Department of Commerce since 2024 of smuggling $2 billion worth of advanced silicon to China.

The backdrop for the situation is that the U.S. has long-standing export controls blocking Nvidia and AMD's most advanced AI accelerator chips from reaching China, among a number of other nations. The allegations were first published last week in the NYT, and are reportedly sourced from unnamed U.S. intelligence officials.

The House says the purpose of the briefing with Jensen Huang is to discuss "Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and [his] interactions with [...] Alice Huang." According to the NYT, the CEO never got a "defensive briefing," essentially a warning for potential targets of foreign espionage, to acquaint them with signs of such activities.

The publication notes that intelligence officials often hesitate to inform potential targets of espionage, as doing so may make the spy aware they're being investigated. The NYT adds that President Trump was briefed on the situation surrounding Megaspeed and Alice Huang a year ago, but chose not to act on it.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

According to the WSJ, Singaporean authorities opened their own probe into Megaspeed, and even reportedly questioned Alice Huang directly. However, an official response from the country told the WSJ that it "does not implement unilateral export controls imposed by foreign jurisdictions," adding that while it's investigating Megaspeed, it's not targeting Alice Huang herself or inspecting her claimed ties with Jensen Huang or China.

The Singaporean does note that the country has "a zero-tolerance stance" on commercial fraud, pointing out that it's charged four companies and four individuals over such wrongdoings, and that they may face up to 20 years in prison.

Meanwhile, Taiwan is also seemingly keeping a close eye on Alice Huang, by inspecting her visits to the nation. The WSJ says that the country's authorities are probing her involvement with China and have her under physical surveillance.

As for Nvidia, the company seemingly reposted today the same comments it offered us last week, stating that "meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The firm adds that "[its] regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security."

passages: Apple HomeView chatbots moved from rumor to code-level evidence on November 8, 2026, when The Verge reported that an iOS 27.3 beta contains groundwork for a new “Conversational Apps” category.
The code reportedly prepares two-way audio routing, session management, and interruptions, which are the plumbing a voice chatbot needs on a smart-home hub.
Apple has not announced third-party chatbot apps for HomeView, so everything beyond the code remains inference.
The reporting credits a code investigator known as pdfu with the discovery.
The headline conclusion is modest: chatbots might be coming to HomeView, and Apple appears to be building the framework that would let them.
The timing matters because Apple announced HomeView on October 13, 2026 and schedules availability for November 13, 2026.
That leaves five days between today and the day the first units reach buyers.
Reporting that cites Apple information puts the price at $299.
Apple’s own assistant, Siri AI, ships inside the device in beta, which means any outside chatbot would arrive in a house where Apple already has a voice in the room.
The device runs on the A18 chip, which suggests Apple wants the hub to handle real intelligence work rather than act as a thin speaker.
For a news desk, the right framing is a three-layer ladder.
In the middle sits the reported code, which suggests an app category for conversation.
At the top sits the speculation, in which named chatbot makers ship named apps on named dates.
Teams building voice products today can already design around those three behaviors.
Whether chatbots join it is a question only Apple can answer, and so far it has not.
On the other side of the ledger, the AI industry changed fast in 2026.
Frontier chatbot makers now court distribution wherever they can find it.
Google has pushed Gemini deeper into its own products, as in our report on the Google Messages redesign with Gemini in the beta .
Buyers who want HomeView on day one should buy it for what Apple sells today.
If third-party chatbots arrive later, treat them as a bonus.
A purchase justified only by a rumored ChatGPT or Claude app rests on an unconfirmed claim.
This analysis separates what Apple has said, what the beta code reportedly shows, and what nobody has confirmed.
Two beta tracks with different version numbers suggest that Apple is staging the rollout.
First-party behavior comes first, and an open door for others, if any, follows.
The first beneficiaries would be the chatbot makers themselves.
Even without confirmed partners, the existence of the code makes the opportunity visible to every company that sells conversational AI.
Siri AI is built into Apple HomeView and is powered by Apple Intelligence.
The claim that OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude will launch as dedicated HomeView apps is unconfirmed, and it remains unconfirmed even though the idea feels natural.
Code that prepares a category is not the same thing as a partner list.

Leaker pdfu said at the start of the month that ChatGPT, Claude and other AI apps “may” be coming to HomeView, after spotting an unused flag for ConversationalApps.
They now say that the beta of iOS 26.3 confirms their suspicion.
The same leaker recently discovered evidence that HomeView will be able to serve as a HomeKit security camera .
Code in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that Apple could add support for chatbots to its smart home hub.
Neither feature has been officially announced by Apple, and there’s no word on when they might become available.
While there are no details about what apps would fall under that heading, it seems reasonable that AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude could be added to HomeView.

According to pdfu on X, that new beta also adds support for bidirectional audio routing and session management, but says it’s “still not fully wired up.” Apple has also added anti-spoofing protection that will require a user to authenticate themselves with an iPhone after three failed attempts.

Apparently, after three spoof attempts for a profile, the user must authenticate with an iPhone to see personal data, and the protection is enabled in HomeView software 27.2.
The software HomeView uses to display apps from a connected iPhone or iPad is said to have gained a " Conversational Apps " category in the latest beta.

HomeView isn't on sale in the European Union because Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS there, and Apple says it is still working with the EU to find a path forward to make it available in the bloc.

extraction.body: Code discovered in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests Apple is laying the groundwork for chatbot apps on its upcoming HomeView smart home hub, according to the code investigator known as pdfu . The software HomeView uses to display apps from a connected iPhone or iPad is said to have gained a " Conversational Apps " category in the latest beta. The update also reportedly adds preparations for two-way audio routing, session management, and interruptions, but pdfu notes that it is "still not fully wired up." Apple hasn't announced chatbot apps for HomeView, and the code doesn't show which apps could use the category or when it could launch, so support for ChatGPT, Claude, or other chatbots is unconfirmed. It's not the first time the possibility has been floated: pdfu suggested on Sunday that chatbot apps might follow based on an unused flag in HomeView's software. In a separate finding, pdfu also discovered that HomeView includes anti-spoofing protection . Apparently, after three spoof attempts for a profile, the user must authenticate with an iPhone to see personal data, and the protection is enabled in HomeView software 27.2. Apple is also said to be working on a lockout cooldown system, similar to what happens when you enter the wrong passcode on an iPhone. A first lockout can be cleared immediately, but a second lockout brings a one-hour wait, a third a four-hour wait, and a fourth (or any further) lockout an eight-hour wait. pdfu adds that the lockout cooldown periods are still in development, so for now any lockout can be cleared immediately by authenticating with an iPhone. Apple hasn't described either feature in its press materials. HomeView launches on November 13 for $299, in both desktop and wall-mounted versions. Here's what Apple has announced so far: HomeView won't have an App Store. However, as we reported last month , it shows CarPlay-style third-party audio and video apps from a connected iPhone or iPad. HomeView isn't on sale in the European Union because Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS there, and Apple says it is still working with the EU to find a path forward to make it available in the bloc. Nvidia's board announced Sunday it is opening an independent investigation into Huang's involvement with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company that the U.S. has suspected of helping China circumvent artificial intelligence chip sales prohibitions. In a memo to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang disclosed he had been intimate with the woman, but the affair was not mentioned in the board's statement. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating, the board said. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said in its statement . "Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," the company told CNBC in a statement. Lawmakers have been calling for an investigation into the relationship and are also questioning what the Trump administration knew about it. "The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt," Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., posted on X on Saturday. "Congress will investigate and get answers." Coons is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when his party takes control of the chamber in January. Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18, a day after the company is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China's] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang . Policymakers in the Trump administration received a memo last spring with intelligence identifying Alice Huang as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security and revealing her relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, the Times first reported on Friday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the memo's creation, the Times reported Sunday, citing people briefed on the matter. The State Department and the White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. When asked by the Times whether Huang would appear before lawmakers to discuss the matter, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo declined to comment. "Our chief executive has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed," Mr. Rizzo said in a statement to the Times. Rizzo said the Nvidia CEO's interactions with Ms. Huang were consistent with meetings he has had with any of Nvidia's customers, the Times reported . Separately, Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn shared a Times article published Saturday reporting that the Trump administration approved a Chinese firm, New Matrix, to assemble chips for Nvidia in Beijing. The Times found little evidence of meaningful operations at its listed address, despite Trump's Commerce Department clearing it for national security risks. Cornyn called the report "outrageous" in his post on X . Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., who sits on the House Committee on Homeland Security, called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify before Congress along with Huang. The lawmakers want Huang to describe what he has been doing with Alice Huang, who is an executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, and how Nvidia secures the secrets of its technology and corporate knowledge from foreign spies. Heres a copy of the three Republican House committee chairs message to Huang in a letter dated November 4 available on the official foreignaffairs.house.gov website: Why are US lawmakers seeking answers from Jensen Huang? Three Republican committee chairmen—Brian Mast (House Foreign Affairs), John Moolenaar (House Select Committee on China) and Rick Crawford (House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence)—made the request. The legislators asked Huang to come to a joint briefing on November 18, in a letter dated November 4. They have requested that he either confirm his availability or suggest another date as soon as November 11. Their concerns follow an investigation published by The New York Times on October 29. As per the newspapers report, US intelligence agencies had examined Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, over suspected links to Beijing. According to The New York Times, Alice Huang was allegedly recruited by Chinas Ministry of State Security to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang. The existence of the intelligence memo and the assessment that Alice Huang was working for Chinas principal intelligence agency had not previously been reported. The report also noted the possibility that her role at Megaspeed may have given her the chance to find out how Nvidia was planning to conduct business and what it was talking to the U.S. government about. Why is Megaspeed involved in the investigation? Singaporean data centre operator Megaspeed grabbed headlines for its business with the advanced Nvidia AI chips. US officials reportedly investigated whether the firm aided Chinese companies access to more sophisticated computer chips, subject to U.S. export controls. Washington has placed restrictions on the sale of some high-performance semiconductors to China, as it attempts to curb its access to technology that could improve its artificial intelligence and military programs. Nvidia occupies a particularly important position in this debate because its graphics processing units (GPUs) are widely used to develop and operate advanced AI systems. Any possible diversion of restricted chips or access to sensitive commercial information therefore carries implications beyond an individual companys business relationships. The congressional committees want to know if Nvidias current security measures are adequate to firewall its technology and information against overseas customers. The NYT report also highlighted Megaspeeds growing role in the AI infrastructure business. The company reportedly began a multibillion-dollar purchase of advanced AI chips around 2024 and has been developing data centres in Southeast Asia. These facilities are then rented to Chinese technology giant Alibaba, potentially providing an indirect route for China to access advanced Nvidia chips that cannot be sold directly to the country under US export restrictions. Nvidia has defended the nature of its chief executives interactions with customers, arguing that meetings with business executives are a routine part of running a global technology company. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told The New York Times that the company does not share classified information with customers. He also described Jensen Huangs interactions with Alice Huang as normal business engagements, consistent with the CEOs regular meetings with thousands of executives who work with Nvidia. Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy rejected the newspapers reporting, calling the allegations unsubstantiated. The company added it receives information and guidance from the US government on security issues regarding entities that it may be concerned with. Nvidia did not confirm or deny whether Huang would be at the proposed Congressional briefing. The report also did not immediately have a comment from Megaspeed. Trumps reported awareness adds another dimension The controversy has also drawn attention to President Donald Trumps earlier awareness of the intelligence findings. According to The New York Times, Trump was briefed about the findings approximately a year before the newspapers report became public. The newspaper reported that he chose not to take action at the time. The development is notable because Trump has maintained close engagement with the American technology industry and has supported efforts to strengthen the countrys position in artificial intelligence. But the questions being raised by lawmakers are different from the intelligence report and the administrations response. Congresss November 18 briefing might allow committees to look into Nvidias business practices, how its sharing information, and internal security practices.

A company spokesperson said Huang engages with thousands of customers annually and expressed confidence that US authorities would alert the chipmaker if they considered an individual a threat to American industry. extraction.body: Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are ramping up calls for congressional investigations into reports of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia's board announced Sunday it is opening an independent investigation into Huang's involvement with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company that the U.S. has suspected of helping China circumvent artificial intelligence chip sales prohibitions. In a memo to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang disclosed he had been intimate with the woman, but the affair was not mentioned in the board's statement. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating, the board said. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said in its statement . "Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," the company told CNBC in a statement. Lawmakers have been calling for an investigation into the relationship and are also questioning what the Trump administration knew about it. "The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt," Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., posted on X on Saturday. "Congress will investigate and get answers." Coons is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when his party takes control of the chamber in January. Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18, a day after the company is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China's] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang . Policymakers in the Trump administration received a memo last spring with intelligence identifying Alice Huang as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security and revealing her relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, the Times first reported on Friday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the memo's creation, the Times reported Sunday, citing people briefed on the matter. The State Department and the White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. When asked by the Times whether Huang would appear before lawmakers to discuss the matter, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo declined to comment. "Our chief executive has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed," Mr. Rizzo said in a statement to the Times. Rizzo said the Nvidia CEO's interactions with Ms. Huang were consistent with meetings he has had with any of Nvidia's customers, the Times reported . Separately, Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn shared a Times article published Saturday reporting that the Trump administration approved a Chinese firm, New Matrix, to assemble chips for Nvidia in Beijing. The Times found little evidence of meaningful operations at its listed address, despite Trump's Commerce Department clearing it for national security risks. Cornyn called the report "outrageous" in his post on X . Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., who sits on the House Committee on Homeland Security, called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify before Congress along with Huang. passages: Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are ramping up calls for congressional investigations into reports of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Nvidia's board announced Sunday it is opening an independent investigation into Huang's involvement with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company that the U.S. has suspected of helping China circumvent artificial intelligence chip sales prohibitions.

In a memo to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang disclosed he had been intimate with the woman, but the affair was not mentioned in the board's statement. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating, the board said.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said in its statement .
"Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," the company told CNBC in a statement.
Lawmakers have been calling for an investigation into the relationship and are also questioning what the Trump administration knew about it.

"The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt," Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., posted on X on Saturday. "Congress will investigate and get answers."
Coons is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when his party takes control of the chamber in January.

Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18, a day after the company is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China's] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang .

Policymakers in the Trump administration received a memo last spring with intelligence identifying Alice Huang as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security and revealing her relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, the Times first reported on Friday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the memo's creation, the Times reported Sunday, citing people briefed on the matter. The State Department and the White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

When asked by the Times whether Huang would appear before lawmakers to discuss the matter, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo declined to comment. "Our chief executive has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed," Mr. Rizzo said in a statement to the Times.
Rizzo said the Nvidia CEO's interactions with Ms. Huang were consistent with meetings he has had with any of Nvidia's customers, the Times reported .

Separately, Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn shared a Times article published Saturday reporting that the Trump administration approved a Chinese firm, New Matrix, to assemble chips for Nvidia in Beijing. The Times found little evidence of meaningful operations at its listed address, despite Trump's Commerce Department clearing it for national security risks.
Cornyn called the report "outrageous" in his post on X .
Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., who sits on the House Committee on Homeland Security, called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify before Congress along with Huang.
Neither Nvidia nor the Commerce Department immediately responded to CNBC's request for comment.

US officials reportedly investigated whether the firm aided Chinese companies access to more sophisticated computer chips, subject to U.S. export controls. According to The New York Times, Trump was briefed about the findings approximately a year before the newspapers report became public. The newspaper reported that he chose not to take action at the time. The development is notable because Trump has maintained close engagement with the American technology industry and has supported efforts to strengthen the countrys position in artificial intelligence. But the questions being raised by lawmakers are different from the intelligence report and the administrations response. Congresss November 18 briefing might allow committees to look into Nvidias business practices, how its sharing information, and internal security practices.

extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing questions from senior US lawmakers over his interactions with an executive at a company whose employee is reportedly being investigated for suspected espionage on behalf of China. Three Republican lawmakers have asked Huang to appear before Congress on November 18, seeking details about the nature of his dealings and the chipmaker's safeguards against potential security threats. The request follows a report by The New York Times last week that Huang Le, an executive at Megaspeed International, had been under US government surveillance over allegations that he supplied information to the Chinese government. The report has raised questions about whether individuals with potential links to Beijing could gain access to sensitive American technology or information through their business relationships with major technology companies. Nvidia has pushed back against any suggestion that its interactions with customers indicate a security concern. A company spokesperson said Huang engages with thousands of customers annually and expressed confidence that US authorities would alert the chipmaker if they considered an individual a threat to American industry. The lawmakers, however, want a more detailed account of the company's interactions with the Megaspeed executive and the measures it takes to protect sensitive technology. Lawmakers seek answers as Nvidia faces China-related scrutiny The letter to Huang was signed by Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, who currently lead three congressional panels dealing with foreign affairs, China and intelligence matters. Chairman @RepMoolenaar, Chairman @RepBrianMast, and Chairman @RepRickCrawford have sent a letter to NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang asking him to appear before their three committees this month. The letter expresses concerns over NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and Mr. Huang’s reported ties to a Chinese intelligence-linked executive of a Singapore-based data center company. — Select Committee on China (@ChinaSelect) November 5, 2026 The lawmakers have proposed a joint, closed-door session focused on Nvidia's security procedures. They argued that the allegations surrounding Megaspeed warranted congressional examination, particularly given the risks associated with China's access to advanced American technology. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive US technology and information," the representatives wrote, referring to the People's Republic of China. They added that Congress needed to establish whether American national security had been compromised. The incoming leadership has signalled plans for closer oversight of corporate conduct, with major Silicon Valley companies likely to face questions about their business practices and the broader implications of their technology. For Huang, the latest request adds to an already difficult relationship with some lawmakers over Nvidia's business in China. Mast, in particular, has repeatedly challenged the company's position on export restrictions. In January, he accused Nvidia and its chief executive of pushing to sell millions of advanced chips to Chinese businesses and even challenged Huang to a televised debate on Fox News. Proposed AI chip restrictions add to tensions The disagreement extends beyond the latest espionage allegations. Nvidia has been at the centre of a wider Washington debate over whether American companies should be allowed to sell their most advanced AI processors to Chinese customers. Earlier this year, Mast helped develop the AI Overwatch Act, a proposed law intended to give Congress greater authority over exports of advanced AI chips. The legislation sought to introduce an approval mechanism similar to the oversight used for certain arms sales, allowing lawmakers to block specific transactions through a joint resolution. Under the proposal, sales of Nvidia's H200 processors could face congressional intervention, while the company's Blackwell generation and subsequent, more advanced chips would be subject to restrictions. The proposed restrictions reflect growing concern in Washington that access to advanced computing hardware could strengthen China's military and technological capabilities. Nvidia, meanwhile, has argued against overly restrictive export policies.

extraction.body: Four years ago the Bank of Russia wanted to ban crypto outright. On November 17 it will do the opposite: let ordinary Russians buy Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether's USDT through licensed brokers and exchanges. The list is short, the limits are strict, and the political subtext is hard to miss. The central bank has finalised the rules that let exchanges admit three assets to public trading for non-qualified investors: Bitcoin, Ether and USDT. From November 17, exchanges may list them, and retail investors can buy through brokers, asset managers or licensed crypto exchanges. Moscow Exchange plans to launch its own crypto trading in December, and the country's largest banks, Sberbank and VTB, are preparing access for their roughly 140 million banking clients. Financial institutions have until July 1, 2027 to align their infrastructure fully with the new framework. The three coins were chosen because they cleared the regulator's liquidity and market-history thresholds. First Deputy Governor Vladimir Chistyukhin has said there are no plans to extend the list for now. How much can Russian retail investors actually buy? Non-qualified investors face an annual purchase cap of 300,000 rubles, roughly 3,600 dollars. Sources differ on whether the cap applies per intermediary or per asset, but either way this is a sandbox, not a free market. Qualified investors, by contrast, can trade any cryptocurrency on exchange or over the counter without a limit.The largest crypto assets compared over 90 days, according to CoinMarketCap data The regulator's own estimate is that retail makes up around 98 percent of market participants. The cap is designed to pull that crowd away from unmonitored peer-to-peer channels and into supervised ones, where every ruble can be tracked. Because the central bank's criteria are liquidity and track record on regulated venues, not market cap. XRP, despite its size and its institutional use inside Russia, did not meet them. Qualified investors can still trade it through Moscow Exchange products; the general public cannot. For a token that has built much of its narrative on bank adoption, being left out by one of the world's most bank-centric crypto frameworks is an awkward headline. A dollar stablecoin issued by a company that complies with US sanctions is now the only stablecoin a Russian retail investor may legally buy. At the same time, Tether has frozen millions in USDT linked to sanctioned Russian exchanges. Russia gets a liquid dollar instrument for domestic investors; Tether gets a market it cannot openly serve. Expect this tension to produce headlines well beyond November 17.The Fear and Greed Index places market sentiment between extreme fear and extreme greed Does Russia's move matter for Bitcoin price? A 3,600 dollar annual cap on a population of retail investors is not the kind of flow that moves a 1.5 trillion dollar asset. Longer term, the signal matters more than the volume: a G20 central bank that called crypto a threat to financial stability in 2022 now builds regulated rails for it. extraction.body: Four years ago the Bank of Russia wanted to ban crypto outright. On November 17 it will do the opposite: let ordinary Russians buy Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether's USDT through licensed brokers and exchanges. The list is short, the limits are strict, and the political subtext is hard to miss. The central bank has finalised the rules that let exchanges admit three assets to public trading for non-qualified investors: Bitcoin, Ether and USDT. From November 17, exchanges may list them, and retail investors can buy through brokers, asset managers or licensed crypto exchanges. Moscow Exchange plans to launch its own crypto trading in December, and the country's largest banks, Sberbank and VTB, are preparing access for their roughly 140 million banking clients. Financial institutions have until July 1, 2027 to align their infrastructure fully with the new framework. The three coins were chosen because they cleared the regulator's liquidity and market-history thresholds. First Deputy Governor Vladimir Chistyukhin has said there are no plans to extend the list for now. How much can Russian retail investors actually buy? Non-qualified investors face an annual purchase cap of 300,000 rubles, roughly 3,600 dollars. Sources differ on whether the cap applies per intermediary or per asset, but either way this is a sandbox, not a free market. Qualified investors, by contrast, can trade any cryptocurrency on exchange or over the counter without a limit.The largest crypto assets compared over 90 days, according to CoinMarketCap data The regulator's own estimate is that retail makes up around 98 percent of market participants. The cap is designed to pull that crowd away from unmonitored peer-to-peer channels and into supervised ones, where every ruble can be tracked. Because the central bank's criteria are liquidity and track record on regulated venues, not market cap. XRP, despite its size and its institutional use inside Russia, did not meet them. Qualified investors can still trade it through Moscow Exchange products; the general public cannot. For a token that has built much of its narrative on bank adoption, being left out by one of the world's most bank-centric crypto frameworks is an awkward headline. A dollar stablecoin issued by a company that complies with US sanctions is now the only stablecoin a Russian retail investor may legally buy. At the same time, Tether has frozen millions in USDT linked to sanctioned Russian exchanges. Russia gets a liquid dollar instrument for domestic investors; Tether gets a market it cannot openly serve. Expect this tension to produce headlines well beyond November 17.The Fear and Greed Index places market sentiment between extreme fear and extreme greed Does Russia's move matter for Bitcoin price? A 3,600 dollar annual cap on a population of retail investors is not the kind of flow that moves a 1.5 trillion dollar asset. Longer term, the signal matters more than the volume: a G20 central bank that called crypto a threat to financial stability in 2022 now builds regulated rails for it. Traders closely monitor these whales due to their substantial financial backing and potential access to better information, though their track record is mixed. From April 12 to May 10, Bitcoin surged 16.1%, rising from $70,661 to $82,018 and catching many short traders off guard.
Whales’ long positions also reversed. In May 2026, they reached a high level of net longs, but Bitcoin subsequently dropped by 28.6% to $58,566 by June 30.

However, the whales had more success in October 2025 when they last held a similar level of short exposure. Bitcoin peaked at $126,080 on October 6, 2025, closed the month at $109,567, then slid 22.7% to $84,676 by November 22, 2025. So far, their current short position is paying off, as Glassnode noted that they first went net short on October 27 , when Bitcoin closed at $80,801, and Bitcoin has fallen about 6% since.

Glassnode tracks only one exchange, leaving gaps in its analysis. A whale might own Bitcoin stored in cold storage, on a centralized exchange, or through an ETF and could short on Hyperliquid to protect their assets without selling, which would still count as a bearish position in Glassnode’s data.
Additionally, most Bitcoin transactions occur on exchange order books that don’t interact with the blockchain, which is why significant whale buying in October did not lead to price increases.

Hyperliquid represents only a small fraction of the total futures market. For context, on November 7, Binance’s BTCUSDT perpetual contracts accounted for 96,471 BTC (approximately $7.3 billion), while Bybit had 69,555 BTC ($5.28 billion) and OKX had 34,497 BTC ($2.62 billion).

Investors have also been selling at a loss for an unusually long stretch . Based on current indicators, it seems more likely that the whales are making a directional call rather than merely hedging, although only they know their true intentions.

At this point, the whales appear to have a stronger stance, especially as ETF investments decline and leveraged longs continue to accumulate beneath them. Their past performance seems to be about even, given the 16.1% rally against them in spring and the 22.7% decline that favored them later in 2025.

When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.
However, the whales had more success in October 2025 when they last held a similar level of short exposure.
Bitcoin peaked at $126,080 on October 6, 2025, closed the month at $109,567, then slid 22.7% to $84,676 by November 22, 2025.
Traders closely monitor these whales due to their substantial financial backing and potential access to better information, though their track record is mixed.
For instance, they last went net short in March and then rebuilt their long positions during Bitcoin’s April rally.
From April 12 to May 10, Bitcoin surged 16.1%, rising from $70,661 to $82,018 and catching many short traders off guard.
Glassnode tracks only one exchange, leaving gaps in its analysis.

A whale might own Bitcoin stored in cold storage, on a centralized exchange, or through an ETF and could short on Hyperliquid to protect their assets without selling, which would still count as a bearish position in Glassnode’s data.

Bitcoin's last five-week slide ended in two very different ways, and ETF outflows, whale shorts, and a key moving average now complicate the comparison.
Funding rates also provide insight into market sentiment.

On November 7, Binance’s funding rate was slightly positive, at 0.0000059, suggesting that the broader market isn’t heavily positioned for a price drop.
Are they hedging a hidden stash or sniffing out the next leg down?
Bitcoin traded around $75,662 on November 8, down 8% over the past 30 days and just under its lowest 30-day close of $75,775 on November 6.
Hyperliquid traders held $612 million in leveraged long positions just a week earlier, on November 2, showing a drastic shift in strategy.
These trades are recorded on Hyperliquid’s public blockchain, enabling Glassnode to analyze the holdings of significant accounts.
In May 2026, they reached a high level of net longs, but Bitcoin subsequently dropped by 28.6% to $58,566 by June 30.
Additionally, most Bitcoin transactions occur on exchange order books that don’t interact with the blockchain, which is why significant whale buying in October did not lead to price increases.
Open interest data indicates a directional bias among traders.
A week of net ETF inflows that surpasses the $1.28 billion that departed in the week ending November 6 could undercut the whales’ short.

If Bitcoin continues to drop, these long positions could face liquidation, an automatic closure of a borrowed position when losses exceed the initial deposit, adding selling pressure in favor of the whales.

In the same SEC filing, Strategy detailed its efforts to support its preferred stock. The company sold 1,178,552 MSTR shares for net proceeds of $164 million and used $208.2 million to repurchase 2,092,035 shares of STRC, its variable-rate preferred stock. STRC pays a 12% annual dividend, and Strategy aims to keep it trading near its $100 par value, the amount owed to investors. STRC recently closed at $99.84, just below par. The company’s dividend cushion is its dollar reserve, reported at $4.79 billion in the November 2 filing. Management has described the reserve as a way to keep paying dividends and interest through market swings, including periods when raising capital is costly. According to its third-quarter report, USD assets of $5.07 billion cover 3.4 years of dividend and interest obligations, while preferred dividends in that quarter alone totaled $419.56 million. Spot Bitcoin ETFs, which are funds that hold Bitcoin and trade on stock exchanges like regular stocks, saw significant outflows totaling $1.28 billion in the week ending November 6. When investors pull out more ETF shares than they purchase, the funds must sell Bitcoin, turning a consistent buyer into a seller. According to SoSoValue, four out of the five trading days in that week saw money leave the funds, including outflows of $398.6 million on November 2, $430.2 million on November 5, and $411.9 million on November 6. This trend of selling started earlier, with the funds reporting a $643.3 million outflow on October 30, the largest one-day exit since at least October 9. Additionally, Bitcoin’s weekly trading volume has increased over the past three weeks leading up to November 8, indicating that sellers are becoming more active as the price continues to drop. Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is on course for its fifth week of losses in a row, marking a Bitcoin losing streak that began in early October. It trades at around $75,662, which is down roughly 3.3% from last week’s close and about 40% below its all-time high of $126,080 recorded on October 6, 2025.

Over the past four weeks, each week closed lower than the one before. Bitcoin started at $86,507 on October 4 and dropped to $78,231 by November 1, culminating in a 2.28% loss that last week. Bitcoin’s last losing streak this long ended on March 1. So, what followed that Bitcoin losing streak, and does the current situation resemble it?

Spot Bitcoin ETFs, which are funds that hold Bitcoin and trade on stock exchanges like regular stocks, saw significant outflows totaling $1.28 billion in the week ending November 6. When investors pull out more ETF shares than they purchase, the funds must sell Bitcoin, turning a consistent buyer into a seller.

According to SoSoValue, four out of the five trading days in that week saw money leave the funds, including outflows of $398.6 million on November 2, $430.2 million on November 5, and $411.9 million on November 6. The only day with net inflows was November 4, when the funds took in $74.6 million.

On November 6, Bitcoin closed at $75,775, marking its lowest closing price in the past month amid heavy ETF selling for two consecutive days. This trend of selling started earlier, with the funds reporting a $643.3 million outflow on October 30, the largest one-day exit since at least October 9.

The flow of money and the price movement often affect each other. When prices fall, ETF holders may feel compelled to sell, further driving prices down. Additionally, Bitcoin’s weekly trading volume has increased over the past three weeks leading up to November 8, indicating that sellers are becoming more active as the price continues to drop.

Extended losing streaks are uncommon for Bitcoin. Even during the downturn in 2018, when Bitcoin closed as low as $3,217 on December 16, it never experienced more than three consecutive losing weeks. The two most recent streaks lasting five weeks or longer ended in very different situations.

In early 2026, Bitcoin faced six weeks of losses, dropping from $93,634 on January 18 to $65,769 on March 1, with a low of $60,001 reached in the week ending February 8. Four weeks later, on March 29, it closed at $65,957, nearly unchanged. By eight weeks after the streak ended, it rose to $78,674 on April 26, a gain of about 20% from the end of the losing streak.

In contrast, the 2022 streak also lasted six weeks, dropping from $39,678 on April 17, 2022, to $29,446 on May 29. Four weeks later, Bitcoin fell to $21,029 on June 26, then dipped to $19,310 on July 3, and by eight weeks out, it had only slightly rebounded to close at $22,601 on July 24, still significantly lower than where the losing streak concluded.

Neither of these situations marked a lasting recovery. The rebound from the spring 2026 drop eventually faded, leading to Bitcoin’s lowest close in a year at $58,566 on June 30. Additionally, the presence of ETFs changes the comparison to 2022 since U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had not yet launched at that time. Now, Bitcoin has a new set of buyers due to these ETFs, but they have also contributed to the current sell-off.

Bitcoin is currently trading below its 20-day moving average of $79,362 and its 50-day average of $81,889. This means most buyers from the past two months are facing losses. It remains about 3% above its 200-day average of $73,194, a benchmark many traders use to tell a pullback apart from a bear market. Each bounce this week, including a high of $81,131, has struggled to exceed the 50-day average.

Moreover, large traders have shifted their stance regarding Bitcoin. On-chain analytics firm Glassnode noted that major traders on Hyperliquid began to take net short positions on October 27, after holding long positions for seven months, and have continued to add to those shorts. A short position profits when prices fall, indicating that they expect further declines.

Bitcoin’s dominance , its share of the overall cryptocurrency market, remains at 60%. Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) decreased by 1.6% over the past week, less than Bitcoin, while Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) saw a decline of 6.1%. Over the past month, though, Bitcoin’s 8.31% loss is still smaller than Ethereum’s 10.19% and Solana’s 18.16%.

Bitcoin’s deeper trading market and a larger base of ETF investors imply that when market players reduce their exposure to cryptocurrency, they typically sell the smaller and more volatile coins first. Ethereum’s relative strength this past week may appear to be a pause in that trend, but it too remains down more than Bitcoin over the month.

A quick recovery from this downturn appears unlikely. In previous long losing streaks, it took at least a month to find a floor, and so far, there has been no sign of returning buyers in the market. To avoid a fifth consecutive loss, Bitcoin will need a significant shift in buying sentiment.

His work focuses on price levels, spot ETF flows, on-chain data and the regulatory decisions that move crypto markets, written so a first-time buyer and a seasoned trader can both use it.

His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites.

Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is on course for its fifth week of losses in a row, marking a Bitcoin losing streak that began in early October.
It trades at around $75,662, which is down roughly 3.3% from last week’s close and about 40% below its all-time high of $126,080 recorded on October 6, 2025.
Bitcoin’s last losing streak this long ended on March 1.
In contrast, the 2022 streak also lasted six weeks, dropping from $39,678 on April 17, 2022, to $29,446 on May 29.

Four weeks later, Bitcoin fell to $21,029 on June 26, then dipped to $19,310 on July 3, and by eight weeks out, it had only slightly rebounded to close at $22,601 on July 24, still significantly lower than where the losing streak concluded.
Additionally, the presence of ETFs changes the comparison to 2022 since U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had not yet launched at that time.
Extended losing streaks are uncommon for Bitcoin.
Even during the downturn in 2018, when Bitcoin closed as low as $3,217 on December 16, it never experienced more than three consecutive losing weeks.
The two most recent streaks lasting five weeks or longer ended in very different situations.
To avoid a fifth consecutive loss, Bitcoin will need a significant shift in buying sentiment.

According to SoSoValue, four out of the five trading days in that week saw money leave the funds, including outflows of $398.6 million on November 2, $430.2 million on November 5, and $411.9 million on November 6.
Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) decreased by 1.6% over the past week, less than Bitcoin, while Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) saw a decline of 6.1%.
Bitcoin ETFs just suffered their worst single day since late June, and Ethereum ETFs have now bled red for 11 straight sessions.

Days earlier, nine civilians were massacred in L'Estère by the Kokorat San Ras gang. The gang’s notorious leader, Fadens “Meyè” Tilus, was later killed by a self-defense group. Residents continue to denounce government inaction as violence intensifies in the Artibonite region. GONAÏVES — At least three officers from the Departmental Law Enforcement Unit (UDMO) were killed on Tuesday, July 22, during an operation in Liancourt—a commune in the lower Artibonite—when their armored vehicle was ambushed and burned by members of the Gran Grif gang. In a separate attack, armed men from Kokorat San Ras, whose leader was killed by a local self-defense brigade, stormed the neighboring Kanpenyen community in L’Estère and murdered at least nine people. These incidents highlight the latest wave of ongoing violence in the region. These police officers, identified by the authorities as Jean Louis Daniel, Dareus Daniel and Fegensly Mertus, distressed, spent hours waiting for reinforcements that never arrived. “We have received information that the police officers were the victims of a criminal act carried out by members of the Gran Grif gang,” Féquière Casséus, spokesperson for the Haitian National Police (PNH) in Artibonite, told The Haitian Times . “We are still compiling the reports before releasing more details.” The Gran Grif gang—designated a terrorist organization earlier this year by the Trump administration— is one of the most feared armed groups in the region. It has been the target of ongoing police operations aimed at reclaiming control of Savien and Liancourt, two communes that have been occupied since as early as 2018. Videos circulating on social media showed the aftermath of the ambush—an immobilized armored police vehicle in flames and the bodies of the slain officers being desecrated by men waving red handkerchiefs. These latest killings echo a 2023 incident in which seven UDMO agents were slain at the Liancourt police station. The attacks have reignited criticism over the government’s failure to curb gang violence and adequately equip the police. “There is no genuine will to combat the armed groups that operate with impunity,” said André Saint-Louis, coordinator of the human rights organization—Committee for Peace Initiative in the Lower Artibonite (KILBA). “The Presidential Transitional Council [CPT] remains inactive and appears unconcerned about the dire situation facing the Haitian people.” “There is no genuine will to combat the armed groups that operate with impunity in the department.” The Minister of Economy and Finance (MEF), Patrick Pélissier, confirmed that on July 18 he disbursed 117,130,000 gourdes, or about $901,000, to mobilize the necessary resources for the PNH’s anti-gang operations. Saint-Louis said the number of officers killed in clashes with Gran Grif in recent days may be as high as four. He added that eight weapons were seized and one armored vehicle torched in the ambush. “The fallen officers were deployed in deplorable conditions, without adequate ammunition or proper equipment,” he said. In addition to Liancourt and L’Estère, other areas in the region like Pont-Sondé, Gros-Morne, Verrettes, Petite-Rivière de l’Artibonite and La Chapelle have been especially affected by rampant gang violence, with residents being consistently killed, kidnapped, extorted or forced to flee their homes. Just days earlier, July 17 to 18, another deadly incident unfolded in Kanpenyen—a community in L’Estère, where members of the Kokorat San Ras gang killed nine civilians. The attack, reportedly in retaliation, came shortly before the gang’s notorious leader, Fadens “Meyè” Tilus, was killed by an armed self-defense group known as the “Coalition.” A source with insider information confirmed Tilus’ death to The Haitian Times , though police officials have not verified it. “We treat this information with the utmost seriousness, but at this time we cannot confirm whether the gang leader has been killed,” said Casseus, PNH spokesperson. The victims in Kapenyen were described as peaceful residents, mostly engaged in agriculture. Their identities have not yet been released. Local authorities said more information will be shared at a forthcoming press briefing in Gonaïves. Government Commissioner Guiverna Guillaume said he, too, learned of the massacre through the media. “We are collaborating with police forces to clarify what happened and restore security in the jurisdiction of Gonaïves,” he told The Haitian Times . In the wake of the violence, the Committee for Demobilization Against Gangs and Insecurity in Artibonite announced new mobilizations against the government’s inaction. The group’s spokesperson, Jécosiasse Pierre, condemned the killings in Kapenyen and demanded the removal of Artibonite’s top police official. “We demand the immediate resignation of Commissioner Kalerb Exantus,” Pierre said. “His inefficiency has only enabled the rise in insecurity.” Pierre also said National Road No. 1 would remain blocked in L’Estère, where supporters of Kokorat San Ras have disrupted traffic. Residents fleeing Kapenyen were seen arriving in Gonaïves with small bags and children in tow, seeking shelter from the violence. passages: Haitian security forces have intensified operations against armed gangs, killing a notorious gang leader in a series of coordinated attacks involving explosive drones as authorities push to reclaim territory controlled by criminal groups.
Caribbean National Weekly — your trusted source for Caribbean news, culture, and community across the diaspora.
Haitian police said Saintil died from multiple gunshot wounds sustained during a security operation.
However, the National Human Rights Defense Network (RNDDH) reported that he was critically injured Thursday night when an explosive drone struck his vehicle and died the following day.

The operations form part of an intensified campaign by Haitian authorities and international security partners to weaken armed gangs and restore government control over communities affected by years of violence.

In a recent national address, he pledged that the Haitian state would not surrender territory to armed groups and insisted that security operations would continue until public order and state authority were restored.
The organization has called attention to reports of civilian casualties as security forces increasingly rely on drone strikes to target gang leaders and their strongholds.
“One less gang leader,” Fils-Aimé declared on social media, reaffirming his government's commitment to dismantling the armed groups responsible for widespread violence and instability across Haiti.
The prime minister has also emphasized that operations must comply with Haitian law and international human rights obligations.

The latest offensive comes amid an expanded international security presence in Haiti, including the deployment of approximately 2,500 Salvadoran troops following the disappearance of four Salvadoran aviation technicians during a gang ambush in October.
Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé confirmed the death of Mathias Saintil, leader of the Boston gang operating in the densely populated Cité Soleil neighborhood of Port-au-Prince.
According to the human rights organization, at least seven explosive drones were deployed during coordinated operations targeting several gang-controlled communities.
Haitian police subsequently recovered the burned-out vehicle in the Santo district of Croix-des-Bouquets, but the four men remain missing.

Authorities have maintained that their objective is to dismantle criminal networks, regain control of gang-held communities and create the security conditions necessary for Haiti's long-awaited elections.

Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé confirmed the death of Mathias Saintil, leader of the Boston gang operating in the densely populated Cité Soleil neighborhood of Port-au-Prince. “One less gang leader,” Fils-Aimé declared on social media, reaffirming his government's commitment to dismantling the armed groups responsible for widespread violence and instability across Haiti. Saintil's gang is affiliated with the powerful Viv Ansanm coalition, an alliance of armed groups that controls significant portions of the capital and has expanded its influence into other regions of the country. Haitian police said Saintil died from multiple gunshot wounds sustained during a security operation. However, the National Human Rights Defense Network (RNDDH) reported that he was critically injured Thursday night when an explosive drone struck his vehicle and died the following day. According to the human rights organization, at least seven explosive drones were deployed during coordinated operations targeting several gang-controlled communities. The RNDDH reported that five gang members were killed and approximately 15 others injured in the attack targeting Saintil, while additional casualties were recorded during separate confrontations. The operations form part of an intensified campaign by Haitian authorities and international security partners to weaken armed gangs and restore government control over communities affected by years of violence. Security forces have also targeted Wilson Joseph, leader of the notorious 400 Mawozo gang, which has been linked to kidnappings and other violent crimes. Joseph's home was reportedly bombed during a recent operation, although he is believed to have survived the attack and gone into hiding. The latest offensive comes amid an expanded international security presence in Haiti, including the deployment of approximately 2,500 Salvadoran troops following the disappearance of four Salvadoran aviation technicians during a gang ambush in October. The technicians went missing on October 18 after armed gangs attacked their vehicle near Port-au-Prince. Haitian police subsequently recovered the burned-out vehicle in the Santo district of Croix-des-Bouquets, but the four men remain missing. The incident has heightened tensions and prompted additional security operations targeting armed groups suspected of involvement in the attack. Meanwhile, the RNDDH has raised concerns about the potential impact of explosive drone operations on civilians living in densely populated neighborhoods. The organization has called attention to reports of civilian casualties as security forces increasingly rely on drone strikes to target gang leaders and their strongholds. Haiti has experienced years of escalating gang violence, with armed groups controlling major roads, neighborhoods and commercial routes, particularly in and around Port-au-Prince. The violence has forced hundreds of thousands of residents to flee their homes, disrupted essential services and severely restricted access to food, healthcare and humanitarian assistance. The latest operations come as Prime Minister Fils-Aimé has identified restoring security and organizing elections as his government's two main priorities. In a recent national address, he pledged that the Haitian state would not surrender territory to armed groups and insisted that security operations would continue until public order and state authority were restored. The prime minister has also emphasized that operations must comply with Haitian law and international human rights obligations. Despite the intensified offensive, questions remain about coordination among Haiti's police, military and international security partners, as well as the effectiveness of drone strikes in reducing gang violence without placing civilians at further risk. Authorities have maintained that their objective is to dismantle criminal networks, regain control of gang-held communities and create the security conditions necessary for Haiti's long-awaited elections. extraction.body: Three officers from the departmental police unit (UDMO ) were killed on July 22 in an ambush by the Gran Grif gang in Liancourt. Days earlier, nine civilians were massacred in L'Estère by the Kokorat San Ras gang. The gang’s notorious leader, Fadens “Meyè” Tilus, was later killed by a self-defense group. Residents continue to denounce government inaction as violence intensifies in the Artibonite region. GONAÏVES — At least three officers from the Departmental Law Enforcement Unit (UDMO) were killed on Tuesday, July 22, during an operation in Liancourt—a commune in the lower Artibonite—when their armored vehicle was ambushed and burned by members of the Gran Grif gang. In a separate attack, armed men from Kokorat San Ras, whose leader was killed by a local self-defense brigade, stormed the neighboring Kanpenyen community in L’Estère and murdered at least nine people. These incidents highlight the latest wave of ongoing violence in the region. These police officers, identified by the authorities as Jean Louis Daniel, Dareus Daniel and Fegensly Mertus, distressed, spent hours waiting for reinforcements that never arrived. “We have received information that the police officers were the victims of a criminal act carried out by members of the Gran Grif gang,” Féquière Casséus, spokesperson for the Haitian National Police (PNH) in Artibonite, told The Haitian Times . “We are still compiling the reports before releasing more details.” The Gran Grif gang—designated a terrorist organization earlier this year by the Trump administration— is one of the most feared armed groups in the region. It has been the target of ongoing police operations aimed at reclaiming control of Savien and Liancourt, two communes that have been occupied since as early as 2018. Videos circulating on social media showed the aftermath of the ambush—an immobilized armored police vehicle in flames and the bodies of the slain officers being desecrated by men waving red handkerchiefs. These latest killings echo a 2023 incident in which seven UDMO agents were slain at the Liancourt police station. The attacks have reignited criticism over the government’s failure to curb gang violence and adequately equip the police. “There is no genuine will to combat the armed groups that operate with impunity,” said André Saint-Louis, coordinator of the human rights organization—Committee for Peace Initiative in the Lower Artibonite (KILBA). “The Presidential Transitional Council [CPT] remains inactive and appears unconcerned about the dire situation facing the Haitian people.” “There is no genuine will to combat the armed groups that operate with impunity in the department.” The Minister of Economy and Finance (MEF), Patrick Pélissier, confirmed that on July 18 he disbursed 117,130,000 gourdes, or about $901,000, to mobilize the necessary resources for the PNH’s anti-gang operations. Saint-Louis said the number of officers killed in clashes with Gran Grif in recent days may be as high as four. He added that eight weapons were seized and one armored vehicle torched in the ambush. “The fallen officers were deployed in deplorable conditions, without adequate ammunition or proper equipment,” he said. In addition to Liancourt and L’Estère, other areas in the region like Pont-Sondé, Gros-Morne, Verrettes, Petite-Rivière de l’Artibonite and La Chapelle have been especially affected by rampant gang violence, with residents being consistently killed, kidnapped, extorted or forced to flee their homes. Just days earlier, July 17 to 18, another deadly incident unfolded in Kanpenyen—a community in L’Estère, where members of the Kokorat San Ras gang killed nine civilians. The attack, reportedly in retaliation, came shortly before the gang’s notorious leader, Fadens “Meyè” Tilus, was killed by an armed self-defense group known as the “Coalition.” A source with insider information confirmed Tilus’ death to The Haitian Times , though police officials have not verified it. “We treat this information with the utmost seriousness, but at this time we cannot confirm whether the gang leader has been killed,” said Casseus, PNH spokesperson. The victims in Kapenyen were described as peaceful residents, mostly engaged in agriculture. Their identities have not yet been released. Local authorities said more information will be shared at a forthcoming press briefing in Gonaïves. Government Commissioner Guiverna Guillaume said he, too, learned of the massacre through the media. “We are collaborating with police forces to clarify what happened and restore security in the jurisdiction of Gonaïves,” he told The Haitian Times . In the wake of the violence, the Committee for Demobilization Against Gangs and Insecurity in Artibonite announced new mobilizations against the government’s inaction. The group’s spokesperson, Jécosiasse Pierre, condemned the killings in Kapenyen and demanded the removal of Artibonite’s top police official. “We demand the immediate resignation of Commissioner Kalerb Exantus,” Pierre said. “His inefficiency has only enabled the rise in insecurity.” Pierre also said National Road No. 1 would remain blocked in L’Estère, where supporters of Kokorat San Ras have disrupted traffic. Residents fleeing Kapenyen were seen arriving in Gonaïves with small bags and children in tow, seeking shelter from the violence. Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé confirmed the death of Mathias Saintil, leader of the Boston gang operating in the densely populated Cité Soleil neighborhood of Port-au-Prince. “One less gang leader,” Fils-Aimé declared on social media, reaffirming his government's commitment to dismantling the armed groups responsible for widespread violence and instability across Haiti. Saintil's gang is affiliated with the powerful Viv Ansanm coalition, an alliance of armed groups that controls significant portions of the capital and has expanded its influence into other regions of the country. Haitian police said Saintil died from multiple gunshot wounds sustained during a security operation. However, the National Human Rights Defense Network (RNDDH) reported that he was critically injured Thursday night when an explosive drone struck his vehicle and died the following day. According to the human rights organization, at least seven explosive drones were deployed during coordinated operations targeting several gang-controlled communities. The RNDDH reported that five gang members were killed and approximately 15 others injured in the attack targeting Saintil, while additional casualties were recorded during separate confrontations. The operations form part of an intensified campaign by Haitian authorities and international security partners to weaken armed gangs and restore government control over communities affected by years of violence. Security forces have also targeted Wilson Joseph, leader of the notorious 400 Mawozo gang, which has been linked to kidnappings and other violent crimes. Joseph's home was reportedly bombed during a recent operation, although he is believed to have survived the attack and gone into hiding. The latest offensive comes amid an expanded international security presence in Haiti, including the deployment of approximately 2,500 Salvadoran troops following the disappearance of four Salvadoran aviation technicians during a gang ambush in October. The technicians went missing on October 18 after armed gangs attacked their vehicle near Port-au-Prince. Haitian police subsequently recovered the burned-out vehicle in the Santo district of Croix-des-Bouquets, but the four men remain missing. The incident has heightened tensions and prompted additional security operations targeting armed groups suspected of involvement in the attack. Meanwhile, the RNDDH has raised concerns about the potential impact of explosive drone operations on civilians living in densely populated neighborhoods. The organization has called attention to reports of civilian casualties as security forces increasingly rely on drone strikes to target gang leaders and their strongholds. Haiti has experienced years of escalating gang violence, with armed groups controlling major roads, neighborhoods and commercial routes, particularly in and around Port-au-Prince. The violence has forced hundreds of thousands of residents to flee their homes, disrupted essential services and severely restricted access to food, healthcare and humanitarian assistance. The latest operations come as Prime Minister Fils-Aimé has identified restoring security and organizing elections as his government's two main priorities. In a recent national address, he pledged that the Haitian state would not surrender territory to armed groups and insisted that security operations would continue until public order and state authority were restored. The prime minister has also emphasized that operations must comply with Haitian law and international human rights obligations. Despite the intensified offensive, questions remain about coordination among Haiti's police, military and international security partners, as well as the effectiveness of drone strikes in reducing gang violence without placing civilians at further risk. Authorities have maintained that their objective is to dismantle criminal networks, regain control of gang-held communities and create the security conditions necessary for Haiti's long-awaited elections.
