sources.title: Kushner proposes NATO-Russia Council model for European security: EU insists that ceasefire in Ukraine is top priority, – WP
passages: According to an official familiar with the talks, Kushner’s model is the NATO-Russia Council, which was established after the end of the Cold War but whose activities were suspended in 2014 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the annexation of Crimea," he writes in his column.

According to the Washington Post, Jared Kushner, an adviser and relative of Donald Trump, is considering the Russia–NATO Council format as a possible model for the future architecture of European security.
At the same time, European diplomats emphasise that reaching a ceasefire in Ukraine remains a key condition.
Kushner seeks to proceed in parallel, whilst the European Union insists that a ceasefire must come first.
It was previously reported that the US, together with its partners, is developing five objectives for a new European security architecture.
By contrast, European officials consider Donald Trump’s statements following talks with Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev about the prospect of a "major deal" to be extremely premature.
There is a consensus in Europe that any contacts with Russia must begin only after a ceasefire has been established.

Kushner has outlined five pillars, including crisis communications and military transparency, if progress is made at the Abu Dhabi trilateral talks on Nov. 10-11. US special presidential envoy Jared Kushner has proposed launching multilateral negotiations between European nations and Russia to design a post-war continental security architecture, modeling the initiative on the defunct NATO- Russia Council, The Washington Post reported. According to a senior official familiar with internal deliberations, Kushner seeks to transition diplomatic engagements into a broader multilateral framework with direct European participation if working-level trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US, and Russia achieve progress in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11 . Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Writing in a statement on X, Kushner outlined five primary pillars for the proposed security architecture: permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications channels, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability. However, European allied governments and Ukrainian leadership have emphasized that any discussions on continental security architecture must remain strictly conditional on first securing a verified ceasefire and an enforceable peace agreement in Ukraine. Kushner’s proposal looks toward the operational template of the NATO -Russia Council, an institutional body established in 2002 to facilitate security coordination and dialogue between the Western alliance and Moscow . The council’s practical operations were suspended in 2014 following Russia’s illegal military invasion and annexation of Ukraine’s Crimean peninsula and its armed incursions into the Donbas region. Diplomatic sources cited by The Washington Post indicated that the proposed mechanism aims to re-engage Moscow across standing security consultations and structured military transparency. European officials who spoke to The Washington Post affirmed their general openness to future dialogue with Moscow, but stressed that an armistice in Ukraine remains a mandatory prerequisite. “Both tracks are on,” messaged a knowledgeable official from a close US ally. However, the official cautioned: “A Ukraine peace agreement has to be settled before an agreement on security architecture.” A senior official from another key European country noted that while European leaders choose to engage rather than isolate themselves from the diplomatic initiative, European capitals maintain a unified red line regarding sequencing. “Many risks for us in this approach, but better to engage than not,” the senior European official explained. “Our approach is still that these issues can be discussed only after the war… Not gonna be easy talks.” The official added that despite willingness among prominent European heads of state to support Kushner’s diplomatic outreach, “broad unity in Europe” exists around the fundamental principle that an operational ceasefire in Ukraine must precede any Europe-Russia discussions. President Volodymyr Zelensky rejected the notion of prioritizing broader European security talks over an end to hostilities , warning that Moscow’s push to discuss continental structures first is dangerous. Speaking in an interview with CNN host Jake Tapper, Zelensky stated that diplomatic sequencing must place the cessation of the war and binding security guarantees for Ukraine before any multilateral framework involving Russia is evaluated. “The idea of discussing a European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelensky said. “I have been very clear with all partners: first, we must discuss how to end Russia’s war against Ukraine. Second, what the security infrastructure for Ukraine will look like. What security guarantees Ukraine will receive.” Zelensky warned that allowing Russia to participate in restructuring continental security while actively striking civilian population centers and energy grids risks repeating historical errors. The president recalled the 1945 Yalta Conference, emphasizing that Ukraine and Europe must avoid a “Yalta 2.0” where great powers negotiate spheres of influence over the heads of sovereign states. Kushner has outlined five pillars, including crisis communications and military transparency, if progress is made at the Abu Dhabi trilateral talks on Nov. 10-11. US special presidential envoy Jared Kushner has proposed launching multilateral negotiations between European nations and Russia to design a post-war continental security architecture, modeling the initiative on the defunct NATO- Russia Council, The Washington Post reported. According to a senior official familiar with internal deliberations, Kushner seeks to transition diplomatic engagements into a broader multilateral framework with direct European participation if working-level trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US, and Russia achieve progress in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11 . Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Writing in a statement on X, Kushner outlined five primary pillars for the proposed security architecture: permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications channels, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability. However, European allied governments and Ukrainian leadership have emphasized that any discussions on continental security architecture must remain strictly conditional on first securing a verified ceasefire and an enforceable peace agreement in Ukraine. Kushner’s proposal looks toward the operational template of the NATO -Russia Council, an institutional body established in 2002 to facilitate security coordination and dialogue between the Western alliance and Moscow . The council’s practical operations were suspended in 2014 following Russia’s illegal military invasion and annexation of Ukraine’s Crimean peninsula and its armed incursions into the Donbas region. Diplomatic sources cited by The Washington Post indicated that the proposed mechanism aims to re-engage Moscow across standing security consultations and structured military transparency. European officials who spoke to The Washington Post affirmed their general openness to future dialogue with Moscow, but stressed that an armistice in Ukraine remains a mandatory prerequisite. “Both tracks are on,” messaged a knowledgeable official from a close US ally. However, the official cautioned: “A Ukraine peace agreement has to be settled before an agreement on security architecture.” A senior official from another key European country noted that while European leaders choose to engage rather than isolate themselves from the diplomatic initiative, European capitals maintain a unified red line regarding sequencing. “Many risks for us in this approach, but better to engage than not,” the senior European official explained. “Our approach is still that these issues can be discussed only after the war… Not gonna be easy talks.” The official added that despite willingness among prominent European heads of state to support Kushner’s diplomatic outreach, “broad unity in Europe” exists around the fundamental principle that an operational ceasefire in Ukraine must precede any Europe-Russia discussions. President Volodymyr Zelensky rejected the notion of prioritizing broader European security talks over an end to hostilities , warning that Moscow’s push to discuss continental structures first is dangerous. Speaking in an interview with CNN host Jake Tapper, Zelensky stated that diplomatic sequencing must place the cessation of the war and binding security guarantees for Ukraine before any multilateral framework involving Russia is evaluated. “The idea of discussing a European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelensky said. “I have been very clear with all partners: first, we must discuss how to end Russia’s war against Ukraine. Second, what the security infrastructure for Ukraine will look like. What security guarantees Ukraine will receive.” Zelensky warned that allowing Russia to participate in restructuring continental security while actively striking civilian population centers and energy grids risks repeating historical errors. The president recalled the 1945 Yalta Conference, emphasizing that Ukraine and Europe must avoid a “Yalta 2.0” where great powers negotiate spheres of influence over the heads of sovereign states. sources.title: Two Chinese companies cleared to buy banned Nvidia AI chips have empty offices and unknown addresses — investigation reveals businesses have ties to sanctioned Chinese military suppliers - Tom's Hardware
passages: An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them.

According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military.
President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors.
The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China .
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra.
The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces.
Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links.
It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center.

An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them. According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military. This news has revealed concerns that the U.S. Department of Commerce is simply rubber-stamping GPU export license applications instead of scrutinizing each one for potential links to Beijing. “I have a ton of concerns that neither the Commerce Department or Nvidia is doing the due diligence needed to ensure that the licensing terms are being followed,” former China director for the White House National Security Council Liza Tobin told the publication. Many of these approved companies include well-known entities like Baidu, BYD, Tesla Shanghai, as well as ZTE , which has previously been blacklisted from the U.S. market, Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance. However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra. The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces. The New Matrix website also reportedly did not contain any information about its owners or its history, although public company records reveal that it was founded by Li Bin, who, along with two other primary owners, are connected to Wise Road, a Chinese private equity firm sanctioned by the U.S. for helping Beijing acquire sensitive chip technologies. Furthermore, Mr. Li chairs Tsinghua Unigroup, a tech conglomerate partly owned by the Chinese government, and owns New H3C Semiconductor Technologies, which has also been added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List for cooperating with the Chinese military. Maginfra, on the other hand, is suspected of being linked to Inspur, which Washington has b lacklisted since 2023 for supporting the People’s Liberation Army, with both companies sharing personnel, patents, and a similar government ownership structure. These two firms aren’t listed as the final users of Nvidia’s AI chips, though. Instead, they’re supposed to assemble them into AI servers, which would then be forwarded to a final user, although it’s unclear who their customers are. Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links. Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology’s executives are reportedly related to the founder of Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group, a data center operator that has sold compute capacity to Chinese military contractors. It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center. President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors. The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China . Beijing’s refusal to give Chinese tech companies the green light to buy the chips for the first few months of the year caused the delay. But once China lifted its import ban on Nvidia chips, several Chinese companies applied for licenses to buy them, and The New York Times reported that around two dozen firms have already received approval, including these questionable ones. An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them. According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military.

This news has revealed concerns that the U.S. Department of Commerce is simply rubber-stamping GPU export license applications instead of scrutinizing each one for potential links to Beijing. “I have a ton of concerns that neither the Commerce Department or Nvidia is doing the due diligence needed to ensure that the licensing terms are being followed,” former China director for the White House National Security Council Liza Tobin told the publication.

Many of these approved companies include well-known entities like Baidu, BYD, Tesla Shanghai, as well as ZTE , which has previously been blacklisted from the U.S. market, Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance. However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra. The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces.

The New Matrix website also reportedly did not contain any information about its owners or its history, although public company records reveal that it was founded by Li Bin, who, along with two other primary owners, are connected to Wise Road, a Chinese private equity firm sanctioned by the U.S. for helping Beijing acquire sensitive chip technologies. Furthermore, Mr. Li chairs Tsinghua Unigroup, a tech conglomerate partly owned by the Chinese government, and owns New H3C Semiconductor Technologies, which has also been added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List for cooperating with the Chinese military.

Maginfra, on the other hand, is suspected of being linked to Inspur, which Washington has b lacklisted since 2023 for supporting the People’s Liberation Army, with both companies sharing personnel, patents, and a similar government ownership structure. These two firms aren’t listed as the final users of Nvidia’s AI chips, though. Instead, they’re supposed to assemble them into AI servers, which would then be forwarded to a final user, although it’s unclear who their customers are.

Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links. Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology’s executives are reportedly related to the founder of Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group, a data center operator that has sold compute capacity to Chinese military contractors. It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center.

President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors. The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China . Beijing’s refusal to give Chinese tech companies the green light to buy the chips for the first few months of the year caused the delay. But once China lifted its import ban on Nvidia chips, several Chinese companies applied for licenses to buy them, and The New York Times reported that around two dozen firms have already received approval, including these questionable ones.

story.title: Two Chinese companies cleared to buy banned Nvidia AI chips have empty offices and unknown addresses — investigation reveals businesses have ties to sanctioned Chinese military suppliers - Tom's Hardware

facts.text: An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them.

According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military.
President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors.
The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China .
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra.
The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces.
Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links.
It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center.

sources.title: Two Chinese companies cleared to buy banned Nvidia AI chips have empty offices and unknown addresses — investigation reveals businesses have ties to sanctioned Chinese military suppliers - Tom's Hardware
passages: An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them.

According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military.
President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors.
The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China .
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra.
The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces.
Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links.
It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center.

An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them. According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military. This news has revealed concerns that the U.S. Department of Commerce is simply rubber-stamping GPU export license applications instead of scrutinizing each one for potential links to Beijing. “I have a ton of concerns that neither the Commerce Department or Nvidia is doing the due diligence needed to ensure that the licensing terms are being followed,” former China director for the White House National Security Council Liza Tobin told the publication. Many of these approved companies include well-known entities like Baidu, BYD, Tesla Shanghai, as well as ZTE , which has previously been blacklisted from the U.S. market, Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance. However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra. The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces. The New Matrix website also reportedly did not contain any information about its owners or its history, although public company records reveal that it was founded by Li Bin, who, along with two other primary owners, are connected to Wise Road, a Chinese private equity firm sanctioned by the U.S. for helping Beijing acquire sensitive chip technologies. Furthermore, Mr. Li chairs Tsinghua Unigroup, a tech conglomerate partly owned by the Chinese government, and owns New H3C Semiconductor Technologies, which has also been added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List for cooperating with the Chinese military. Maginfra, on the other hand, is suspected of being linked to Inspur, which Washington has b lacklisted since 2023 for supporting the People’s Liberation Army, with both companies sharing personnel, patents, and a similar government ownership structure. These two firms aren’t listed as the final users of Nvidia’s AI chips, though. Instead, they’re supposed to assemble them into AI servers, which would then be forwarded to a final user, although it’s unclear who their customers are. Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links. Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology’s executives are reportedly related to the founder of Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group, a data center operator that has sold compute capacity to Chinese military contractors. It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center. President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors. The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China . Beijing’s refusal to give Chinese tech companies the green light to buy the chips for the first few months of the year caused the delay. But once China lifted its import ban on Nvidia chips, several Chinese companies applied for licenses to buy them, and The New York Times reported that around two dozen firms have already received approval, including these questionable ones. An investigation has found that addresses for two Chinese companies approved to purchase Nvidia H200 chips led to empty offices, and the receptionists at the buildings were unfamiliar with them. According to The New York Times , these companies didn’t just have empty offices; their executives are often linked to other firms sanctioned by the United States for working with and providing advanced technology to the Chinese military.

This news has revealed concerns that the U.S. Department of Commerce is simply rubber-stamping GPU export license applications instead of scrutinizing each one for potential links to Beijing. “I have a ton of concerns that neither the Commerce Department or Nvidia is doing the due diligence needed to ensure that the licensing terms are being followed,” former China director for the White House National Security Council Liza Tobin told the publication.

Many of these approved companies include well-known entities like Baidu, BYD, Tesla Shanghai, as well as ZTE , which has previously been blacklisted from the U.S. market, Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance. However, the outfit’s investigation also revealed approval for two relatively unknown firms: New Matrix and Maginfra. The offices for both companies were empty shells with some office furniture, and people working nearby said they’d never heard of the company or seen anyone go to the deserted spaces.

The New Matrix website also reportedly did not contain any information about its owners or its history, although public company records reveal that it was founded by Li Bin, who, along with two other primary owners, are connected to Wise Road, a Chinese private equity firm sanctioned by the U.S. for helping Beijing acquire sensitive chip technologies. Furthermore, Mr. Li chairs Tsinghua Unigroup, a tech conglomerate partly owned by the Chinese government, and owns New H3C Semiconductor Technologies, which has also been added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List for cooperating with the Chinese military.

Maginfra, on the other hand, is suspected of being linked to Inspur, which Washington has b lacklisted since 2023 for supporting the People’s Liberation Army, with both companies sharing personnel, patents, and a similar government ownership structure. These two firms aren’t listed as the final users of Nvidia’s AI chips, though. Instead, they’re supposed to assemble them into AI servers, which would then be forwarded to a final user, although it’s unclear who their customers are.

Aside from these questionable non-entities, another company that received a license to purchase H200 GPUs has some suspicious links. Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology’s executives are reportedly related to the founder of Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group, a data center operator that has sold compute capacity to Chinese military contractors. It’s also reportedly partly operating out of a Range data center.

President Donald Trump banned the export of Nvidia AI GPUs in April 2025 , even those customized to meet the performance ceiling Washington set for AI processors. The president reversed the decision late last year in exchange for a 25% cut of the sale, but it still took more than eight months for the first H200 shipments to arrive in China . Beijing’s refusal to give Chinese tech companies the green light to buy the chips for the first few months of the year caused the delay. But once China lifted its import ban on Nvidia chips, several Chinese companies applied for licenses to buy them, and The New York Times reported that around two dozen firms have already received approval, including these questionable ones.

passages: The early iPhone Duo reviews were a bit hard on Apple’s new foldable for the lack of Duo-optimized apps available at the time of launch.
But Apple says things are changing quickly on the software front.

The Duo has also proven to be more popular than perhaps Apple had planned for, given its high price point. (It starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model.) The device quickly sold out within hours of orders opening up, and now, Duo ship times have shifted into the next year.
On its earnings call this week, Apple said it’s “hard to predict” when the Duo constraints leading to those delays will improve .
The company said that more than 2,000 app developers attended its over 50 in-person workshops that were hosted across 19 cities worldwide.

“It’s been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we’re grateful for their creativity and innovation,” said Susan Prescott, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations, in a statement referring to the 100,000-app milestone. “The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we’re excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo,” she added.
Spotify, for instance, is still showing the black bar on the side, and the App Store doesn’t yet say an update is available on our review unit of the Duo.
However, given that this list comes directly from Apple, we expect to see these updates soon.

extraction.body: The early iPhone Duo reviews were a bit hard on Apple’s new foldable for the lack of Duo-optimized apps available at the time of launch. But Apple says things are changing quickly on the software front. The company on Friday announced there are now over 100,000 apps built for the Duo live on the App Store, and it’s seeing thousands more being added to the store every day. The news was timed alongside the release of over a dozen more notable Duo-ready apps, including Microsoft Word and Outlook, Zoom, sports apps from the NBA and NHL, shopping apps like Etsy and LTK, productivity apps like Goodnotes and Extra, the Halide Mark III camera app, and others. These join the iPhone Duo-optimized apps that were already available, like Netflix, YouTube, Instagram, and WhatsApp. Non-optimized apps are definitely less than ideal, as they come with a black bar on the side of the screen, which takes up valuable space. Sometimes, they hide important functions under an overflow menu. Apple’s data seems to suggest that at least some iOS developers may have needed extra time to get their apps ready for its latest form factor. extraction.body: When I tried a prototype of Snap’s Specs at CES in Las Vegas earlier this year, the experience left something to be desired. The company’s AR glasses — which the company calls a “new kind of computer” — were heavy (they weighed around 8 ounces) and fit rather uncomfortably on my face. The device was also hot, and made my face feel tingly — a common side-effect of smart glasses where massive computing is happening under the hood. Fast forward to late October, when I met back up with the Snap team at a Four Seasons in downtown San Francisco. By this time, the company had debuted Specs publicly during an event with CEO Evan Spiegel, and pre-orders of the company’s long-gestating headset were already underway. What I can say is this: Specs has improved the form factor significantly since my first brush with the device. The glasses now weigh nearly half of what the previous version did, slimming down to 132 grams, or approximately 4.6 ounces. They were quite comfortable and, during the hour-ish that I demo-ed the device, it did not heat up like the previous version had. Specs now comes in two sizes — 47mm and 52mm. The purpose here is purely to accommodate different head sizes, ensuring the glasses fit snugly on whoever’s face happens to be wearing them. They also now come equipped with spring hinges, which make the device more flexible and comfortable. However, if the body of the device has improved greatly, its soul is still a work-in-progress. The glasses can be fun — but they also still seem to lack a dedicated purpose, and one struggles to imagine how, specifically, this expensive head gear ($2,200 a pop) would prove useful in a daily capacity. When I asked Snap staff what the device was really for — fun and games or productivity — the answer was vague. The device attempts to be a bunch of things at once and, in the process, ends up feeling a little rudderless. I have racked my brain to come up with some daily use-cases for Specs. Some of the things I came up with were: By contrast, here are some of the areas I’m still not totally sold on as Specs use-cases: Specs is impressive for how the Snap team has managed to integrate a variety of user experiences into one unified device. There are a lot of impressive achievements here — specifically the spatial synching tech that allows two users to see the same thing simultaneously — that, with some further development, could be deployed towards some really interesting use cases. The bottom line is that Snap’s device can continue to grow and transform as the company iterates. sources.title: Weakening AI copyright law will spell ‘disaster for creativity’, global music body warns Albanese - The Guardian
passages: Australia weakening copyright protections to aid AI companies would be “ridiculous and dangerous”, the global peak body for the music recording industry has warned as it watches with concern how the Albanese government responds to big tech’s demands.

While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, promised “the strongest possible protection” , warning it would be “theft” if creatives were not paid for their work, creative industries were alarmed after AI companies requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material.
“We’ve been talking to capitals around the world, saying ‘are you seeing what’s going on in Australia?’ We think this is a disaster for creativity.”

Why would a sophisticated, democratic country that has a phenomenal cultural power of its own choose to make this very odd decision and buy into the promises of a few large AI companies, and throw away their own culture and creativity?” Victoria Oakley, the chief executive of IFPI, told Guardian Australia.

In recent answers to a parliamentary committee on AI, responding to questions from the independent senator David Pocock about why it couldn’t replicate the kind of deals Spotify had made, OpenAI said the music streaming giant “has a different business, where it primarily transmits un-transformed copyrighted content, so would be expected to license content that it streams”.

extraction.body: Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australia weakening copyright protections to aid AI companies would be “ridiculous and dangerous”, the global peak body for the music recording industry has warned as it watches with concern how the Albanese government responds to big tech’s demands. While local creatives have raised constitutional issues and threatened political backlash , the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), representing recording industry bodies worldwide, said its members were worried about Australia potentially agreeing to demands other nations had rejected. “Why would Australia do this? Why would a sophisticated, democratic country that has a phenomenal cultural power of its own choose to make this very odd decision and buy into the promises of a few large AI companies, and throw away their own culture and creativity?” Victoria Oakley, the chief executive of IFPI, told Guardian Australia. “I don’t think Australia wants to be the weakest link in this situation, the one that believed the promises and gave in and threw creativity under the bus on behalf of everyone else. That doesn’t feel very Australian to me. “You just need one safe harbour, because then you can train on music from anywhere in the world. So this isn’t just about Australian music and Australian culture; it’s about music and culture everywhere.” Labor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of policy overhauls around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, promised “the strongest possible protection” , warning it would be “theft” if creatives were not paid for their work, creative industries were alarmed after AI companies requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material. Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model that would allow it to scrape content unless rights holders signalled an objection. Large AI companies say they need legal certainty on issues such as copyright before making investments in Australia or training their models here. Oakley said AI companies had made similar proposals in the US, UK and other nations and that Australia should not accept such a bargain. “I just don’t think it’s true that you will only get investment or growth, or be seen as pro-innovation, if you entirely give in to the demands of AI companies,” Oakley said. “We’ve been talking to capitals around the world, saying ‘are you seeing what’s going on in Australia?’ We think this is a disaster for creativity.” The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said via a spokesperson last week that the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”. Oakley said she worried about AI and copyright “everywhere” but feared “Australia appears to be threatening to do something really ridiculous and dangerous”. She said creative industries worried about “contagion” of copyright relaxation if Australia caved in, and that copyright material from anywhere in the world could be affected. She declined to speculate on any potential legal or constitutional challenges, as raised by the Australian Recording Industry Association, but said it would be reputational damage to Australia’s standing in the creative world. “It would be a huge mistake and I think the prize is not worth what you’re throwing away,” she said. In recent answers to a parliamentary committee on AI, responding to questions from the independent senator David Pocock about why it couldn’t replicate the kind of deals Spotify had made, OpenAI said the music streaming giant “has a different business, where it primarily transmits un-transformed copyrighted content, so would be expected to license content that it streams”. But Oakley said music labels had already inked dozens of licensing deals with smaller AI companies around the world. “It is perfectly possible to license. I’m almost shocked that these words are coming out of the mouths of some of the larger AI companies … We already know how to license music to tech platforms because that’s exactly how Spotify works, or Amazon Music, Apple, or Tidal,” she said. “You have a ready, willing set of rights holders who want to license with a history of licensing in the streaming world, but also current evidence of licensing to AI firms. Let’s let the market do what it needs to do. Come to us and we’ll make it work.”

extraction.body: MPs, local authorities, lawyers, schools and more are receiving floods of grievances, requests and legal challenges, often complex to read and respond to “I t started as a trickle in 2024 and now it’s an onslaught.” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, is explaining the daily reality of dealing with surging volumes of artificial intelligence-generated correspondence. “Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” she says, adding that this has made requests and complaints much more complex and time-consuming to read and deal with, despite her decade of experience in the role. “It is definitely more taxing.” At the start of this decade, applying for a job, writing a complaint or objecting to a local planning application typically required considerable effort: time to research a topic, fill in a form or write a formal-sounding email, with specialist knowledge often also required. The developers of AI tools promised huge productivity gains for employers and their staff: dull, routine tasks could be automated and carried out far more quickly, giving the human workforce more time for creative endeavours. There are signs of those gains in parts of the economy, with AI credited for some of this year’s better than expected UK GDP growth. However, UK businesses, local authorities, courts, schools and other public bodies are reporting being swamped by a flood of AI-generated complaints, letters and legal challenges that are massively increasing their workload , at a time of already stretched resources . This phenomenon has been called “AI clog” by commenters. With the concept of low-quality “AI slop” now mainstream, organisations are sounding the alarm that their operations are being gummed up by ever greater volumes of correspondence. These only take moments for users to create, but huge amounts of time for human employees to sift through and respond to. Bombarding public bodies with AI-generated requests has been labelled “agentic flooding” by researchers at the centre for digital governance at the Hertie School in Berlin, the Cooperative AI Foundation and GovAI. “Every sector is experiencing very similar issues,” says Deborah Evans, the chief executive of Lawyers in Local Government (LLG), an organisation that represents 5,600 lawyers working in local authorities. “Obviously AI is a wonderful tool that enables people to do things very, very quickly and it can make a complaint sound incredibly professional, very formal.” Local authorities are experiencing surging numbers of complaints, which can relate to issues from adult social care services to missed bin collections or objections to planning applications. “Local authorities have one pot of money and don’t get extra money because of more complaints,” Evans says. Local authorities believe the length of correspondence is an indication that it has been artificially generated, as does the inclusion of certain phrases or use of bullet points. “It’s a real problem,” says councillor Alessandro Georgiou, the leader of Enfield council. “More and more residents are using it to appeal decisions of the council, such as a significant uptick in parking appeals.” The information rights watchdog, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) , found that many public authorities received more requests in 2025. It noted that AI-generated requests can be “very long, repetitive and contain unrelated comments or misdirected demands”, have a greater scope, and be written in a way that makes it harder to identify what information is being requested. Before the widespread use of chatbots, the average length of complaints received by local authorities was about two pages. The majority are now 10 times longer, says Evans. “You get some huge ones. The worst one I’m aware of at the moment is about 200 pages long,” she says. Despite this, the ICO cautions that requests that appear to be drafted using AI and contain inaccuracies still need to be answered by humans. AI tools can often treat complaints as a legal claim, Evans says. “It will start referring to statute and pull out case law, but not necessarily tied to the jurisdictional boundaries in which you operate. It might find some great case law from Canada or somewhere. [AI] is also slightly prone to hallucinations so it does occasionally make things up.” Some business owners worry that AI’s tendency to be overly supportive and validating can give people misplaced confidence to pursue a legal case. “Everyone’s got a free lawyer now,” complains the founder of one technology start-up. One of its former employees, who was let go on performance grounds, is challenging their dismissal through an employment tribunal, although the entrepreneur insists the process was handled correctly. “You can tell by the wording [that the complaint is AI-generated] and it has a different tone.” Amid a long backlog of employment tribunal cases, the founder expects they will have spent £30,000 on legal fees by the time the case is heard. The number of employment tribunal claims opened between April and June soared by 28% compared with a year earlier, representing 14,000 cases from single claimants, according to the most recent government figures. The number of concluded cases also fell during the quarter, resulting in 70,000 open single claims at the end of June. The founder’s experience is by no means unique, according to Jim Moore, an employee relations expert at Hamilton Nash. Many of his clients are receiving correspondence that is either entirely AI-generated or relies heavily on wording from AI tools. The complaints received by employers are described as “unnecessarily verbose” and containing “embellished or exaggerated claims that portray relatively minor incidents as major offences”. Moore says many AI-generated complaints “miss out on the most important point of a complaint – what resolution are you looking for? Most of the time, they’re worded to sound intimidating but forget to set out what solution the complainant wants.” The statutory response times for some requests are putting further pressure on public bodies clogged up by AI-generated correspondence. Transport for London (TfL), the public body responsible for the capital’s public transport system, received a record 4,769 freedom of information (FoI) requests in 2025-26, a 5% increase on the previous peak in 2023-24. The number of appeals sent to TfL is also rising, according to the minutes of a recent meeting of its audit and assurance committee. It reported a “noted increase” in appeals that appeared to be generated by AI “which often contain highly technical and often inaccurate assertions and assumptions”. The offices of some MPs are also struggling to cope. Vonnie Sandlan, the head of office for Graeme Downie, the Labour MP for Dunfermline and Dollar, says dealing with a surge in AI-generated requests has left her staff “exhausted”. “They are stretched to the limits and working more hours than they are paid,” she says. She notes that AI agents could aid those who would struggle to draft correspondence without help, but says her office has recently decided to stop responding to automated “click to email your MP” campaigns, to allow them to focus on constituents’ requests. The GMB union, which represents MPs’ office staff, has found soaring casework levels to be widespread. “AI is not lightening the load in MPs’ offices,” says Lisa Gillmore, the president of the MPs’ and peers’ staff branch. “Where offices keep their own figures, that casework has doubled or more and staff are carrying it with no let-up.” Evans warns that every pound spent by local authorities on dealing with complaints “is a pound that’s not being spent on something else, which is why getting things under control is important”. Some ombudsman services are now imposing word limits for complaints, she says, or designing online templates to restrict how much information can be attached. Others fear that organisations might start using AI tools to sift through AI-generated correspondence, with machine talking to machine. But this doesn’t come without cost and “losing the human touch”, as Evans puts it. Wiltshire council has said it is exploring using AI tools to summarise long emails and draft initial responses, while a committee at Stroud district council in Gloucestershire has discussed how it uses Microsoft’s Copilot to help with writing reports and presenting information. The UK government has issued civil servants with advice on using AI tools, including verifying facts provided, not inputting personal data and making sure humans review the work and take final decisions. The technology journalist Jamie Bartlett has been approached by many people sharing their experiences of AI clog. “Public bodies and companies are probably going to have to use some form of AI to start filtering things out, or set stricter rules on what they’ll accept and what they won’t,” he says. “Otherwise I worry they’re going to get completely overwhelmed.”

With the concept of low-quality “AI slop” now mainstream, organisations are sounding the alarm that their operations are being gummed up by ever greater volumes of correspondence. These only take moments for users to create, but huge amounts of time for human employees to sift through and respond to. Bombarding public bodies with AI-generated requests has been labelled “agentic flooding” by researchers at the centre for digital governance at the Hertie School in Berlin, the Cooperative AI Foundation and GovAI. “Every sector is experiencing very similar issues,” says Deborah Evans, the chief executive of Lawyers in Local Government (LLG), an organisation that represents 5,600 lawyers working in local authorities. “Obviously AI is a wonderful tool that enables people to do things very, very quickly and it can make a complaint sound incredibly professional, very formal.” Local authorities are experiencing surging numbers of complaints, which can relate to issues from adult social care services to missed bin collections or objections to planning applications. “Local authorities have one pot of money and don’t get extra money because of more complaints,” Evans says. The worst one I’m aware of at the moment is about 200 pages long,” she says. Despite this, the ICO cautions that requests that appear to be drafted using AI and contain inaccuracies still need to be answered by humans. AI tools can often treat complaints as a legal claim, Evans says. “It will start referring to statute and pull out case law, but not necessarily tied to the jurisdictional boundaries in which you operate. Many of his clients are receiving correspondence that is either entirely AI-generated or relies heavily on wording from AI tools. The complaints received by employers are described as “unnecessarily verbose” and containing “embellished or exaggerated claims that portray relatively minor incidents as major offences”. Most of the time, they’re worded to sound intimidating but forget to set out what solution the complainant wants.” The statutory response times for some requests are putting further pressure on public bodies clogged up by AI-generated correspondence. The number of appeals sent to TfL is also rising, according to the minutes of a recent meeting of its audit and assurance committee. It reported a “noted increase” in appeals that appeared to be generated by AI “which often contain highly technical and often inaccurate assertions and assumptions”. The offices of some MPs are also struggling to cope. Vonnie Sandlan, the head of office for Graeme Downie, the Labour MP for Dunfermline and Dollar, says dealing with a surge in AI-generated requests has left her staff “exhausted”. “They are stretched to the limits and working more hours than they are paid,” she says. She notes that AI agents could aid those who would struggle to draft correspondence without help, but says her office has recently decided to stop responding to automated “click to email your MP” campaigns, to allow them to focus on constituents’ requests. The GMB union, which represents MPs’ office staff, has found soaring casework levels to be widespread. “AI is not lightening the load in MPs’ offices,” says Lisa Gillmore, the president of the MPs’ and peers’ staff branch. “Where offices keep their own figures, that casework has doubled or more and staff are carrying it with no let-up.” Evans warns that every pound spent by local authorities on dealing with complaints “is a pound that’s not being spent on something else, which is why getting things under control is important”. Some ombudsman services are now imposing word limits for complaints, she says, or designing online templates to restrict how much information can be attached. Others fear that organisations might start using AI tools to sift through AI-generated correspondence, with machine talking to machine. But this doesn’t come without cost and “losing the human touch”, as Evans puts it. Wiltshire council has said it is exploring using AI tools to summarise long emails and draft initial responses, while a committee at Stroud district council in Gloucestershire has discussed how it uses Microsoft’s Copilot to help with writing reports and presenting information. The UK government has issued civil servants with advice on using AI tools, including verifying facts provided, not inputting personal data and making sure humans review the work and take final decisions. sources.title: The Duo apps are coming, says Apple
passages: The early iPhone Duo reviews were a bit hard on Apple’s new foldable for the lack of Duo-optimized apps available at the time of launch.
But Apple says things are changing quickly on the software front.

The Duo has also proven to be more popular than perhaps Apple had planned for, given its high price point. (It starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model.) The device quickly sold out within hours of orders opening up, and now, Duo ship times have shifted into the next year.
On its earnings call this week, Apple said it’s “hard to predict” when the Duo constraints leading to those delays will improve .
The company said that more than 2,000 app developers attended its over 50 in-person workshops that were hosted across 19 cities worldwide.

“It’s been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we’re grateful for their creativity and innovation,” said Susan Prescott, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations, in a statement referring to the 100,000-app milestone. “The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we’re excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo,” she added.
Spotify, for instance, is still showing the black bar on the side, and the App Store doesn’t yet say an update is available on our review unit of the Duo.
However, given that this list comes directly from Apple, we expect to see these updates soon.

extraction.body: The early iPhone Duo reviews were a bit hard on Apple’s new foldable for the lack of Duo-optimized apps available at the time of launch. But Apple says things are changing quickly on the software front. The company on Friday announced there are now over 100,000 apps built for the Duo live on the App Store, and it’s seeing thousands more being added to the store every day. The news was timed alongside the release of over a dozen more notable Duo-ready apps, including Microsoft Word and Outlook, Zoom, sports apps from the NBA and NHL, shopping apps like Etsy and LTK, productivity apps like Goodnotes and Extra, the Halide Mark III camera app, and others. These join the iPhone Duo-optimized apps that were already available, like Netflix, YouTube, Instagram, and WhatsApp. Non-optimized apps are definitely less than ideal, as they come with a black bar on the side of the screen, which takes up valuable space. Sometimes, they hide important functions under an overflow menu. Apple’s data seems to suggest that at least some iOS developers may have needed extra time to get their apps ready for its latest form factor. The company said that more than 2,000 app developers attended its over 50 in-person workshops that were hosted across 19 cities worldwide. Here, the developers could use the Duo and work on their apps with Apple’s support. The Duo has also proven to be more popular than perhaps Apple had planned for, given its high price point. (It starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model.) The device quickly sold out within hours of orders opening up, and now, Duo ship times have shifted into the next year. Other notable apps that have been updated for iOS 27 and optimized for the iPhone Duo include the following: Spotify, CBS, Tubi, BBC iPlayer (U.K.), Yahoo Fantasy Sports, Sportsnet (Canada), Facebook Messenger, Google Chat, ChatGPT, Grok Bot, Microsoft Copilot, Excel, PowerPoint, SAP Concur, monday.com, PDF Expert, Documents, iA Writer, Substack, The Washington Post, Yahoo News, FOX News, Kalshi, Yahoo Finance, Canva, Suno, Tinder, Google Translate, Strava, Alma, Withings, MyFitnessPal, Bevel, Transit, Citi Bike, ParkMobile, Viator, Tesla Robotaxi, Priceline, Kroger, Domino’s, Taco Bell, Untappd, The Weather Channel, FOX Weather, and RainViewer. Not all these updates have yet to fully roll out, we should note. Spotify, for instance, is still showing the black bar on the side, and the App Store doesn’t yet say an update is available on our review unit of the Duo. However, given that this list comes directly from Apple, we expect to see these updates soon.

extraction.body: Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. For years, mysterious electrical anomalies have been flummoxing grid managers around the world. Every 60 seconds, the frequency on the grid would drop a tiny bit. Even weirder: The sags happened at the exact same time on power grids across countries and continents. It was a mystery that Dirk Witthaut, a researcher at Forschungszentrum Jülich in Germany, couldn’t pass up. Germany’s largest transmission system operator, Tennet Germany, brought the puzzle to Witthaut, and it took years of investigative and modeling work to determine the cause. From Europe to Australia, the U.S. to Malaysia, the same pattern shows up in the data. Hydropower plants have historically been a main driver of so-called ultra-low frequency oscillations (UFLOs). Every turbine vibrates, and if those vibrations occur with a certain regularity, known as the resonant frequency, they can magnify, sometimes to dangerous levels. Think of a wine glass breaking before an opera singer’s mighty pipes — that’s resonance. So Witthaut and his team started investigating hydropower, the most obvious potential culprit. They used a computer model of a hydropower plant control system on the Scandinavian grid to test the hypothesis. While they managed to find conditions that could generate a resonance that peaked once per minute, they couldn’t explain why it persisted for so long. Typically, resonances in mechanical systems will come and go, and so will the accompanying signal on the electrical grid. But this frequency drop kept happening minute after minute after minute. Every 60 seconds, without fail. It then dawned on the team that anything operating with such clockwork required, well, a clock. How else could they explain the uncanny timing? To that hypothesis, the researchers started close to home, installing more than 80 smart power quality meters around the Jülich campus. The research site is outfitted with medium- and low-voltage distribution lines, transformers, solar panels, and battery energy storage systems that serve as uninterruptible power supplies (UPS). It also has a high-performance computer system as well as the usual office computers powered by much smaller UPS devices. The power quality meters sampled a range of attributes, including frequency, voltage, current, and power, once every three seconds. Before long, the research team had its answer. The measurements recorded on the transformer attached to the battery energy storage system peaked every minute, just like on the bigger power grids. It turns out that many stationary batteries, from data center UPSes to large grid-scale batteries , check their state-of-charge every minute. Since these devices are internet-connected, their clocks are in near perfect synchronicity. Every time one checks its charge, the disturbance is imperceptible on the wide grid. But when they all do it together, that disruption becomes apparent. To find evidence that UPSes were the main culprit on the grid, Witthaut and his team turned to data provided by grid operators. They found their answer in Ireland. There, data centers have grown to consume a large fraction of the country’s electricity. By 2022, data centers represented 18% of the load on Ireland’s grid, and each facility is served by a fleet of UPSes. Sure enough, between 2016 and 2021, the minute-by-minute frequency drop on the Irish grid quadrupled from 3 milli-Hertz (mHz) in 2016 to 12 mHz in 2021. More recently, some drops have exceeded 20 mHz. The problem is entirely preventable. Rather than check state-of-charge exactly on the minute, Witthaus and team recommend that UPS and grid-scale battery manufacturers add some randomization to the schedule. While UPSes are driving the problem today, there’s a risk that the phenomenon could persist. The researchers also tested IoT devices. In devices as diverse as a smart oven and Raspberry Pi clusters, they were able to detect periodic power fluctuations. The fix is also a simple software patch, but many IoT devices go unpatched. A recent study found that less than 3% of IoT devices are running the latest firmware. Regulators may soon have to step in to demand changes, but they can only address their corner of the grid. Given the global nature of the issue, it’ll ultimately require global coordination. The mystery may be solved, but the problem could remain for years to come. Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. He received his PhD in environmental science, policy, and management from the University of California, Berkeley, and his BA degree in environmental studies, English, and biology from St. Olaf College. You can contact or verify outreach from Tim by emailing [email protected] .

sources.title: Sequoia partners reportedly blindsided when Roelof Botha joined SpaceX board
passages: The break between Botha and his old firm reportedly deepened after Botha joined the SpaceX board this summer. (Botha and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk previously worked together at PayPal.) A source told the FT that Sequoia’s partners were blindsided by the announcement, because Botha “didn’t ask compliance, he didn’t get sign off from the partnership” — even though his new role could complicate the firm’s ability to trade its $20 billion stake.
Apparently, not everyone is on-board with the changes, with another source firing back that this seems like an “erasure of Sequoia’s heritage, not Roelof’s legacy.”
A Sequoia spokesperson said that the firm continues to “collaborate closely” with Botha.

According to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence has been aware of her activities for over a year already and has even briefed President Donald Trump on the situation.
However, Trump reportedly chose not to do anything about the information, as he apparently did not want to affect Nvidia sales or antagonize China.

The investigation into the firm began when the U.S.

This raised suspicion that the machines were either just shipped in or about to be shipped out, instead of being installed on the site.

As for Jensen, U.S. officials do not believe that he is aware of Ms. Huang’s intelligence activities. Multiple sources claim that a top executive at a Singapore AI firm suspected of steering Nvidia AI GPUs to China and who has close business ties with Jensen Huang was apparently passing information to Beijing as a Chinese intelligence asset. According to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence has been aware of her activities for over a year already and has even briefed President Donald Trump on the situation. However, Trump reportedly chose not to do anything about the information, as he apparently did not want to affect Nvidia sales or antagonize China.

The suspect, Alice Huang or Huang Le, was listed as the managing director of Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed, an Nvidia cloud partner that builds data centers and rents out the compute to Chinese firms like Alibaba. The investigation into the firm began when the U.S. Commerce Department visited the firm’s Malaysia data center and found the Nvidia equipment that it ordered still packed in boxes. This raised suspicion that the machines were either just shipped in or about to be shipped out, instead of being installed on the site. However, it remains unclear what made U.S. intelligence agencies investigate Ms. Huang. Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips last year .

There have been multiple instances where Ms. Huang was spotted in public with the Nvidia chief. She was photographed sitting beside Jensen Huang alongside other executives in an informal event around Computex 2024 in a LinkedIn post by NetThunder, identified as Megaspeed Chairwoman Alice Wong. About a year later, around the same time as Computex 2025 , she was once again seen with Jensen Huang leaving a restaurant in Taipei alongside other business associates.

“Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Tom's Hardware . “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security ." Still, the possibility that Chinese intelligence is targeting a senior figure close to President Trump is apparently troubling some U.S. officials.

The Chinese embassy in Washington denied the allegations, saying that it was merely “groundless smears and slanders” against China. Nevertheless, it would also make sense for Beijing to keep tabs on senior executives of the top American firms that arguably single-handedly fueled the AI boom. And given Jensen Huang’s status as a celebrity CEO , it’s not surprising that he is surrounded by all kinds of people from both the U.S. and China. Sources cited in the report claimed that Mr. Huang hasn’t yet been given a defensive briefing — a warning that U.S. counterintelligence agencies would sometimes give to American citizens who have been targeted by foreign intelligence services — even though the surveillance against Alice Huang continues. The report speculates it is possible this was done to avoid alerting Alice Huang that she was being investigated.

As for Jensen, U.S. officials do not believe that he is aware of Ms. Huang’s intelligence activities. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," Nvidia told Tom’s Hardware . "We often receive updates from the U.S. government regarding parties and entities of concern and always act accordingly."

Nvidia's board of directors announced Sunday that it's launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a Chinese spy operation . Nvidia also published a message that Huang to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia's CEO. "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Jensen Huang wrote. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Huang added that he'd "fallen short' of his responsibility to the company. "To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me," he said. AI chips, including those created by Nvidia, have been a focus in the trade war between the United States and China . In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers.
As the AI race between the United States and China heats up , chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus .

According to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence has been aware of her activities for over a year already and has even briefed President Donald Trump on the situation.

The investigation into the firm began when the U.S.
Commerce Department visited the firm’s Malaysia data center and found the Nvidia equipment that it ordered still packed in boxes.
This raised suspicion that the machines were either just shipped in or about to be shipped out, instead of being installed on the site.
Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips last year .
The Chinese embassy in Washington denied the allegations, saying that it was merely “groundless smears and slanders” against China.
Nevertheless, it would also make sense for Beijing to keep tabs on senior executives of the top American firms that arguably single-handedly fueled the AI boom.

passages: Multiple sources claim that a top executive at a Singapore AI firm suspected of steering Nvidia AI GPUs to China and who has close business ties with Jensen Huang was apparently passing information to Beijing as a Chinese intelligence asset.
According to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence has been aware of her activities for over a year already and has even briefed President Donald Trump on the situation.
However, Trump reportedly chose not to do anything about the information, as he apparently did not want to affect Nvidia sales or antagonize China.
“Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers.

The suspect, Alice Huang or Huang Le, was listed as the managing director of Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed, an Nvidia cloud partner that builds data centers and rents out the compute to Chinese firms like Alibaba.
The investigation into the firm began when the U.S.
Commerce Department visited the firm’s Malaysia data center and found the Nvidia equipment that it ordered still packed in boxes.
This raised suspicion that the machines were either just shipped in or about to be shipped out, instead of being installed on the site.
Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips last year .
The Chinese embassy in Washington denied the allegations, saying that it was merely “groundless smears and slanders” against China.
Nevertheless, it would also make sense for Beijing to keep tabs on senior executives of the top American firms that arguably single-handedly fueled the AI boom.

Huang hasn’t yet been given a defensive briefing — a warning that U.S. counterintelligence agencies would sometimes give to American citizens who have been targeted by foreign intelligence services — even though the surveillance against Alice Huang continues.
The report speculates it is possible this was done to avoid alerting Alice Huang that she was being investigated.
Huang was spotted in public with the Nvidia chief.
She was photographed sitting beside Jensen Huang alongside other executives in an informal event around Computex 2024 in a LinkedIn post by NetThunder, identified as Megaspeed Chairwoman Alice Wong.

Some U.S. officials are worried that Beijing may be targeting close allies of President Trump. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Multiple sources claim that a top executive at a Singapore AI firm suspected of steering Nvidia AI GPUs to China and who has close business ties with Jensen Huang was apparently passing information to Beijing as a Chinese intelligence asset. According to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence has been aware of her activities for over a year already and has even briefed President Donald Trump on the situation. However, Trump reportedly chose not to do anything about the information, as he apparently did not want to affect Nvidia sales or antagonize China. The suspect, Alice Huang or Huang Le, was listed as the managing director of Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed, an Nvidia cloud partner that builds data centers and rents out the compute to Chinese firms like Alibaba. The investigation into the firm began when the U.S. Commerce Department visited the firm’s Malaysia data center and found the Nvidia equipment that it ordered still packed in boxes. This raised suspicion that the machines were either just shipped in or about to be shipped out, instead of being installed on the site. However, it remains unclear what made U.S. intelligence agencies investigate Ms. Huang. Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips last year . There have been multiple instances where Ms. Huang was spotted in public with the Nvidia chief. She was photographed sitting beside Jensen Huang alongside other executives in an informal event around Computex 2024 in a LinkedIn post by NetThunder, identified as Megaspeed Chairwoman Alice Wong. About a year later, around the same time as Computex 2025 , she was once again seen with Jensen Huang leaving a restaurant in Taipei alongside other business associates. “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Tom's Hardware . “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security ." Still, the possibility that Chinese intelligence is targeting a senior figure close to President Trump is apparently troubling some U.S. officials. The Chinese embassy in Washington denied the allegations, saying that it was merely “groundless smears and slanders” against China. Nevertheless, it would also make sense for Beijing to keep tabs on senior executives of the top American firms that arguably single-handedly fueled the AI boom. And given Jensen Huang’s status as a celebrity CEO , it’s not surprising that he is surrounded by all kinds of people from both the U.S. and China. Sources cited in the report claimed that Mr. Huang hasn’t yet been given a defensive briefing — a warning that U.S. counterintelligence agencies would sometimes give to American citizens who have been targeted by foreign intelligence services — even though the surveillance against Alice Huang continues. The report speculates it is possible this was done to avoid alerting Alice Huang that she was being investigated. As for Jensen, U.S. officials do not believe that he is aware of Ms. Huang’s intelligence activities. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," Nvidia told Tom’s Hardware . "We often receive updates from the U.S. government regarding parties and entities of concern and always act accordingly." Multiple sources claim that a top executive at a Singapore AI firm suspected of steering Nvidia AI GPUs to China and who has close business ties with Jensen Huang was apparently passing information to Beijing as a Chinese intelligence asset.
According to The New York Times , U.S. intelligence has been aware of her activities for over a year already and has even briefed President Donald Trump on the situation.
However, Trump reportedly chose not to do anything about the information, as he apparently did not want to affect Nvidia sales or antagonize China.
“Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers.

The suspect, Alice Huang or Huang Le, was listed as the managing director of Singaporean AI firm Megaspeed, an Nvidia cloud partner that builds data centers and rents out the compute to Chinese firms like Alibaba.
The investigation into the firm began when the U.S.
Commerce Department visited the firm’s Malaysia data center and found the Nvidia equipment that it ordered still packed in boxes.
This raised suspicion that the machines were either just shipped in or about to be shipped out, instead of being installed on the site.
Megaspeed was accused of helping smuggle $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips last year .
The Chinese embassy in Washington denied the allegations, saying that it was merely “groundless smears and slanders” against China.
Nevertheless, it would also make sense for Beijing to keep tabs on senior executives of the top American firms that arguably single-handedly fueled the AI boom.

Huang hasn’t yet been given a defensive briefing — a warning that U.S. counterintelligence agencies would sometimes give to American citizens who have been targeted by foreign intelligence services — even though the surveillance against Alice Huang continues.
The report speculates it is possible this was done to avoid alerting Alice Huang that she was being investigated.
Huang was spotted in public with the Nvidia chief.
She was photographed sitting beside Jensen Huang alongside other executives in an informal event around Computex 2024 in a LinkedIn post by NetThunder, identified as Megaspeed Chairwoman Alice Wong.
