extraction.body: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working for Beijing's intelligence services, according to an email obtained by Axios, prompting an independent investigation into whether the affair compromised U.S. national security or the chipmaker's closely guarded technology. The disclosure has raised concerns about potential foreign influence over one of the world's most powerful technology executives, who has been a prominent advocate in Washington for easing restrictions on exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China amid intensifying competition between the two countries. "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang wrote in a draft email to Nvidia employees obtained by Axios. There is no excuse for what I did." Huang said he took "full responsibility" for his actions, acknowledging that he had fallen short of his obligations to Nvidia employees, the company's board of directors and shareholders. "Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life," he wrote. "I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence." Nvidia announced Sunday that its board had authorized an independent investigation following media reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The inquiry will be conducted by an independent committee with the assistance of outside legal counsel. The company emphasized that it had no reason to believe either U.S. national security or Nvidia's proprietary information had been compromised. The board also expressed confidence in Huang's leadership, saying he fully supported the investigation and had committed to cooperating with it. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," John Rizzo, Nvidia's head of public policy communications, said in a statement. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a separate request for comment on the Axios report. The allegations center on Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman and senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. Despite sharing a surname, she and Jensen Huang are not related. According to people familiar with U.S. intelligence and reports in American and European media, including The New York Times and Britain's Financial Times, Alice Huang was recruited by a Chinese intelligence agency to gather information about Nvidia's advanced AI chips and influence the company's export policies. The alleged intelligence operation reportedly involved cultivating a personal relationship with the Nvidia chief executive that eventually became romantic. U.S. intelligence agencies monitored the relationship for more than a year, according to the reports. In June 2024, Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were reportedly documented together at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan. Around the same period, Megaspeed, which emerged from a little-known Chinese gaming company, began purchasing billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia's advanced chips. The circumstances have drawn scrutiny over whether the relationship could have provided Chinese intelligence with access to sensitive commercial information or opportunities to influence Huang's positions on U.S. export controls. The New York Times reported in October that Huang had maintained a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing. Following that report, senior Republican lawmakers in the U.S. House of Representatives called on Huang to brief Congress this month about the allegations. The controversy comes as Nvidia occupies a central position in the technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing. Its advanced processors are essential to developing and operating powerful AI systems, making restrictions on their export to China a major issue in U.S. national security policy. Huang has been among the most prominent technology executives urging Washington to ease those restrictions. He has argued that maintaining American technology companies' presence in the Chinese market strengthens U.S. competitiveness and helps prevent China from developing domestic alternatives that could eventually surpass American chips. His position has placed him at the center of a debate over whether restricting access to U.S. technology slows China's AI development or instead accelerates Beijing's efforts to achieve technological independence. The allegations involving Alice Huang have added a new dimension to that debate, raising questions about possible attempts by Chinese intelligence to influence a leading advocate for continued technology exports. However, the existence of a romantic relationship does not establish that Huang knowingly assisted a foreign intelligence operation or disclosed sensitive information. Nvidia's board said its investigation would examine all available information, while maintaining that it had found no reason to conclude that national security or company secrets had been compromised. For now, Huang remains at the helm of the chipmaker, with the company's leadership publicly backing him as the independent review proceeds.

extraction.body: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working for Beijing's intelligence services, according to an email obtained by Axios, prompting an independent investigation into whether the affair compromised U.S. national security or the chipmaker's closely guarded technology. The disclosure has raised concerns about potential foreign influence over one of the world's most powerful technology executives, who has been a prominent advocate in Washington for easing restrictions on exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China amid intensifying competition between the two countries. "I owe my family and all of you an apology," Huang wrote in a draft email to Nvidia employees obtained by Axios. There is no excuse for what I did." Huang said he took "full responsibility" for his actions, acknowledging that he had fallen short of his obligations to Nvidia employees, the company's board of directors and shareholders. "Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life," he wrote. "I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence." Nvidia announced Sunday that its board had authorized an independent investigation following media reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The inquiry will be conducted by an independent committee with the assistance of outside legal counsel. The company emphasized that it had no reason to believe either U.S. national security or Nvidia's proprietary information had been compromised. The board also expressed confidence in Huang's leadership, saying he fully supported the investigation and had committed to cooperating with it. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," John Rizzo, Nvidia's head of public policy communications, said in a statement. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a separate request for comment on the Axios report. The allegations center on Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese businesswoman and senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. Despite sharing a surname, she and Jensen Huang are not related. According to people familiar with U.S. intelligence and reports in American and European media, including The New York Times and Britain's Financial Times, Alice Huang was recruited by a Chinese intelligence agency to gather information about Nvidia's advanced AI chips and influence the company's export policies. The alleged intelligence operation reportedly involved cultivating a personal relationship with the Nvidia chief executive that eventually became romantic. U.S. intelligence agencies monitored the relationship for more than a year, according to the reports. In June 2024, Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were reportedly documented together at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan. Around the same period, Megaspeed, which emerged from a little-known Chinese gaming company, began purchasing billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia's advanced chips. The circumstances have drawn scrutiny over whether the relationship could have provided Chinese intelligence with access to sensitive commercial information or opportunities to influence Huang's positions on U.S. export controls. The New York Times reported in October that Huang had maintained a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing. Following that report, senior Republican lawmakers in the U.S. House of Representatives called on Huang to brief Congress this month about the allegations. The controversy comes as Nvidia occupies a central position in the technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing. Its advanced processors are essential to developing and operating powerful AI systems, making restrictions on their export to China a major issue in U.S. national security policy. Huang has been among the most prominent technology executives urging Washington to ease those restrictions. He has argued that maintaining American technology companies' presence in the Chinese market strengthens U.S. competitiveness and helps prevent China from developing domestic alternatives that could eventually surpass American chips. His position has placed him at the center of a debate over whether restricting access to U.S. technology slows China's AI development or instead accelerates Beijing's efforts to achieve technological independence. The allegations involving Alice Huang have added a new dimension to that debate, raising questions about possible attempts by Chinese intelligence to influence a leading advocate for continued technology exports. However, the existence of a romantic relationship does not establish that Huang knowingly assisted a foreign intelligence operation or disclosed sensitive information. Nvidia's board said its investigation would examine all available information, while maintaining that it had found no reason to conclude that national security or company secrets had been compromised. For now, Huang remains at the helm of the chipmaker, with the company's leadership publicly backing him as the independent review proceeds.

Back in June, Apple hiked prices for all of its entire line-up of MacBooks and iPads, with the MacBook Air rising by $200. Thanks to Amazon, you can pick up the 2026 MacBook Air with M5 chip with that $200 price rise removed, bringing the price down to just $1,099 for its 16GB RAM and 512GB SSD model. It's also dropped the 16GB / 1TB model to $1,399 , with the 24GB / 1TB model costing $1,599 , both receiving the same $200 price drops. We saw these prices during the Prime Day sales earlier this week, but Amazon doesn't look like it's raised its prices on these models just yet.
● Grab this Apple MacBook Air deal at Amazon

Few can rival the MacBook for build quality and design: that's why they're so popular. The Air is its lightest laptop design, with this base-edition 13.6-inch model shipping with 16GB of memory and a 512GB SSD for storage. This latest M5 chip from Apple uses a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, giving you incremental gains in performance and speed compared to the last-gen M4.

These ultra-light and slim-line laptops get the N1 wireless chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity, along with that 13.6-inch Liquid Retina display, giving you stunning clear images. You also have a 12MP Center Stage camera for video calls, along with Touch ID for biometric security.

Other specs are available, including the 16GB/1TB model that we mentioned for $1,399 and the 24GB/1TB model for $1,599.9. They're identical in design to the $1,099 model, with the same price available for the Sky Blue, Starlight (yellow), classic Silver, and Sky Blue colorways, all featuring the same M5 chip. You're just paying more for extra storage or memory, depending on whether you need it or not.
This 13.6-Inch MacBook Air is complete with Apple's Liquid Retina display, 16GB of unified memory, a 512GB SSD, 12MP center stage camera, touch ID, and Wi-Fi 7 connectivity.
This model is the same shape and design as the one above, but you get a boost in storage. This MacBook Air comes with a 1TB SSD instead.
The best spec'd model on sale at Amazon right now for the MacBook Air 13 2026. This model has a 1TB SSD and 24GB of unified memory.

Apple only raised its prices back in June, with Amazon's pricing following shortly afterward. You can't get them at these prices from Apple directly, either.

Whether you go for the $1,099 16GB/512GB MacBook Air , the $1,299 16GB/1TB upgrade , or the higher-spec 24GB/1TB edition for $1,599 , these are great deals for a new Apple laptop in the current market. Don't expect them to be around for long, though. The $1,099 edition is already limited stock in the Sky Blue colorway, for instance, and Apple could raise its prices at any time.

It’s still the jack-of-all-trades laptop I recommend to most people, with a thin-and-light build, fantastic battery life, and — compared to the M4 — more memory and faster storage.
Unfortunately, these prices might be as low as they can possibly go for now as companies grapple with the rising cost of device components, memory, and storage.
This means consumers are paying 15% to 25% more now than they would have on the same device a couple of months ago.
While Amazon has changed its prices to match, some of the latest MacBook Air models are still less expensive there than at Apple.

With the recent launch of Meta Platforms ' (NASDAQ: META) popular Muse app , which can autonomously complete personal tasks such as booking a flight and shopping online, it's clear that Siri still doesn't measure up.
That's a problem for Apple -- and I think it's one the company can solve. But there's a lot at stake if it keeps getting agentic AI wrong.

Most of my personal devices are Apple products, and I've been less than enthused by Siri for years now. The latest update was a big leap forward, but it essentially caught Apple up with where OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude were several years ago.

Meta's Muse easily helps users with all sorts of tasks, including booking flights, reserving tables at restaurants, ordering groceries, buying clothes online, and more. It's the type of personal AI assistant that many tech companies have talked about for years, finally built into a simple app.

Muse has reached the top of Apple's App Store and has more than 3 million weekly users. That rapid adoption is a good sign that consumers want these capabilities, and there are some important reasons Apple should take notice.

The bulk of Apple's revenue -- around 50% -- comes from selling its high-margin iPhones. The margins have taken a bit of a hit recently because of soaring memory prices, but management still estimates gross margins will be around 47%.
For decades, Apple has paired high-end devices with top-notch software that consumers mostly love. But Muse and other agents could chip away at this sentiment by offering superior capabilities.

Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan is concerned about this threat. Mohan said in an investor note last month that Muse could cut into Apple's services revenue by completing online transactions outside of Apple's ecosystem.

What's more, if more consumers view Muse as essential to their daily routines, they could shift their smartphone buying habits away from expensive iPhones and toward cheaper Android devices that run Muse just as well.

It's still too early to tell whether that will happen, but as users grow more accustomed to highly capable AI agents, paying premium prices for Apple hardware without robust AI built in may not make sense for many smartphone buyers.

The biggest hurdle for Muse, and Apple's biggest advantage, is that most users don't trust Meta with their data. A recent Oppenheimer survey found that just 8% of respondents said they trust Meta with their passwords. In contrast, 28% of respondents said they would trust Apple with their passwords.

Trust isn't the only factor in winning the agentic AI space, but it's a start. The next step is, of course, for Apple to design Siri to work better within third-party apps to complete autonomous tasks. The real problem for Apple isn't the technical know-how; it may be whether Apple's management believes the company needs to make such a leap with Siri to stay relevant.

The latest version of Siri is a step in the right direction, but as an Apple shareholder myself, I wonder how long it will be before Siri catches up to other AI agents. If Apple is in the same place it is now a year from now, after the next iteration of Siri has presumably debuted, Apple's AI software miss could turn into a hardware sales problem.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

extraction.body: Apple CEO John Ternus is putting intense pressure on AI chief Craig Federighi to transform Siri into a full-fledged agentic assistant capable of competing with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. While Federighi delivered a functional Siri AI on a compressed timeline, the company knows it's falling behind in the race to build powerful AI agents that can autonomously handle complex tasks across apps and services. Apple is scrambling to catch up in the agentic AI wars. CEO John Ternus isn't satisfied with Siri's current trajectory and is leaning hard on software chief Craig Federighi to deliver something that can actually go toe-to-toe with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports. While Federighi's team managed to ship a working version of Siri AI on what insiders describe as an "incredibly short timeline," Apple executives privately admit they're not keeping pace with rivals who've already deployed AI agents capable of autonomous, multi-step tasks. It's a rare admission of vulnerability from a company that typically sets the industry tempo. Two significant capability upgrades are headed to Siri in the coming months, according to Gurman's sources. The first will give the assistant granular control over Apple's native apps - think rotating and cropping images directly in Photos, organizing Safari tabs by topic, or managing complex Mail workflows without constant user prompting. OpenAI just closed an $11 billion funding round that values the ChatGPT maker at $1.25 trillion, cementing its position as the world's most valuable startup. Its Dots agent can already handle sophisticated tasks like booking travel, managing schedules, and coordinating across multiple services with minimal human intervention. Meta, meanwhile, has been aggressively rolling out Muse across its family of apps, giving billions of users access to agentic capabilities. Apple's challenge is architectural as much as it is competitive. The company built its reputation on tightly controlled, privacy-first experiences, but modern AI agents demand access to vast amounts of user data and cross-app coordination to function effectively. Federighi's team is essentially trying to build a competitive agent while maintaining Apple's privacy guardrails - a technical high-wire act that's proving harder than anticipated. The pressure from Ternus suggests Apple views agentic AI as existential, not incremental. The company recently began integrating ChatGPT support into its HomeView smart hub, signaling a willingness to partner with rivals when its own technology lags. But relying on OpenAI for core assistant functionality undermines Apple's ecosystem lock-in and puts user data in third-party hands - exactly the scenario Cupertino has spent decades avoiding. Industry observers note that Apple's historical playbook - wait, watch, then perfect - doesn't work when competitors are shipping transformative capabilities to hundreds of millions of users every quarter. Amazon just launched its own text-to-shop Alexa feature after blocking Meta's Muse from its platform, showing how quickly the agentic landscape is fragmenting. The internal roadmap acceleration also reflects concerns about developer momentum. If third-party apps optimize for OpenAI and Meta agents first, Apple risks becoming a second-class citizen in the AI ecosystem it desperately wants to control. The company needs Siri to become genuinely useful - not just incrementally better - to keep developers building for Apple Intelligence first. What remains unclear is whether Apple can compress its development timeline enough to matter. The company's methodical approach to shipping polished products has served it well in hardware, but software moves faster, and AI moves faster still. Federighi delivered functional Siri AI quickly, but "functional" isn't the bar anymore. Users expect agents that anticipate needs, coordinate complex workflows, and actually save time - capabilities that require fundamentally different architectures than what Siri was built on. The coming months will reveal whether Apple's internal pressure translates to external progress. Ternus isn't just asking for iterative improvements; he's demanding a competitive agent that can stand alongside the industry's best. That's a tall order for a company that's spent the past year playing catch-up while rivals sprint ahead. Apple's internal urgency around Siri signals a broader shift in how the company views AI competition. This isn't about adding features to maintain parity - it's about building an agent capable of genuinely competing with OpenAI and Meta's offerings before the window closes. For users, the promise of fine-grained app control and deeper automation sounds compelling, but the real question is whether Apple can deliver transformative agentic capabilities while maintaining the privacy and polish that define its brand. The key insight: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported on November 8 that Apple wants to make Siri more agent-like, possibly as early as next year in Gurman’s view, contrasting Siri’s request-based actions with ChatGPT Dots, Meta Muse and Grok, which Gurman said keep working between conversations. Apple also gave engineers six weeks of coding instead of four in the first iOS 28 milestone, which by our arithmetic is 50% more coding time in that stage. Gurman wrote that today’s Siri AI “can properly answer questions, write emails and text messages, set reminders, pull information from the open web, serve up news and take basic actions inside apps”. Gurman described its biggest development this year as the ability to draw context from what is on a user’s display and from private information on Apple devices, such as emails and text messages. The iOS 27.3 beta adds precise control over Apple ’s own apps, Gurman reported, with examples including organising Safari tabs, sorting Files folders, unsending an iMessage and multistep Photos edits. Gurman wrote that support for Apple ’s apps “could come as early as December” and that third-party app support probably won’t arrive until the spring. Our earlier piece reported Apple opening Siri AI to any app . Gurman also posted that Apple is changing how it develops iOS 28, iPadOS 28 and macOS 28, giving engineers more time to explore and build new features before locking them in. The newsletter puts the change at six weeks of coding and two of convergence in the first milestone, instead of four and four. Apple is exploring turning Siri into a background AI agent similar to OpenAI ’s ChatGPT Dots as part of an iOS 28 shake-up, according to Bloomberg. Apple is still delivering the Siri overhaul it promised years ago. Now it is already exploring the architecture that could make that version look obsolete. An X user posting as cryptopunk7213 (Ejaaz) shared a personal take on Gurman’s report at 17:07 UTC on 8 November. The post describes the reported feature as letting third-party apps integrate with Siri so it can act across apps, and argues that Apple’s installed base of devices is an advantage; that argument and the 3.5 billion devices figure are the poster’s, not Bloomberg’s. Gurman wrote that these features are “nothing close to what you can do with something like ChatGPT ’s Dots, Meta ’s Muse and Elon Musk ’s Grok”. Gurman listed what those agents do: they “can remember projects and preferences over time, monitor connected sources for changes, proactively surface information, and decide when to pause and resume work”. In Gurman’s summary, Siri “can now execute more complicated requests and integrate more deeply with third-party software ”, while Dots, Muse and Grok “can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step”. Apple ultimately wants to go in that direction, Gurman wrote, citing people Gurman spoke to. Apple CEO John Ternus said on the company’s earnings call, as quoted by Bloomberg, that Siri is “primarily request-based today” but “built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand its capabilities over time”. For M1 of this cycle, covering Bell (iOS 28 and iPadOS 28) and Poppy (macOS 28), engineers got six weeks of coding, exploration and feature development and two weeks of convergence, according to the newsletter. Development of the M2 milestone kicks off on Monday, and that is the period when Apple will start to finalise what it plans to include, according to the report. Our coverage has also included Anthropic’s Claude ‘Dreams’ memory research and Perplexity’s launch of Teammates . As we read the newsletter, the gap Gurman describes is less about what Siri can do in a single request and more about whether it can hold a goal over time and act without being asked. As we read the iOS 28 change, giving engineers six weeks to explore before converging is a process signal that Apple is making room for new features before it locks the 2027 releases in. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) launched a new version of Siri just last month, and it's undoubtedly the best version of the personal agent the company has ever released. Siri can now interact like other artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots by answering more in-depth questions; it also has on-screen awareness and more personal context than before because it can search through photos, emails, and texts. But as helpful as all of this is, just a few weeks after its launch, Siri still feels dated. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » With the recent launch of Meta Platforms ' (NASDAQ: META) popular Muse app , which can autonomously complete personal tasks such as booking a flight and shopping online, it's clear that Siri still doesn't measure up. That's a problem for Apple -- and I think it's one the company can solve. But there's a lot at stake if it keeps getting agentic AI wrong. Most of my personal devices are Apple products, and I've been less than enthused by Siri for years now. The latest update was a big leap forward, but it essentially caught Apple up with where OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude were several years ago. Meta's Muse easily helps users with all sorts of tasks, including booking flights, reserving tables at restaurants, ordering groceries, buying clothes online, and more. It's the type of personal AI assistant that many tech companies have talked about for years, finally built into a simple app. Muse has reached the top of Apple's App Store and has more than 3 million weekly users. That rapid adoption is a good sign that consumers want these capabilities, and there are some important reasons Apple should take notice. The bulk of Apple's revenue -- around 50% -- comes from selling its high-margin iPhones. The margins have taken a bit of a hit recently because of soaring memory prices, but management still estimates gross margins will be around 47%. For decades, Apple has paired high-end devices with top-notch software that consumers mostly love. But Muse and other agents could chip away at this sentiment by offering superior capabilities. Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan is concerned about this threat. Mohan said in an investor note last month that Muse could cut into Apple's services revenue by completing online transactions outside of Apple's ecosystem. What's more, if more consumers view Muse as essential to their daily routines, they could shift their smartphone buying habits away from expensive iPhones and toward cheaper Android devices that run Muse just as well. It's still too early to tell whether that will happen, but as users grow more accustomed to highly capable AI agents, paying premium prices for Apple hardware without robust AI built in may not make sense for many smartphone buyers. The biggest hurdle for Muse, and Apple's biggest advantage, is that most users don't trust Meta with their data. A recent Oppenheimer survey found that just 8% of respondents said they trust Meta with their passwords. In contrast, 28% of respondents said they would trust Apple with their passwords. Trust isn't the only factor in winning the agentic AI space, but it's a start. The next step is, of course, for Apple to design Siri to work better within third-party apps to complete autonomous tasks. The real problem for Apple isn't the technical know-how; it may be whether Apple's management believes the company needs to make such a leap with Siri to stay relevant. The latest version of Siri is a step in the right direction, but as an Apple shareholder myself, I wonder how long it will be before Siri catches up to other AI agents. Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) launched a new version of Siri just last month, and it's undoubtedly the best version of the personal agent the company has ever released. Siri can now interact like other artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots by answering more in-depth questions; it also has on-screen awareness and more personal context than before because it can search through photos, emails, and texts.
But as helpful as all of this is, just a few weeks after its launch, Siri still feels dated.

With the recent launch of Meta Platforms ' (NASDAQ: META) popular Muse app , which can autonomously complete personal tasks such as booking a flight and shopping online, it's clear that Siri still doesn't measure up.
That's a problem for Apple -- and I think it's one the company can solve. But there's a lot at stake if it keeps getting agentic AI wrong.

Most of my personal devices are Apple products, and I've been less than enthused by Siri for years now. The latest update was a big leap forward, but it essentially caught Apple up with where OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude were several years ago.

Meta's Muse easily helps users with all sorts of tasks, including booking flights, reserving tables at restaurants, ordering groceries, buying clothes online, and more. It's the type of personal AI assistant that many tech companies have talked about for years, finally built into a simple app.

Muse has reached the top of Apple's App Store and has more than 3 million weekly users. That rapid adoption is a good sign that consumers want these capabilities, and there are some important reasons Apple should take notice.

The bulk of Apple's revenue -- around 50% -- comes from selling its high-margin iPhones. The margins have taken a bit of a hit recently because of soaring memory prices, but management still estimates gross margins will be around 47%.
For decades, Apple has paired high-end devices with top-notch software that consumers mostly love. But Muse and other agents could chip away at this sentiment by offering superior capabilities.

Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan is concerned about this threat. Mohan said in an investor note last month that Muse could cut into Apple's services revenue by completing online transactions outside of Apple's ecosystem.

What's more, if more consumers view Muse as essential to their daily routines, they could shift their smartphone buying habits away from expensive iPhones and toward cheaper Android devices that run Muse just as well.

It's still too early to tell whether that will happen, but as users grow more accustomed to highly capable AI agents, paying premium prices for Apple hardware without robust AI built in may not make sense for many smartphone buyers.

The biggest hurdle for Muse, and Apple's biggest advantage, is that most users don't trust Meta with their data. A recent Oppenheimer survey found that just 8% of respondents said they trust Meta with their passwords. In contrast, 28% of respondents said they would trust Apple with their passwords.

Trust isn't the only factor in winning the agentic AI space, but it's a start. The next step is, of course, for Apple to design Siri to work better within third-party apps to complete autonomous tasks. The real problem for Apple isn't the technical know-how; it may be whether Apple's management believes the company needs to make such a leap with Siri to stay relevant.

sources.title: Apple CEO Pushes Siri Agent Overhaul to Match OpenAI, Meta
passages: Apple CEO John Ternus is putting intense pressure on AI chief Craig Federighi to transform Siri into a full-fledged agentic assistant capable of competing with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.
If third-party apps optimize for OpenAI and Meta agents first, Apple risks becoming a second-class citizen in the AI ecosystem it desperately wants to control.

While Federighi's team managed to ship a working version of Siri AI on what insiders describe as an "incredibly short timeline," Apple executives privately admit they're not keeping pace with rivals who've already deployed AI agents capable of autonomous, multi-step tasks.
Meta, meanwhile, has been aggressively rolling out Muse across its family of apps, giving billions of users access to agentic capabilities.
The company needs Siri to become genuinely useful - not just incrementally better - to keep developers building for Apple Intelligence first.
Users expect agents that anticipate needs, coordinate complex workflows, and actually save time - capabilities that require fundamentally different architectures than what Siri was built on.
Apple's internal urgency around Siri signals a broader shift in how the company views AI competition.
But relying on OpenAI for core assistant functionality undermines Apple's ecosystem lock-in and puts user data in third-party hands - exactly the scenario Cupertino has spent decades avoiding.
Apple is scrambling to catch up in the agentic AI wars.
The pressure from Ternus suggests Apple views agentic AI as existential, not incremental.

For users, the promise of fine-grained app control and deeper automation sounds compelling, but the real question is whether Apple can deliver transformative agentic capabilities while maintaining the privacy and polish that define its brand.

extraction.body: Apple CEO John Ternus is putting intense pressure on AI chief Craig Federighi to transform Siri into a full-fledged agentic assistant capable of competing with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. While Federighi delivered a functional Siri AI on a compressed timeline, the company knows it's falling behind in the race to build powerful AI agents that can autonomously handle complex tasks across apps and services. Apple is scrambling to catch up in the agentic AI wars. CEO John Ternus isn't satisfied with Siri's current trajectory and is leaning hard on software chief Craig Federighi to deliver something that can actually go toe-to-toe with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports. While Federighi's team managed to ship a working version of Siri AI on what insiders describe as an "incredibly short timeline," Apple executives privately admit they're not keeping pace with rivals who've already deployed AI agents capable of autonomous, multi-step tasks. It's a rare admission of vulnerability from a company that typically sets the industry tempo. Two significant capability upgrades are headed to Siri in the coming months, according to Gurman's sources. The first will give the assistant granular control over Apple's native apps - think rotating and cropping images directly in Photos, organizing Safari tabs by topic, or managing complex Mail workflows without constant user prompting. OpenAI just closed an $11 billion funding round that values the ChatGPT maker at $1.25 trillion, cementing its position as the world's most valuable startup. Its Dots agent can already handle sophisticated tasks like booking travel, managing schedules, and coordinating across multiple services with minimal human intervention. Meta, meanwhile, has been aggressively rolling out Muse across its family of apps, giving billions of users access to agentic capabilities. Apple's challenge is architectural as much as it is competitive. The company built its reputation on tightly controlled, privacy-first experiences, but modern AI agents demand access to vast amounts of user data and cross-app coordination to function effectively. Federighi's team is essentially trying to build a competitive agent while maintaining Apple's privacy guardrails - a technical high-wire act that's proving harder than anticipated. The pressure from Ternus suggests Apple views agentic AI as existential, not incremental. The company recently began integrating ChatGPT support into its HomeView smart hub, signaling a willingness to partner with rivals when its own technology lags. But relying on OpenAI for core assistant functionality undermines Apple's ecosystem lock-in and puts user data in third-party hands - exactly the scenario Cupertino has spent decades avoiding. Industry observers note that Apple's historical playbook - wait, watch, then perfect - doesn't work when competitors are shipping transformative capabilities to hundreds of millions of users every quarter. Amazon just launched its own text-to-shop Alexa feature after blocking Meta's Muse from its platform, showing how quickly the agentic landscape is fragmenting. The internal roadmap acceleration also reflects concerns about developer momentum. If third-party apps optimize for OpenAI and Meta agents first, Apple risks becoming a second-class citizen in the AI ecosystem it desperately wants to control. The company needs Siri to become genuinely useful - not just incrementally better - to keep developers building for Apple Intelligence first. What remains unclear is whether Apple can compress its development timeline enough to matter. The company's methodical approach to shipping polished products has served it well in hardware, but software moves faster, and AI moves faster still. Federighi delivered functional Siri AI quickly, but "functional" isn't the bar anymore. Users expect agents that anticipate needs, coordinate complex workflows, and actually save time - capabilities that require fundamentally different architectures than what Siri was built on. The coming months will reveal whether Apple's internal pressure translates to external progress. Ternus isn't just asking for iterative improvements; he's demanding a competitive agent that can stand alongside the industry's best. That's a tall order for a company that's spent the past year playing catch-up while rivals sprint ahead. Apple's internal urgency around Siri signals a broader shift in how the company views AI competition. This isn't about adding features to maintain parity - it's about building an agent capable of genuinely competing with OpenAI and Meta's offerings before the window closes. For users, the promise of fine-grained app control and deeper automation sounds compelling, but the real question is whether Apple can deliver transformative agentic capabilities while maintaining the privacy and polish that define its brand. The pressure from Ternus suggests the company knows it's running out of time to prove it can.

story.title: Apple is racing to make Siri more agentic

facts.text: Trust isn't the only factor in winning the agentic AI space, but it's a start.
The next step is, of course, for Apple to design Siri to work better within third-party apps to complete autonomous tasks.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) launched a new version of Siri just last month, and it's undoubtedly the best version of the personal agent the company has ever released.

Siri can now interact like other artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots by answering more in-depth questions; it also has on-screen awareness and more personal context than before because it can search through photos, emails, and texts.
Most of my personal devices are Apple products, and I've been less than enthused by Siri for years now.
The latest update was a big leap forward, but it essentially caught Apple up with where OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude were several years ago.
If Apple is in the same place it is now a year from now, after the next iteration of Siri has presumably debuted, Apple's AI software miss could turn into a hardware sales problem.
But as helpful as all of this is, just a few weeks after its launch, Siri still feels dated.

With the recent launch of Meta Platforms ' (NASDAQ: META) popular Muse app , which can autonomously complete personal tasks such as booking a flight and shopping online, it's clear that Siri still doesn't measure up.
Apple is expected to push Siri to become more agentic and enable features that will allow it to perform ongoing tasks, not just one-offs.

Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says CEO John Ternus is pressuring AI czar Craig Federighi to accelerate the Siri roadmap and deliver a powerful AI agent that can compete with OpenAI’s Dots or Meta’s Muse.
Two significant improvements are expected to be made to Siri in the coming months.
One will give the assistant fine-grained control over Apple’s first-party apps, allowing it to do things like rotate and crop images in Photos and organize Safari tabs.
That would let Siri place an order through Grubhub or book a dinner reservation through OpenTable, for example.

Apple CEO John Ternus is putting intense pressure on AI chief Craig Federighi to transform Siri into a full-fledged agentic assistant capable of competing with OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.
If third-party apps optimize for OpenAI and Meta agents first, Apple risks becoming a second-class citizen in the AI ecosystem it desperately wants to control.

While Federighi's team managed to ship a working version of Siri AI on what insiders describe as an "incredibly short timeline," Apple executives privately admit they're not keeping pace with rivals who've already deployed AI agents capable of autonomous, multi-step tasks.
Meta, meanwhile, has been aggressively rolling out Muse across its family of apps, giving billions of users access to agentic capabilities.
The company needs Siri to become genuinely useful - not just incrementally better - to keep developers building for Apple Intelligence first.
Users expect agents that anticipate needs, coordinate complex workflows, and actually save time - capabilities that require fundamentally different architectures than what Siri was built on.
Apple's internal urgency around Siri signals a broader shift in how the company views AI competition.
But relying on OpenAI for core assistant functionality undermines Apple's ecosystem lock-in and puts user data in third-party hands - exactly the scenario Cupertino has spent decades avoiding.

passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a man who likely attends numerous meetings, and today one more was added to his busy schedule.
Congress wants to have a closed-door chat with Huang over mounting concerns about national security .
The congressmen bidding for his time say last week's report spurred the move that he may be the target of espionage by a reported Chinese asset: Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (family unrelated).
The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) further claims that she was recruited by Chinese authorities due to her existing relationship with Jensen Huang.

As for Nvidia, the company seemingly reposted today the same comments it offered us last week, stating that "meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The firm adds that "[its] regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security."
According to the WSJ, Singaporean authorities opened their own probe into Megaspeed, and even reportedly questioned Alice Huang directly.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a man who likely attends numerous meetings, and today one more was added to his busy schedule. The U.S. Congress wants to have a closed-door chat with Huang over mounting concerns about national security . The congressmen bidding for his time say last week's report spurred the move that he may be the target of espionage by a reported Chinese asset: Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (family unrelated). The meeting was set up by Republican House representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford, respective Chairs of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence. In the House's letter on the matter, the lawmakers say the aforementioned reports "raise significant national security concerns" about China gaining access to U.S. technology and information. The previously reported claim is that Alice Huang is a Chinese plant in Singaporean data center outfit Megaspeed, siphoning information to Beijing. The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) further claims that she was recruited by Chinese authorities due to her existing relationship with Jensen Huang. Megaspeed reportedly bought and continues to buy billions' worth of Nvidia's chips, according to The New York Times (NYT), and stands accused by the Department of Commerce since 2024 of smuggling $2 billion worth of advanced silicon to China. The backdrop for the situation is that the U.S. has long-standing export controls blocking Nvidia and AMD's most advanced AI accelerator chips from reaching China, among a number of other nations. The allegations were first published last week in the NYT, and are reportedly sourced from unnamed U.S. intelligence officials. The House says the purpose of the briefing with Jensen Huang is to discuss "Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and [his] interactions with [...] Alice Huang." According to the NYT, the CEO never got a "defensive briefing," essentially a warning for potential targets of foreign espionage, to acquaint them with signs of such activities. The publication notes that intelligence officials often hesitate to inform potential targets of espionage, as doing so may make the spy aware they're being investigated. The NYT adds that President Trump was briefed on the situation surrounding Megaspeed and Alice Huang a year ago, but chose not to act on it. Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. According to the WSJ, Singaporean authorities opened their own probe into Megaspeed, and even reportedly questioned Alice Huang directly. However, an official response from the country told the WSJ that it "does not implement unilateral export controls imposed by foreign jurisdictions," adding that while it's investigating Megaspeed, it's not targeting Alice Huang herself or inspecting her claimed ties with Jensen Huang or China. The Singaporean does note that the country has "a zero-tolerance stance" on commercial fraud, pointing out that it's charged four companies and four individuals over such wrongdoings, and that they may face up to 20 years in prison. Meanwhile, Taiwan is also seemingly keeping a close eye on Alice Huang, by inspecting her visits to the nation. The WSJ says that the country's authorities are probing her involvement with China and have her under physical surveillance. As for Nvidia, the company seemingly reposted today the same comments it offered us last week, stating that "meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The firm adds that "[its] regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security." Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a man who likely attends numerous meetings, and today one more was added to his busy schedule. The U.S. Congress wants to have a closed-door chat with Huang over mounting concerns about national security . The congressmen bidding for his time say last week's report spurred the move that he may be the target of espionage by a reported Chinese asset: Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (family unrelated).

The meeting was set up by Republican House representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford, respective Chairs of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence. In the House's letter on the matter, the lawmakers say the aforementioned reports "raise significant national security concerns" about China gaining access to U.S. technology and information.

The previously reported claim is that Alice Huang is a Chinese plant in Singaporean data center outfit Megaspeed, siphoning information to Beijing. The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) further claims that she was recruited by Chinese authorities due to her existing relationship with Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed reportedly bought and continues to buy billions' worth of Nvidia's chips, according to The New York Times (NYT), and stands accused by the Department of Commerce since 2024 of smuggling $2 billion worth of advanced silicon to China.

The backdrop for the situation is that the U.S. has long-standing export controls blocking Nvidia and AMD's most advanced AI accelerator chips from reaching China, among a number of other nations. The allegations were first published last week in the NYT, and are reportedly sourced from unnamed U.S. intelligence officials.

The House says the purpose of the briefing with Jensen Huang is to discuss "Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and [his] interactions with [...] Alice Huang." According to the NYT, the CEO never got a "defensive briefing," essentially a warning for potential targets of foreign espionage, to acquaint them with signs of such activities.

The publication notes that intelligence officials often hesitate to inform potential targets of espionage, as doing so may make the spy aware they're being investigated. The NYT adds that President Trump was briefed on the situation surrounding Megaspeed and Alice Huang a year ago, but chose not to act on it.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

According to the WSJ, Singaporean authorities opened their own probe into Megaspeed, and even reportedly questioned Alice Huang directly. However, an official response from the country told the WSJ that it "does not implement unilateral export controls imposed by foreign jurisdictions," adding that while it's investigating Megaspeed, it's not targeting Alice Huang herself or inspecting her claimed ties with Jensen Huang or China.

The Singaporean does note that the country has "a zero-tolerance stance" on commercial fraud, pointing out that it's charged four companies and four individuals over such wrongdoings, and that they may face up to 20 years in prison.

Meanwhile, Taiwan is also seemingly keeping a close eye on Alice Huang, by inspecting her visits to the nation. The WSJ says that the country's authorities are probing her involvement with China and have her under physical surveillance.

As for Nvidia, the company seemingly reposted today the same comments it offered us last week, stating that "meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The firm adds that "[its] regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security."

coreStoryFacts.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a man who likely attends numerous meetings, and today one more was added to his busy schedule.
Congress wants to have a closed-door chat with Huang over mounting concerns about national security .
The congressmen bidding for his time say last week's report spurred the move that he may be the target of espionage by a reported Chinese asset: Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (family unrelated).
The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) further claims that she was recruited by Chinese authorities due to her existing relationship with Jensen Huang.

As for Nvidia, the company seemingly reposted today the same comments it offered us last week, stating that "meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The firm adds that "[its] regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security."
According to the WSJ, Singaporean authorities opened their own probe into Megaspeed, and even reportedly questioned Alice Huang directly.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware.

The backdrop for the situation is that the U.S. has long-standing export controls blocking Nvidia and AMD's most advanced AI accelerator chips from reaching China, among a number of other nations.
The allegations were first published last week in the NYT, and are reportedly sourced from unnamed U.S. intelligence officials.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.
Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.
It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.
Congress has summoned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to directly explain his relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The backdrop for the situation is that the U.S. has long-standing export controls blocking Nvidia and AMD's most advanced AI accelerator chips from reaching China, among a number of other nations.
The allegations were first published last week in the NYT, and are reportedly sourced from unnamed U.S. intelligence officials.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.
Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.
It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.
Congress has summoned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to directly explain his relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

According to Axios on the 5th (local time), Representative Brian Mast, Republican Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Representative John Moolenaar, Chairman of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and Representative Rick Crawford, member of the Intelligence Committee, sent a letter to Jensen Huang that day, requesting his attendance at a joint, closed-door briefing by the three committees.
Alice Huang herself reportedly flaunted her ties by posting photos with Jensen Huang on social media, which she allegedly used to raise investment funds.

The Chinese government previously dismissed allegations of Chinese espionage targeting Nvidia as "groundless speculation." (Photo: Capture of a NetThunder LinkedIn post, Yonhap News) ※ Please note: This article was translated by AI and may contain errors.
In the letter, they asked Huang to explain Nvidia's security systems designed to protect the company from foreign adversaries, as well as his interactions with Alice Huang.
Nvidia has not released a statement regarding the House's summons.

Three House Republican committee chairs have asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to brief Congress behind closed doors on his reported relationship with a businesswoman accused of passing information to China.

Nvidia's Jensen Huang’s Close Friend Alleged To Be A Chinese SpyWhat lawmakers want to knowThe chairs are seeking details of Huang's interactions with Alice Huang and of Nvidia's security protocols against espionage by foreign adversaries, Implicator reported.

The Chinese government has previously called allegations that it was spying on Nvidia "groundless speculation."Nvidia says their interactions were “not unusual,” and no wrongdoing by Huang is alleged.Megaspeed and Nvidia chipsThe US government has suspected Megaspeed of helping China get around export curbs and gain access to Nvidia's AI chips.
Their letter, dated November 4, asks him for a closed-door briefing on November 18, the day after Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings, Reuters and Implicator reported.

The letter was signed by Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, John Moolenaar of the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and Rick Crawford of the House Intelligence Committee.Who Is Alice Huang?

The letter says recent reports raise national security concerns about China's access to sensitive US technology, and that Congress needs to determine how far American security may have been put at risk.

The backdrop for the situation is that the U.S. has long-standing export controls blocking Nvidia and AMD's most advanced AI accelerator chips from reaching China, among a number of other nations.
The allegations were first published last week in the NYT, and are reportedly sourced from unnamed U.S. intelligence officials.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.
Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.
It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.
Congress has summoned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to directly explain his relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

According to Axios on the 5th (local time), Representative Brian Mast, Republican Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Representative John Moolenaar, Chairman of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and Representative Rick Crawford, member of the Intelligence Committee, sent a letter to Jensen Huang that day, requesting his attendance at a joint, closed-door briefing by the three committees.
Alice Huang herself reportedly flaunted her ties by posting photos with Jensen Huang on social media, which she allegedly used to raise investment funds.

The Chinese government previously dismissed allegations of Chinese espionage targeting Nvidia as "groundless speculation." (Photo: Capture of a NetThunder LinkedIn post, Yonhap News) ※ Please note: This article was translated by AI and may contain errors.
In the letter, they asked Huang to explain Nvidia's security systems designed to protect the company from foreign adversaries, as well as his interactions with Alice Huang.
Nvidia has not released a statement regarding the House's summons.

Three House Republican committee chairs have asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to brief Congress behind closed doors on his reported relationship with a businesswoman accused of passing information to China.

Nvidia's Jensen Huang’s Close Friend Alleged To Be A Chinese SpyWhat lawmakers want to knowThe chairs are seeking details of Huang's interactions with Alice Huang and of Nvidia's security protocols against espionage by foreign adversaries, Implicator reported.

The Chinese government has previously called allegations that it was spying on Nvidia "groundless speculation."Nvidia says their interactions were “not unusual,” and no wrongdoing by Huang is alleged.Megaspeed and Nvidia chipsThe US government has suspected Megaspeed of helping China get around export curbs and gain access to Nvidia's AI chips.
Their letter, dated November 4, asks him for a closed-door briefing on November 18, the day after Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings, Reuters and Implicator reported.

The letter was signed by Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, John Moolenaar of the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and Rick Crawford of the House Intelligence Committee.Who Is Alice Huang?

The letter says recent reports raise national security concerns about China's access to sensitive US technology, and that Congress needs to determine how far American security may have been put at risk.

passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a man who likely attends numerous meetings, and today one more was added to his busy schedule.
Congress wants to have a closed-door chat with Huang over mounting concerns about national security .
The congressmen bidding for his time say last week's report spurred the move that he may be the target of espionage by a reported Chinese asset: Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (family unrelated).
The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) further claims that she was recruited by Chinese authorities due to her existing relationship with Jensen Huang.

As for Nvidia, the company seemingly reposted today the same comments it offered us last week, stating that "meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The firm adds that "[its] regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security."
According to the WSJ, Singaporean authorities opened their own probe into Megaspeed, and even reportedly questioned Alice Huang directly.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware.

sources.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned by Congress over Chinese espionage concerns
passages: Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.
Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.
It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.

NetThunder, a company that posted this photo on social media, introduced Alice Huang as "Megaspeed Chairperson Alice Wong." The U.S. Congress has summoned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to directly explain his relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. According to Axios on the 5th (local time), Representative Brian Mast, Republican Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Representative John Moolenaar, Chairman of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and Representative Rick Crawford, member of the Intelligence Committee, sent a letter to Jensen Huang that day, requesting his attendance at a joint, closed-door briefing by the three committees. In the letter, they asked Huang to explain Nvidia's security systems designed to protect the company from foreign adversaries, as well as his interactions with Alice Huang. They stated, "Recent reports raise serious national security concerns regarding the possibility of China accessing sensitive U.S. technologies and information," adding, "The issues of Chinese infiltration and access to advanced U.S. technology are core investigative matters for the three committees during this session." They emphasized, "It is crucial for Congress to understand the extent to which U.S. national security has been exposed to risk." This request indicates growing congressional pressure surrounding the investigation into the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who is suspected of Chinese espionage. Alice Huang is a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-headquartered data center company. She was photographed drinking alongside Jensen Huang and other artificial intelligence (AI) company executives at a bar in Taiwan in June 2024, and was spotted with him again in May of last year. Alice Huang herself reportedly flaunted her ties by posting photos with Jensen Huang on social media, which she allegedly used to raise investment funds. Previously, The New York Times (NYT) reported that Alice Huang is suspected of maintaining a close relationship with Jensen Huang and leaking information to China. The NYT also reported that President Donald Trump was briefed on the matter by intelligence agencies but took no action. The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that authorities in at least three countries are concerned that Alice Huang may have leaked sensitive information regarding Nvidia chips to the Chinese government. However, Nvidia has denied the allegations, stating that Jensen Huang's contact with Alice Huang was merely routine business interaction and that no national security-related information was leaked. Nvidia has not released a statement regarding the House's summons. The Chinese government previously dismissed allegations of Chinese espionage targeting Nvidia as "groundless speculation." (Photo: Capture of a NetThunder LinkedIn post, Yonhap News) ※ Please note: This article was translated by AI and may contain errors.

The backdrop for the situation is that the U.S. has long-standing export controls blocking Nvidia and AMD's most advanced AI accelerator chips from reaching China, among a number of other nations.
The allegations were first published last week in the NYT, and are reportedly sourced from unnamed U.S. intelligence officials.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.
Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.
Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.
It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.
The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.
The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.
Congress has summoned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to directly explain his relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

According to Axios on the 5th (local time), Representative Brian Mast, Republican Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Representative John Moolenaar, Chairman of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and Representative Rick Crawford, member of the Intelligence Committee, sent a letter to Jensen Huang that day, requesting his attendance at a joint, closed-door briefing by the three committees.
Alice Huang herself reportedly flaunted her ties by posting photos with Jensen Huang on social media, which she allegedly used to raise investment funds.

The Chinese government previously dismissed allegations of Chinese espionage targeting Nvidia as "groundless speculation." (Photo: Capture of a NetThunder LinkedIn post, Yonhap News) ※ Please note: This article was translated by AI and may contain errors.
In the letter, they asked Huang to explain Nvidia's security systems designed to protect the company from foreign adversaries, as well as his interactions with Alice Huang.
Nvidia has not released a statement regarding the House's summons.

Three House Republican committee chairs have asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to brief Congress behind closed doors on his reported relationship with a businesswoman accused of passing information to China.

Nvidia's Jensen Huang’s Close Friend Alleged To Be A Chinese SpyWhat lawmakers want to knowThe chairs are seeking details of Huang's interactions with Alice Huang and of Nvidia's security protocols against espionage by foreign adversaries, Implicator reported.

The Chinese government has previously called allegations that it was spying on Nvidia "groundless speculation."Nvidia says their interactions were “not unusual,” and no wrongdoing by Huang is alleged.Megaspeed and Nvidia chipsThe US government has suspected Megaspeed of helping China get around export curbs and gain access to Nvidia's AI chips.
Their letter, dated November 4, asks him for a closed-door briefing on November 18, the day after Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings, Reuters and Implicator reported.

The letter was signed by Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, John Moolenaar of the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and Rick Crawford of the House Intelligence Committee.Who Is Alice Huang?

The letter says recent reports raise national security concerns about China's access to sensitive US technology, and that Congress needs to determine how far American security may have been put at risk.

coreFacts.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a man who likely attends numerous meetings, and today one more was added to his busy schedule.
Congress wants to have a closed-door chat with Huang over mounting concerns about national security .
The congressmen bidding for his time say last week's report spurred the move that he may be the target of espionage by a reported Chinese asset: Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (family unrelated).
The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) further claims that she was recruited by Chinese authorities due to her existing relationship with Jensen Huang.

As for Nvidia, the company seemingly reposted today the same comments it offered us last week, stating that "meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The firm adds that "[its] regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security."
According to the WSJ, Singaporean authorities opened their own probe into Megaspeed, and even reportedly questioned Alice Huang directly.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware.

sources.title: Chatbots might be coming to Apple’s HomeView
passages: Code in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that Apple could add support for chatbots to its smart home hub.
Neither feature has been officially announced by Apple, and there’s no word on when they might become available.
While there are no details about what apps would fall under that heading, it seems reasonable that AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude could be added to HomeView.

According to pdfu on X, that new beta also adds support for bidirectional audio routing and session management, but says it’s “still not fully wired up.” Apple has also added anti-spoofing protection that will require a user to authenticate themselves with an iPhone after three failed attempts.

passages: Apple hasn't announced chatbot apps for HomeView, and the code doesn't show which apps could use the category or when it could launch, so support for ChatGPT, Claude, or other chatbots is unconfirmed.
It's not the first time the possibility has been floated: pdfu suggested on Sunday that chatbot apps might follow based on an unused flag in HomeView's software.
In a separate finding, pdfu also discovered that HomeView includes anti-spoofing protection .
Apparently, after three spoof attempts for a profile, the user must authenticate with an iPhone to see personal data, and the protection is enabled in HomeView software 27.2.
The software HomeView uses to display apps from a connected iPhone or iPad is said to have gained a " Conversational Apps " category in the latest beta.

HomeView isn't on sale in the European Union because Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS there, and Apple says it is still working with the EU to find a path forward to make it available in the bloc.

The update also reportedly adds preparations for two-way audio routing, session management, and interruptions, but pdfu notes that it is "still not fully wired up." Apple hasn't announced chatbot apps for HomeView, and the code doesn't show which apps could use the category or when it could launch, so support for ChatGPT, Claude, or other chatbots is unconfirmed. It's not the first time the possibility has been floated: pdfu suggested on Sunday that chatbot apps might follow based on an unused flag in HomeView's software. In a separate finding, pdfu also discovered that HomeView includes anti-spoofing protection . Apparently, after three spoof attempts for a profile, the user must authenticate with an iPhone to see personal data, and the protection is enabled in HomeView software 27.2. Apple is also said to be working on a lockout cooldown system, similar to what happens when you enter the wrong passcode on an iPhone. A first lockout can be cleared immediately, but a second lockout brings a one-hour wait, a third a four-hour wait, and a fourth (or any further) lockout an eight-hour wait. pdfu adds that the lockout cooldown periods are still in development, so for now any lockout can be cleared immediately by authenticating with an iPhone. Apple hasn't described either feature in its press materials. HomeView launches on November 13 for $299, in both desktop and wall-mounted versions. Here's what Apple has announced so far: HomeView won't have an App Store. However, as we reported last month , it shows CarPlay-style third-party audio and video apps from a connected iPhone or iPad. HomeView isn't on sale in the European Union because Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS there, and Apple says it is still working with the EU to find a path forward to make it available in the bloc.
