New features and lesser-known changes to check out if you're upgrading. Siri AI improvements, Suggestions in Messages, Apple Music rebrand, and more. Apple's iPhone Duo is in customers' hands, and our dedicated how-to series explains the new features worth trying first. Spec bump to the M6 chip for the low-end 14-inch model, plus new high-end PROLED XDR models with touchscreen displays. 8.5-inch OLED display, A20 Pro chip, IP67 water and dust resistance, and a thinner and lighter design. Apple's smart home hub with 7-inch square display, A18 chip with Siri AI support, and more. MacRumors attracts a broad audience of both consumers and professionals interested in the latest technologies and products. The Verge’s report centers on a find in an iOS 27.3 beta. Code in that build reportedly includes a category named “Conversational Apps” along with preparations for two-way audio routing, session management, and interruptions. The reporting credits a code investigator known as pdfu with the discovery. The headline conclusion is modest: chatbots might be coming to HomeView, and Apple appears to be building the framework that would let them. The same report carries a caution that readers should not skip. The code is “still not fully wired up,” per the reporting. Unfinished code in a beta shows direction, not a commitment. Apple regularly ships groundwork in betas that never reaches customers in the form people expect, and it sometimes ships features months after the first traces appear. What the report does not say matters as much as what it says. It does not name ChatGPT. It does not name Claude. It does not give a date. Apple has not announced third-party chatbot apps for HomeView, and the company has not responded to the code discovery in any form that appears in our fact base. Any article that treats the code as a launch announcement overshoots the evidence. For a news desk, the right framing is a three-layer ladder. At the bottom sits the confirmed product, a $299 hub with Apple’s own assistant. In the middle sits the reported code, which suggests an app category for conversation. At the top sits the speculation, in which named chatbot makers ship named apps on named dates. Only the bottom layer is solid today. Apple HomeView is a smart-home hub that Apple announced on October 13, 2026. Availability is scheduled for November 13, 2026. Reporting that cites Apple information lists the price at $299. The device runs on the A18 chip, which suggests Apple wants the hub to handle real intelligence work rather than act as a thin speaker. Apple Intelligence powers the assistant experience on the device. A hub built around a modern chip and a modern assistant stack is the kind of product that can host a conversational app framework without feeling bolted on. We are deliberately not listing screen size, speaker configuration, memory, or storage here. Our verified fact sheet does not include those specifications, and guessing at them would violate basic reporting standards. Buyers who need those details should wait for Apple’s product page and early hands-on coverage around the November 13 availability date. Siri AI is built into Apple HomeView and is powered by Apple Intelligence. It is available in beta on HomeView software version 27.2. Apple lists Siri AI as supporting open-ended questions and back-and-forth conversations on the device. That is notable, because back-and-forth conversation is exactly the behavior people associate with chatbots. This creates a real strategic puzzle. If Siri AI already handles open-ended conversation, why would Apple prepare a “Conversational Apps” category for outside developers? There are at least three plausible answers. Apple may want specialist assistants for tasks Siri AI does not cover. It may want to let users pick a preferred model for certain conversations. Or the category may serve something unrelated to chatbots, such as language tutors, storytelling apps, or customer-support voices from retailers. The code alone cannot settle which. The beta label also deserves attention. Apple is shipping its first-party conversational assistant on this hub as a beta on version 27.2, while the possible third-party framework sits in a separate iOS 27.3 beta. Two beta tracks with different version numbers suggest that Apple is staging the rollout. First-party behavior comes first, and an open door for others, if any, follows. The table below sorts every claim in circulation into what the verified record supports and what it does not. Treat the right-hand column as a reading guide, not a prediction. Two rows deserve extra emphasis. The claim that OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude will launch as dedicated HomeView apps is unconfirmed, and it remains unconfirmed even though the idea feels natural. Code that prepares a category is not the same thing as a partner list. A chatbot on a phone has a screen, a keyboard, and a person holding it. A chatbot on a hub has none of that. It lives on a shelf or a kitchen counter, hears a room full of voices, and answers to whoever speaks first. That changes the engineering and the product design. Then there is latency. Voice conversation feels natural only when responses start fast. A hub with an A18 chip can do some work on-device, yet large chatbot models usually run in the cloud, which adds round-trip delay. Interruption handling helps hide that delay because users can cut in when the assistant rambles. Our piece on the AI bill shock and the limits Forrester wants on agents shows the other side of that cloud dependency, where always-on conversations can turn into surprise costs for whoever pays the model provider. Finally, there is the question of who answers when two assistants could respond. If Siri AI and a third-party chatbot both live on the hub, the system needs a clear rule for who hears the wake word and who owns the thread. Apple’s emphasis on audio routing and session ownership in the reported code reads like an attempt to write that rule into the operating system. Apple enters a market where rival platform owners already pair their home devices with their own large language models. Amazon and Google both sell home hardware tied to their own assistants. We do not have verified specifications or prices for those rival products in our fact base, so this section compares strategy rather than spec sheets. Google builds its own Gemini model family. Our Claude versus Gemini comparison shows how close the top frontier models now sit on independent indexes, which weakens the argument that any single platform owner must lock users into a house model. If the best models are near parity, a hub that lets users choose becomes more attractive than a hub that forces one. Apple’s possible third path would split the difference. Siri AI would remain the default voice, powered by Apple Intelligence, while a conversational app layer would let outside models plug in under Apple’s rules for audio, sessions, and interruptions. Frontier chatbot makers now court distribution wherever they can find it. Google has pushed Gemini deeper into its own products, as in our report on the Google Messages redesign with Gemini in the beta . A hub that hosts third-party chatbots would be Apple’s answer to that distribution race, if the company chooses to run it. The first beneficiaries would be the chatbot makers themselves. A voice app on a $299 hub gives a model provider a daily-use surface in the home, which is hard to buy through advertising. Even without confirmed partners, the existence of the code makes the opportunity visible to every company that sells conversational AI. The second group is independent developers. A “Conversational Apps” category could create room for small teams to build specialized voice experiences, such as cooking guides, study partners, or accessibility tools, without training their own foundation models. coreStoryFacts.text: Code discovered in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that HomeView is set to gain support for third-party AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude.
Leaker pdfu said at the start of the month that ChatGPT, Claude and other AI apps “may” be coming to HomeView, after spotting an unused flag for ConversationalApps.
They now say that the beta of iOS 26.3 confirms their suspicion.
The same leaker recently discovered evidence that HomeView will be able to serve as a HomeKit security camera .
Code in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that Apple could add support for chatbots to its smart home hub.
Neither feature has been officially announced by Apple, and there’s no word on when they might become available.
While there are no details about what apps would fall under that heading, it seems reasonable that AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude could be added to HomeView.

According to pdfu on X, that new beta also adds support for bidirectional audio routing and session management, but says it’s “still not fully wired up.” Apple has also added anti-spoofing protection that will require a user to authenticate themselves with an iPhone after three failed attempts.

Apple hasn't announced chatbot apps for HomeView, and the code doesn't show which apps could use the category or when it could launch, so support for ChatGPT, Claude, or other chatbots is unconfirmed.
It's not the first time the possibility has been floated: pdfu suggested on Sunday that chatbot apps might follow based on an unused flag in HomeView's software.
In a separate finding, pdfu also discovered that HomeView includes anti-spoofing protection .
Apparently, after three spoof attempts for a profile, the user must authenticate with an iPhone to see personal data, and the protection is enabled in HomeView software 27.2.
The software HomeView uses to display apps from a connected iPhone or iPad is said to have gained a " Conversational Apps " category in the latest beta.

HomeView isn't on sale in the European Union because Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS there, and Apple says it is still working with the EU to find a path forward to make it available in the bloc.

They now say that the beta of iOS 26.3 confirms their suspicion.
The same leaker recently discovered evidence that HomeView will be able to serve as a HomeKit security camera .

sources.title: Chatbots might be coming to Apple’s HomeView
passages: Code in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that Apple could add support for chatbots to its smart home hub.
Neither feature has been officially announced by Apple, and there’s no word on when they might become available.
While there are no details about what apps would fall under that heading, it seems reasonable that AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude could be added to HomeView.

According to pdfu on X, that new beta also adds support for bidirectional audio routing and session management, but says it’s “still not fully wired up.” Apple has also added anti-spoofing protection that will require a user to authenticate themselves with an iPhone after three failed attempts.

extraction.body: Code discovered in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests Apple is laying the groundwork for chatbot apps on its upcoming HomeView smart home hub, according to the code investigator known as pdfu . The software HomeView uses to display apps from a connected iPhone or iPad is said to have gained a " Conversational Apps " category in the latest beta. The update also reportedly adds preparations for two-way audio routing, session management, and interruptions, but pdfu notes that it is "still not fully wired up." Apple hasn't announced chatbot apps for HomeView, and the code doesn't show which apps could use the category or when it could launch, so support for ChatGPT, Claude, or other chatbots is unconfirmed. It's not the first time the possibility has been floated: pdfu suggested on Sunday that chatbot apps might follow based on an unused flag in HomeView's software. In a separate finding, pdfu also discovered that HomeView includes anti-spoofing protection . Apparently, after three spoof attempts for a profile, the user must authenticate with an iPhone to see personal data, and the protection is enabled in HomeView software 27.2. Apple is also said to be working on a lockout cooldown system, similar to what happens when you enter the wrong passcode on an iPhone. A first lockout can be cleared immediately, but a second lockout brings a one-hour wait, a third a four-hour wait, and a fourth (or any further) lockout an eight-hour wait. pdfu adds that the lockout cooldown periods are still in development, so for now any lockout can be cleared immediately by authenticating with an iPhone. Apple hasn't described either feature in its press materials. HomeView launches on November 13 for $299, in both desktop and wall-mounted versions. Here's what Apple has announced so far: HomeView won't have an App Store. However, as we reported last month , it shows CarPlay-style third-party audio and video apps from a connected iPhone or iPad. HomeView isn't on sale in the European Union because Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS there, and Apple says it is still working with the EU to find a path forward to make it available in the bloc. The Verge’s report centers on a find in an iOS 27.3 beta. Code in that build reportedly includes a category named “Conversational Apps” along with preparations for two-way audio routing, session management, and interruptions. The reporting credits a code investigator known as pdfu with the discovery. The headline conclusion is modest: chatbots might be coming to HomeView, and Apple appears to be building the framework that would let them. The same report carries a caution that readers should not skip. The code is “still not fully wired up,” per the reporting. Unfinished code in a beta shows direction, not a commitment. Apple regularly ships groundwork in betas that never reaches customers in the form people expect, and it sometimes ships features months after the first traces appear. What the report does not say matters as much as what it says. It does not name ChatGPT. It does not name Claude. It does not give a date. Apple has not announced third-party chatbot apps for HomeView, and the company has not responded to the code discovery in any form that appears in our fact base. Any article that treats the code as a launch announcement overshoots the evidence. For a news desk, the right framing is a three-layer ladder. At the bottom sits the confirmed product, a $299 hub with Apple’s own assistant. In the middle sits the reported code, which suggests an app category for conversation. At the top sits the speculation, in which named chatbot makers ship named apps on named dates. Only the bottom layer is solid today. Apple HomeView is a smart-home hub that Apple announced on October 13, 2026. Availability is scheduled for November 13, 2026. Reporting that cites Apple information lists the price at $299. The device runs on the A18 chip, which suggests Apple wants the hub to handle real intelligence work rather than act as a thin speaker. Apple Intelligence powers the assistant experience on the device. A hub built around a modern chip and a modern assistant stack is the kind of product that can host a conversational app framework without feeling bolted on. We are deliberately not listing screen size, speaker configuration, memory, or storage here. Our verified fact sheet does not include those specifications, and guessing at them would violate basic reporting standards. Buyers who need those details should wait for Apple’s product page and early hands-on coverage around the November 13 availability date. Siri AI is built into Apple HomeView and is powered by Apple Intelligence. It is available in beta on HomeView software version 27.2. Apple lists Siri AI as supporting open-ended questions and back-and-forth conversations on the device. That is notable, because back-and-forth conversation is exactly the behavior people associate with chatbots. This creates a real strategic puzzle. If Siri AI already handles open-ended conversation, why would Apple prepare a “Conversational Apps” category for outside developers? There are at least three plausible answers. Apple may want specialist assistants for tasks Siri AI does not cover. It may want to let users pick a preferred model for certain conversations. Or the category may serve something unrelated to chatbots, such as language tutors, storytelling apps, or customer-support voices from retailers. The code alone cannot settle which. The beta label also deserves attention. Apple is shipping its first-party conversational assistant on this hub as a beta on version 27.2, while the possible third-party framework sits in a separate iOS 27.3 beta. Two beta tracks with different version numbers suggest that Apple is staging the rollout. First-party behavior comes first, and an open door for others, if any, follows. The table below sorts every claim in circulation into what the verified record supports and what it does not. Treat the right-hand column as a reading guide, not a prediction. Two rows deserve extra emphasis. The claim that OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude will launch as dedicated HomeView apps is unconfirmed, and it remains unconfirmed even though the idea feels natural. Code that prepares a category is not the same thing as a partner list. A chatbot on a phone has a screen, a keyboard, and a person holding it. A chatbot on a hub has none of that. It lives on a shelf or a kitchen counter, hears a room full of voices, and answers to whoever speaks first. That changes the engineering and the product design. Then there is latency. Voice conversation feels natural only when responses start fast. A hub with an A18 chip can do some work on-device, yet large chatbot models usually run in the cloud, which adds round-trip delay. Interruption handling helps hide that delay because users can cut in when the assistant rambles. Our piece on the AI bill shock and the limits Forrester wants on agents shows the other side of that cloud dependency, where always-on conversations can turn into surprise costs for whoever pays the model provider. Finally, there is the question of who answers when two assistants could respond. If Siri AI and a third-party chatbot both live on the hub, the system needs a clear rule for who hears the wake word and who owns the thread. Apple’s emphasis on audio routing and session ownership in the reported code reads like an attempt to write that rule into the operating system. Apple enters a market where rival platform owners already pair their home devices with their own large language models. Amazon and Google both sell home hardware tied to their own assistants. We do not have verified specifications or prices for those rival products in our fact base, so this section compares strategy rather than spec sheets. Google builds its own Gemini model family. Our Claude versus Gemini comparison shows how close the top frontier models now sit on independent indexes, which weakens the argument that any single platform owner must lock users into a house model. If the best models are near parity, a hub that lets users choose becomes more attractive than a hub that forces one. Apple’s possible third path would split the difference. Siri AI would remain the default voice, powered by Apple Intelligence, while a conversational app layer would let outside models plug in under Apple’s rules for audio, sessions, and interruptions. That would give Apple control of the experience without requiring it to win every model benchmark. It would also hand Apple a gatekeeper role over which chatbots reach the living room. The table below frames the three strategic options for a hub maker. It uses no vendor-specific numbers, because our verified record does not support them. The company has also shown a pattern of building infrastructure first and opening it later. Betas often contain framework code months before a public rollout, and some of it never graduates. The phrase “still not fully wired up,” as relayed in the reporting, fits that pattern. It marks the code as scaffolding. On the other side of the ledger, the AI industry changed fast in 2026. Frontier chatbot makers now court distribution wherever they can find it. Google has pushed Gemini deeper into its own products, as in our report on the Google Messages redesign with Gemini in the beta . A hub that hosts third-party chatbots would be Apple’s answer to that distribution race, if the company chooses to run it. The first beneficiaries would be the chatbot makers themselves. A voice app on a $299 hub gives a model provider a daily-use surface in the home, which is hard to buy through advertising. Even without confirmed partners, the existence of the code makes the opportunity visible to every company that sells conversational AI. The second group is independent developers. A “Conversational Apps” category could create room for small teams to build specialized voice experiences, such as cooking guides, study partners, or accessibility tools, without training their own foundation models. That depends on Apple publishing developer tools, which it has not done in anything we can verify. We would update these quickly on two triggers. A developer-facing document from Apple would raise the odds of a broad opening. A statement from a named chatbot maker would move the ChatGPT and Claude rumor from unconfirmed to reported. Buyers who want HomeView on day one should buy it for what Apple sells today. That means a $299 hub with the A18 chip and Siri AI in beta. If third-party chatbots arrive later, treat them as a bonus. A purchase justified only by a rumored ChatGPT or Claude app rests on an unconfirmed claim. Developers have more to track. Watch Apple’s beta release notes for the iOS 27.3 cycle and any HomeView software notes after version 27.2. If a documented API appears, the three named capabilities, two-way audio routing, session management, and interruptions, will tell you what the platform expects from a conversational app. Teams building voice products today can already design around those three behaviors. Teams also need a cost plan. Always-on voice sessions can drive inference spend, a point we raised in the bill shock coverage above. And for companies exploring agent-style products, our report on Perplexity Teammates and the $200 Max agents launch shows how fast the market is moving toward assistants that carry ongoing work, which is the same session-management idea Apple’s code reportedly prepares. The takeaway: the code is real enough to report, early enough to doubt, and silent on every detail that would let anyone plan a launch. Apple HomeView ships on November 13 with Siri AI. Whether chatbots join it is a question only Apple can answer, and so far it has not. Not confirmed. Apple has not announced third-party chatbot apps for HomeView, and support for ChatGPT, Claude, or other chatbots is unconfirmed. A claim that both will launch as dedicated HomeView apps is also unconfirmed. The Verge reported code that includes a “Conversational Apps” category and preparations for two-way audio routing, session management, and interruptions. The code investigator identified in the reporting is pdfu. The reporting says the code is “still not fully wired up.” Apple announced HomeView on October 13, 2026, and availability is scheduled for November 13, 2026. Reporting that cites Apple information puts the price at $299. Yes. Siri AI is built in and powered by Apple Intelligence. In the middle sits the reported code, which suggests an app category for conversation. At the top sits the speculation, in which named chatbot makers ship named apps on named dates. Only the bottom layer is solid today.

Apple HomeView is a smart-home hub that Apple announced on October 13, 2026. Availability is scheduled for November 13, 2026. Reporting that cites Apple information lists the price at $299. The device runs on the A18 chip, which suggests Apple wants the hub to handle real intelligence work rather than act as a thin speaker.

Apple Intelligence powers the assistant experience on the device. A hub built around a modern chip and a modern assistant stack is the kind of product that can host a conversational app framework without feeling bolted on.

We are deliberately not listing screen size, speaker configuration, memory, or storage here. Our verified fact sheet does not include those specifications, and guessing at them would violate basic reporting standards. Buyers who need those details should wait for Apple’s product page and early hands-on coverage around the November 13 availability date.

Siri AI is built into Apple HomeView and is powered by Apple Intelligence. It is available in beta on HomeView software version 27.2. Apple lists Siri AI as supporting open-ended questions and back-and-forth conversations on the device. That is notable, because back-and-forth conversation is exactly the behavior people associate with chatbots.

This creates a real strategic puzzle. If Siri AI already handles open-ended conversation, why would Apple prepare a “Conversational Apps” category for outside developers? There are at least three plausible answers. Apple may want specialist assistants for tasks Siri AI does not cover. It may want to let users pick a preferred model for certain conversations. Or the category may serve something unrelated to chatbots, such as language tutors, storytelling apps, or customer-support voices from retailers. The code alone cannot settle which.

The beta label also deserves attention. Apple is shipping its first-party conversational assistant on this hub as a beta on version 27.2, while the possible third-party framework sits in a separate iOS 27.3 beta. Two beta tracks with different version numbers suggest that Apple is staging the rollout. First-party behavior comes first, and an open door for others, if any, follows.
The table below sorts every claim in circulation into what the verified record supports and what it does not. Treat the right-hand column as a reading guide, not a prediction.

Two rows deserve extra emphasis. The claim that OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude will launch as dedicated HomeView apps is unconfirmed, and it remains unconfirmed even though the idea feels natural. Code that prepares a category is not the same thing as a partner list.

A chatbot on a phone has a screen, a keyboard, and a person holding it. A chatbot on a hub has none of that. It lives on a shelf or a kitchen counter, hears a room full of voices, and answers to whoever speaks first. That changes the engineering and the product design.

Then there is latency. Voice conversation feels natural only when responses start fast. A hub with an A18 chip can do some work on-device, yet large chatbot models usually run in the cloud, which adds round-trip delay. Interruption handling helps hide that delay because users can cut in when the assistant rambles. Our piece on the AI bill shock and the limits Forrester wants on agents shows the other side of that cloud dependency, where always-on conversations can turn into surprise costs for whoever pays the model provider.

Finally, there is the question of who answers when two assistants could respond. If Siri AI and a third-party chatbot both live on the hub, the system needs a clear rule for who hears the wake word and who owns the thread. Apple’s emphasis on audio routing and session ownership in the reported code reads like an attempt to write that rule into the operating system.

Apple enters a market where rival platform owners already pair their home devices with their own large language models. Amazon and Google both sell home hardware tied to their own assistants. We do not have verified specifications or prices for those rival products in our fact base, so this section compares strategy rather than spec sheets.

Google builds its own Gemini model family. Our Claude versus Gemini comparison shows how close the top frontier models now sit on independent indexes, which weakens the argument that any single platform owner must lock users into a house model. If the best models are near parity, a hub that lets users choose becomes more attractive than a hub that forces one.

Apple’s possible third path would split the difference. Siri AI would remain the default voice, powered by Apple Intelligence, while a conversational app layer would let outside models plug in under Apple’s rules for audio, sessions, and interruptions. That would give Apple control of the experience without requiring it to win every model benchmark. It would also hand Apple a gatekeeper role over which chatbots reach the living room.
The table below frames the three strategic options for a hub maker. It uses no vendor-specific numbers, because our verified record does not support them.

The company has also shown a pattern of building infrastructure first and opening it later. Betas often contain framework code months before a public rollout, and some of it never graduates. The phrase “still not fully wired up,” as relayed in the reporting, fits that pattern. It marks the code as scaffolding.

On the other side of the ledger, the AI industry changed fast in 2026. Frontier chatbot makers now court distribution wherever they can find it. Google has pushed Gemini deeper into its own products, as in our report on the Google Messages redesign with Gemini in the beta . A hub that hosts third-party chatbots would be Apple’s answer to that distribution race, if the company chooses to run it.

The first beneficiaries would be the chatbot makers themselves. A voice app on a $299 hub gives a model provider a daily-use surface in the home, which is hard to buy through advertising. Even without confirmed partners, the existence of the code makes the opportunity visible to every company that sells conversational AI.

The second group is independent developers. A “Conversational Apps” category could create room for small teams to build specialized voice experiences, such as cooking guides, study partners, or accessibility tools, without training their own foundation models. That depends on Apple publishing developer tools, which it has not done in anything we can verify.

We would update these quickly on two triggers. A developer-facing document from Apple would raise the odds of a broad opening. A statement from a named chatbot maker would move the ChatGPT and Claude rumor from unconfirmed to reported.

Buyers who want HomeView on day one should buy it for what Apple sells today. That means a $299 hub with the A18 chip and Siri AI in beta. If third-party chatbots arrive later, treat them as a bonus. A purchase justified only by a rumored ChatGPT or Claude app rests on an unconfirmed claim.

Developers have more to track. Watch Apple’s beta release notes for the iOS 27.3 cycle and any HomeView software notes after version 27.2. If a documented API appears, the three named capabilities, two-way audio routing, session management, and interruptions, will tell you what the platform expects from a conversational app. Teams building voice products today can already design around those three behaviors.

Teams also need a cost plan. Always-on voice sessions can drive inference spend, a point we raised in the bill shock coverage above. And for companies exploring agent-style products, our report on Perplexity Teammates and the $200 Max agents launch shows how fast the market is moving toward assistants that carry ongoing work, which is the same session-management idea Apple’s code reportedly prepares.

The takeaway: the code is real enough to report, early enough to doubt, and silent on every detail that would let anyone plan a launch. Apple HomeView ships on November 13 with Siri AI. Whether chatbots join it is a question only Apple can answer, and so far it has not.

story.title: Chatbots might be coming to Apple’s HomeView

facts.text: Code discovered in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that HomeView is set to gain support for third-party AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude.
Leaker pdfu said at the start of the month that ChatGPT, Claude and other AI apps “may” be coming to HomeView, after spotting an unused flag for ConversationalApps.
They now say that the beta of iOS 26.3 confirms their suspicion.
The same leaker recently discovered evidence that HomeView will be able to serve as a HomeKit security camera .
Code in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that Apple could add support for chatbots to its smart home hub.
Neither feature has been officially announced by Apple, and there’s no word on when they might become available.
While there are no details about what apps would fall under that heading, it seems reasonable that AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude could be added to HomeView.

According to pdfu on X, that new beta also adds support for bidirectional audio routing and session management, but says it’s “still not fully wired up.” Apple has also added anti-spoofing protection that will require a user to authenticate themselves with an iPhone after three failed attempts.

Apple hasn't announced chatbot apps for HomeView, and the code doesn't show which apps could use the category or when it could launch, so support for ChatGPT, Claude, or other chatbots is unconfirmed.
It's not the first time the possibility has been floated: pdfu suggested on Sunday that chatbot apps might follow based on an unused flag in HomeView's software.
In a separate finding, pdfu also discovered that HomeView includes anti-spoofing protection .
Apparently, after three spoof attempts for a profile, the user must authenticate with an iPhone to see personal data, and the protection is enabled in HomeView software 27.2.
The software HomeView uses to display apps from a connected iPhone or iPad is said to have gained a " Conversational Apps " category in the latest beta.

HomeView isn't on sale in the European Union because Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS there, and Apple says it is still working with the EU to find a path forward to make it available in the bloc.

sources.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces bipartisan congressional scrutiny over reported China spy link - CNBC
passages: Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are ramping up calls for congressional investigations into reports of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Policymakers in the Trump administration received a memo last spring with intelligence identifying Alice Huang as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security and revealing her relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, the Times first reported on Friday.
The State Department and the White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," the company told CNBC in a statement.

Nvidia's board announced Sunday it is opening an independent investigation into Huang's involvement with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company that the U.S. has suspected of helping China circumvent artificial intelligence chip sales prohibitions.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China's] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang .
When asked by the Times whether Huang would appear before lawmakers to discuss the matter, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo declined to comment.

extraction.body: Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are ramping up calls for congressional investigations into reports of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia's board announced Sunday it is opening an independent investigation into Huang's involvement with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech company that the U.S. has suspected of helping China circumvent artificial intelligence chip sales prohibitions. In a memo to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang disclosed he had been intimate with the woman, but the affair was not mentioned in the board's statement. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating, the board said. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said in its statement . "Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," the company told CNBC in a statement. Lawmakers have been calling for an investigation into the relationship and are also questioning what the Trump administration knew about it. "The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt," Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., posted on X on Saturday. "Congress will investigate and get answers." Coons is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when his party takes control of the chamber in January. Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18, a day after the company is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China's] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang . Policymakers in the Trump administration received a memo last spring with intelligence identifying Alice Huang as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security and revealing her relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, the Times first reported on Friday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the memo's creation, the Times reported Sunday, citing people briefed on the matter. The State Department and the White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. When asked by the Times whether Huang would appear before lawmakers to discuss the matter, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo declined to comment. "Our chief executive has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed," Mr. Rizzo said in a statement to the Times. Rizzo said the Nvidia CEO's interactions with Ms. Huang were consistent with meetings he has had with any of Nvidia's customers, the Times reported . Separately, Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn shared a Times article published Saturday reporting that the Trump administration approved a Chinese firm, New Matrix, to assemble chips for Nvidia in Beijing. The Times found little evidence of meaningful operations at its listed address, despite Trump's Commerce Department clearing it for national security risks. Cornyn called the report "outrageous" in his post on X . Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., who sits on the House Committee on Homeland Security, called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify before Congress along with Huang. Neither Nvidia nor the Commerce Department immediately responded to CNBC's request for comment. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. The lawmakers want Huang to describe what he has been doing with Alice Huang, who is an executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, and how Nvidia secures the secrets of its technology and corporate knowledge from foreign spies. Heres a copy of the three Republican House committee chairs message to Huang in a letter dated November 4 available on the official foreignaffairs.house.gov website: Why are US lawmakers seeking answers from Jensen Huang? Three Republican committee chairmen—Brian Mast (House Foreign Affairs), John Moolenaar (House Select Committee on China) and Rick Crawford (House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence)—made the request. The legislators asked Huang to come to a joint briefing on November 18, in a letter dated November 4. They have requested that he either confirm his availability or suggest another date as soon as November 11. Their concerns follow an investigation published by The New York Times on October 29. As per the newspapers report, US intelligence agencies had examined Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, over suspected links to Beijing. According to The New York Times, Alice Huang was allegedly recruited by Chinas Ministry of State Security to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang. The existence of the intelligence memo and the assessment that Alice Huang was working for Chinas principal intelligence agency had not previously been reported. The report also noted the possibility that her role at Megaspeed may have given her the chance to find out how Nvidia was planning to conduct business and what it was talking to the U.S. government about. Why is Megaspeed involved in the investigation? Singaporean data centre operator Megaspeed grabbed headlines for its business with the advanced Nvidia AI chips. US officials reportedly investigated whether the firm aided Chinese companies access to more sophisticated computer chips, subject to U.S. export controls. Washington has placed restrictions on the sale of some high-performance semiconductors to China, as it attempts to curb its access to technology that could improve its artificial intelligence and military programs. Nvidia occupies a particularly important position in this debate because its graphics processing units (GPUs) are widely used to develop and operate advanced AI systems. Any possible diversion of restricted chips or access to sensitive commercial information therefore carries implications beyond an individual companys business relationships. The congressional committees want to know if Nvidias current security measures are adequate to firewall its technology and information against overseas customers. The NYT report also highlighted Megaspeeds growing role in the AI infrastructure business. The company reportedly began a multibillion-dollar purchase of advanced AI chips around 2024 and has been developing data centres in Southeast Asia. These facilities are then rented to Chinese technology giant Alibaba, potentially providing an indirect route for China to access advanced Nvidia chips that cannot be sold directly to the country under US export restrictions. Nvidia has defended the nature of its chief executives interactions with customers, arguing that meetings with business executives are a routine part of running a global technology company. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told The New York Times that the company does not share classified information with customers. He also described Jensen Huangs interactions with Alice Huang as normal business engagements, consistent with the CEOs regular meetings with thousands of executives who work with Nvidia. Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy rejected the newspapers reporting, calling the allegations unsubstantiated. The company added it receives information and guidance from the US government on security issues regarding entities that it may be concerned with. Nvidia did not confirm or deny whether Huang would be at the proposed Congressional briefing. The report also did not immediately have a comment from Megaspeed. Trumps reported awareness adds another dimension The controversy has also drawn attention to President Donald Trumps earlier awareness of the intelligence findings. According to The New York Times, Trump was briefed about the findings approximately a year before the newspapers report became public. The newspaper reported that he chose not to take action at the time. The development is notable because Trump has maintained close engagement with the American technology industry and has supported efforts to strengthen the countrys position in artificial intelligence. But the questions being raised by lawmakers are different from the intelligence report and the administrations response. Congresss November 18 briefing might allow committees to look into Nvidias business practices, how its sharing information, and internal security practices.

passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing questions from senior US lawmakers over his interactions with an executive at a company whose employee is reportedly being investigated for suspected espionage on behalf of China.

Huang’s reported ties to a Chinese intelligence-linked executive of a Singapore-based data center company. — Select Committee on China (@ChinaSelect) November 5, 2026 The lawmakers have proposed a joint, closed-door session focused on Nvidia's security procedures.

Lawmakers seek answers as Nvidia faces China-related scrutiny The letter to Huang was signed by Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, who currently lead three congressional panels dealing with foreign affairs, China and intelligence matters.
For Huang, the latest request adds to an already difficult relationship with some lawmakers over Nvidia's business in China.

Three Republican lawmakers have asked Huang to appear before Congress on November 18, seeking details about the nature of his dealings and the chipmaker's safeguards against potential security threats.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive US technology and information," the representatives wrote, referring to the People's Republic of China.
The lawmakers, however, want a more detailed account of the company's interactions with the Megaspeed executive and the measures it takes to protect sensitive technology.
The proposed restrictions reflect growing concern in Washington that access to advanced computing hardware could strengthen China's military and technological capabilities.

extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing questions from senior US lawmakers over his interactions with an executive at a company whose employee is reportedly being investigated for suspected espionage on behalf of China. Three Republican lawmakers have asked Huang to appear before Congress on November 18, seeking details about the nature of his dealings and the chipmaker's safeguards against potential security threats. The request follows a report by The New York Times last week that Huang Le, an executive at Megaspeed International, had been under US government surveillance over allegations that he supplied information to the Chinese government. The report has raised questions about whether individuals with potential links to Beijing could gain access to sensitive American technology or information through their business relationships with major technology companies. Nvidia has pushed back against any suggestion that its interactions with customers indicate a security concern. A company spokesperson said Huang engages with thousands of customers annually and expressed confidence that US authorities would alert the chipmaker if they considered an individual a threat to American industry. The lawmakers, however, want a more detailed account of the company's interactions with the Megaspeed executive and the measures it takes to protect sensitive technology. Lawmakers seek answers as Nvidia faces China-related scrutiny The letter to Huang was signed by Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, who currently lead three congressional panels dealing with foreign affairs, China and intelligence matters. Chairman @RepMoolenaar, Chairman @RepBrianMast, and Chairman @RepRickCrawford have sent a letter to NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang asking him to appear before their three committees this month. The letter expresses concerns over NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and Mr. Huang’s reported ties to a Chinese intelligence-linked executive of a Singapore-based data center company. — Select Committee on China (@ChinaSelect) November 5, 2026 The lawmakers have proposed a joint, closed-door session focused on Nvidia's security procedures. They argued that the allegations surrounding Megaspeed warranted congressional examination, particularly given the risks associated with China's access to advanced American technology. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive US technology and information," the representatives wrote, referring to the People's Republic of China. They added that Congress needed to establish whether American national security had been compromised. The incoming leadership has signalled plans for closer oversight of corporate conduct, with major Silicon Valley companies likely to face questions about their business practices and the broader implications of their technology. For Huang, the latest request adds to an already difficult relationship with some lawmakers over Nvidia's business in China. Mast, in particular, has repeatedly challenged the company's position on export restrictions. In January, he accused Nvidia and its chief executive of pushing to sell millions of advanced chips to Chinese businesses and even challenged Huang to a televised debate on Fox News. Proposed AI chip restrictions add to tensions The disagreement extends beyond the latest espionage allegations. Nvidia has been at the centre of a wider Washington debate over whether American companies should be allowed to sell their most advanced AI processors to Chinese customers. Earlier this year, Mast helped develop the AI Overwatch Act, a proposed law intended to give Congress greater authority over exports of advanced AI chips. The legislation sought to introduce an approval mechanism similar to the oversight used for certain arms sales, allowing lawmakers to block specific transactions through a joint resolution. Under the proposal, sales of Nvidia's H200 processors could face congressional intervention, while the company's Blackwell generation and subsequent, more advanced chips would be subject to restrictions. The proposed restrictions reflect growing concern in Washington that access to advanced computing hardware could strengthen China's military and technological capabilities. Nvidia, meanwhile, has argued against overly restrictive export policies.

In a memo to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang disclosed he had been intimate with the woman, but the affair was not mentioned in the board's statement. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating, the board said. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said in its statement . Chris Coons, D-Del., posted on X on Saturday. "Congress will investigate and get answers." Coons is in line to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when his party takes control of the chamber in January. Three House Republican committee chairs sent a letter to Huang on Wednesday asking him to sit for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18, a day after the company is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China's] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang . Policymakers in the Trump administration received a memo last spring with intelligence identifying Alice Huang as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security and revealing her relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, the Times first reported on Friday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the memo's creation, the Times reported Sunday, citing people briefed on the matter. The State Department and the White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. When asked by the Times whether Huang would appear before lawmakers to discuss the matter, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo declined to comment. "Our chief executive has an outstanding security team that accompanies him where needed," Mr. Rizzo said in a statement to the Times. Cornyn called the report "outrageous" in his post on X . Rep. extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing questions from senior US lawmakers over his interactions with an executive at a company whose employee is reportedly being investigated for suspected espionage on behalf of China. Three Republican lawmakers have asked Huang to appear before Congress on November 18, seeking details about the nature of his dealings and the chipmaker's safeguards against potential security threats. The request follows a report by The New York Times last week that Huang Le, an executive at Megaspeed International, had been under US government surveillance over allegations that he supplied information to the Chinese government. The report has raised questions about whether individuals with potential links to Beijing could gain access to sensitive American technology or information through their business relationships with major technology companies. Nvidia has pushed back against any suggestion that its interactions with customers indicate a security concern. A company spokesperson said Huang engages with thousands of customers annually and expressed confidence that US authorities would alert the chipmaker if they considered an individual a threat to American industry. The lawmakers, however, want a more detailed account of the company's interactions with the Megaspeed executive and the measures it takes to protect sensitive technology. Lawmakers seek answers as Nvidia faces China-related scrutiny The letter to Huang was signed by Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, who currently lead three congressional panels dealing with foreign affairs, China and intelligence matters. Chairman @RepMoolenaar, Chairman @RepBrianMast, and Chairman @RepRickCrawford have sent a letter to NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang asking him to appear before their three committees this month. The letter expresses concerns over NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and Mr. Huang’s reported ties to a Chinese intelligence-linked executive of a Singapore-based data center company. — Select Committee on China (@ChinaSelect) November 5, 2026 The lawmakers have proposed a joint, closed-door session focused on Nvidia's security procedures. They argued that the allegations surrounding Megaspeed warranted congressional examination, particularly given the risks associated with China's access to advanced American technology. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive US technology and information," the representatives wrote, referring to the People's Republic of China. They added that Congress needed to establish whether American national security had been compromised. The incoming leadership has signalled plans for closer oversight of corporate conduct, with major Silicon Valley companies likely to face questions about their business practices and the broader implications of their technology. For Huang, the latest request adds to an already difficult relationship with some lawmakers over Nvidia's business in China. Mast, in particular, has repeatedly challenged the company's position on export restrictions. In January, he accused Nvidia and its chief executive of pushing to sell millions of advanced chips to Chinese businesses and even challenged Huang to a televised debate on Fox News. Proposed AI chip restrictions add to tensions The disagreement extends beyond the latest espionage allegations. Nvidia has been at the centre of a wider Washington debate over whether American companies should be allowed to sell their most advanced AI processors to Chinese customers. Earlier this year, Mast helped develop the AI Overwatch Act, a proposed law intended to give Congress greater authority over exports of advanced AI chips. The legislation sought to introduce an approval mechanism similar to the oversight used for certain arms sales, allowing lawmakers to block specific transactions through a joint resolution. Under the proposal, sales of Nvidia's H200 processors could face congressional intervention, while the company's Blackwell generation and subsequent, more advanced chips would be subject to restrictions. The proposed restrictions reflect growing concern in Washington that access to advanced computing hardware could strengthen China's military and technological capabilities. Nvidia, meanwhile, has argued against overly restrictive export policies.

extraction.body: Four years ago the Bank of Russia wanted to ban crypto outright. On November 17 it will do the opposite: let ordinary Russians buy Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether's USDT through licensed brokers and exchanges. The list is short, the limits are strict, and the political subtext is hard to miss. The central bank has finalised the rules that let exchanges admit three assets to public trading for non-qualified investors: Bitcoin, Ether and USDT. From November 17, exchanges may list them, and retail investors can buy through brokers, asset managers or licensed crypto exchanges. Moscow Exchange plans to launch its own crypto trading in December, and the country's largest banks, Sberbank and VTB, are preparing access for their roughly 140 million banking clients. Financial institutions have until July 1, 2027 to align their infrastructure fully with the new framework. The three coins were chosen because they cleared the regulator's liquidity and market-history thresholds. First Deputy Governor Vladimir Chistyukhin has said there are no plans to extend the list for now. How much can Russian retail investors actually buy? Non-qualified investors face an annual purchase cap of 300,000 rubles, roughly 3,600 dollars. Sources differ on whether the cap applies per intermediary or per asset, but either way this is a sandbox, not a free market. Qualified investors, by contrast, can trade any cryptocurrency on exchange or over the counter without a limit.The largest crypto assets compared over 90 days, according to CoinMarketCap data The regulator's own estimate is that retail makes up around 98 percent of market participants. The cap is designed to pull that crowd away from unmonitored peer-to-peer channels and into supervised ones, where every ruble can be tracked. Because the central bank's criteria are liquidity and track record on regulated venues, not market cap. XRP, despite its size and its institutional use inside Russia, did not meet them. Qualified investors can still trade it through Moscow Exchange products; the general public cannot. For a token that has built much of its narrative on bank adoption, being left out by one of the world's most bank-centric crypto frameworks is an awkward headline. A dollar stablecoin issued by a company that complies with US sanctions is now the only stablecoin a Russian retail investor may legally buy. At the same time, Tether has frozen millions in USDT linked to sanctioned Russian exchanges. Russia gets a liquid dollar instrument for domestic investors; Tether gets a market it cannot openly serve. Expect this tension to produce headlines well beyond November 17.The Fear and Greed Index places market sentiment between extreme fear and extreme greed Does Russia's move matter for Bitcoin price? A 3,600 dollar annual cap on a population of retail investors is not the kind of flow that moves a 1.5 trillion dollar asset. Longer term, the signal matters more than the volume: a G20 central bank that called crypto a threat to financial stability in 2022 now builds regulated rails for it. From November 17, exchanges may list them, and retail investors can buy through brokers, asset managers or licensed crypto exchanges.
Expect this tension to produce headlines well beyond November 17.The Fear and Greed Index places market sentiment between extreme fear and extreme greed Does Russia's move matter for Bitcoin price?

Qualified investors, by contrast, can trade any cryptocurrency on exchange or over the counter without a limit.The largest crypto assets compared over 90 days, according to CoinMarketCap data The regulator's own estimate is that retail makes up around 98 percent of market participants.
The central bank has finalised the rules that let exchanges admit three assets to public trading for non-qualified investors: Bitcoin, Ether and USDT.
A 3,600 dollar annual cap on a population of retail investors is not the kind of flow that moves a 1.5 trillion dollar asset.
Moscow Exchange plans to launch its own crypto trading in December, and the country's largest banks, Sberbank and VTB, are preparing access for their roughly 140 million banking clients.
How much can Russian retail investors actually buy?
A dollar stablecoin issued by a company that complies with US sanctions is now the only stablecoin a Russian retail investor may legally buy.
Four years ago the Bank of Russia wanted to ban crypto outright.
Russia gets a liquid dollar instrument for domestic investors; Tether gets a market it cannot openly serve.

sources.title: Russia allows retail investors to buy Bitcoin, Ether, and USDT with strict limits from Nov 17.
passages: Starting November 17, Russian retail investors can legally buy Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tether's USDT through licensed brokers and exchanges under new rules by the Bank of Russia.
Regarding Russia's new retail crypto trading rules, here is Pluang's market snapshot as of Nov 07, 2026 15:41 WIB: Among 50 major cryptocurrencies, 31 rose while 17 fell.
The annual purchase cap for non-qualified investors is 300,000 rubles (about $3,600), aiming to move retail trading into regulated channels.
XRP is excluded due to regulatory criteria, and the inclusion of USDT raises interesting dynamics amid sanctions.
Qualified investors face no limits and can trade any cryptocurrency.

sources.title: Russia Is Opening Bitcoin and Ethereum to Retail Investors This Month. Can a 300,000-Ruble Cap Move the BTC and ETH Price? - 24/7 Wall St.
passages: Russia’s central bank opened the crypto market to retail investors.

Under a new Bank of Russia regulation, investors who aren’t classified as professional buyers can start buying Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), and the Tether ( CRYPTO:USDT ) stablecoin from November 17.
However, purchases through any one intermediary are capped at 300,000 rubles a year, roughly $3,662 at the November 8 exchange rate.
Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst and the editor of 24/7 Wall St.'s Crypto Desk, where he covers Bitcoin, XRP, Ethereum, Solana and the altcoins investors search for most.
His work focuses on price levels, spot ETF flows, on-chain data and the regulatory decisions that move crypto markets, written so a first-time buyer and a seasoned trader can both use it.
Sam has written about crypto professionally since 2019 and has published more than 2,000 articles.
His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites.
He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives.
When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.
On the current evidence, the 300,000-ruble cap seems unlikely to move Bitcoin’s price much, and Ethereum looks even less likely to benefit.
Bitcoin trades below its 20-day average of $79,362 and has slipped below its 30-day low close of $75,775, suggesting selling by US fund holders is a far bigger factor than potential Russian buying.
US-listed crypto stocks showed little reaction.
Coinbase ( NASDAQ:COIN | COIN Price Prediction ) fell 1.5% to $134.76 on November 6, while Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ:MSTR ) dipped 0.3% to $128.93.
Bitcoin trades at $75,662 and Ethereum at $2,226 today.
So can a cap this small move either coin’s price?
While the rules are clear, how retail buyers will reach the market remains uncertain.
On November 2, Moscow Exchange announced plans to start Bitcoin, Ethereum, and USDT trading on December 1, beginning with pilot trades.
However, Russia hasn’t disclosed how many brokers it will license at launch, nor has it shared a demand forecast.
Strategy holds about 848,517 BTC but has no retail customers.
Executive Chairman Michael Saylor told analysts on February 5 that crypto is moving from an asset class few could buy to one where everyone is competing to offer access.
Russia just handed ordinary citizens a legal path to Bitcoin and Ethereum, yet Coinbase and Strategy shrugged.
Between sanctions, broker bottlenecks, and heavy ETF outflows in the US, one number may matter far less than headlines suggest.
When El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender on September 7, 2021, Bitcoin dropped that same day sharply.
Our look at Ethereum’s year-end outlook runs the longer numbers.
That makes the theoretical ceiling look large on paper.
Even so, the knowledge test, a potentially long licensing process, and restrictions on moving coins to private wallets could significantly reduce actual demand.

extraction.body: Four years ago the Bank of Russia wanted to ban crypto outright. On November 17 it will do the opposite: let ordinary Russians buy Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether's USDT through licensed brokers and exchanges. The list is short, the limits are strict, and the political subtext is hard to miss. The central bank has finalised the rules that let exchanges admit three assets to public trading for non-qualified investors: Bitcoin, Ether and USDT. From November 17, exchanges may list them, and retail investors can buy through brokers, asset managers or licensed crypto exchanges. Moscow Exchange plans to launch its own crypto trading in December, and the country's largest banks, Sberbank and VTB, are preparing access for their roughly 140 million banking clients. Financial institutions have until July 1, 2027 to align their infrastructure fully with the new framework. The three coins were chosen because they cleared the regulator's liquidity and market-history thresholds. First Deputy Governor Vladimir Chistyukhin has said there are no plans to extend the list for now. How much can Russian retail investors actually buy? Non-qualified investors face an annual purchase cap of 300,000 rubles, roughly 3,600 dollars. Sources differ on whether the cap applies per intermediary or per asset, but either way this is a sandbox, not a free market. Qualified investors, by contrast, can trade any cryptocurrency on exchange or over the counter without a limit.The largest crypto assets compared over 90 days, according to CoinMarketCap data The regulator's own estimate is that retail makes up around 98 percent of market participants. The cap is designed to pull that crowd away from unmonitored peer-to-peer channels and into supervised ones, where every ruble can be tracked. Because the central bank's criteria are liquidity and track record on regulated venues, not market cap. XRP, despite its size and its institutional use inside Russia, did not meet them. Qualified investors can still trade it through Moscow Exchange products; the general public cannot. For a token that has built much of its narrative on bank adoption, being left out by one of the world's most bank-centric crypto frameworks is an awkward headline. A dollar stablecoin issued by a company that complies with US sanctions is now the only stablecoin a Russian retail investor may legally buy. At the same time, Tether has frozen millions in USDT linked to sanctioned Russian exchanges. Russia gets a liquid dollar instrument for domestic investors; Tether gets a market it cannot openly serve. Expect this tension to produce headlines well beyond November 17.The Fear and Greed Index places market sentiment between extreme fear and extreme greed Does Russia's move matter for Bitcoin price? A 3,600 dollar annual cap on a population of retail investors is not the kind of flow that moves a 1.5 trillion dollar asset. Longer term, the signal matters more than the volume: a G20 central bank that called crypto a threat to financial stability in 2022 now builds regulated rails for it. Hyperliquid whales, the exchange’s largest Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) traders, have made a major strategic shift, going net short on Bitcoin for the first time in seven months. According to on-chain analytics firm Glassnode, which reported the shift, these whales moved from a net long position to a net short one, and their current short position is the largest since October 2025. Bitcoin traded around $75,662 on November 8, down 8% over the past 30 days and just under its lowest 30-day close of $75,775 on November 6. Hyperliquid traders held $612 million in leveraged long positions just a week earlier, on November 2, showing a drastic shift in strategy. So, are the Hyperliquid whales predicting a further drop in Bitcoin’s price, or just hedging their existing holdings elsewhere? Hyperliquid is a decentralized exchange that offers perpetual futures contracts, which track Bitcoin’s price without any expiration date, allowing traders to use borrowed funds for their positions. These trades are recorded on Hyperliquid’s public blockchain, enabling Glassnode to analyze the holdings of significant accounts. A net short position means that positions profiting from a price drop outweigh those profiting from a price rise. Traders closely monitor these whales due to their substantial financial backing and potential access to better information, though their track record is mixed. For instance, they last went net short in March and then rebuilt their long positions during Bitcoin’s April rally. From April 12 to May 10, Bitcoin surged 16.1%, rising from $70,661 to $82,018 and catching many short traders off guard. Whales’ long positions also reversed. In May 2026, they reached a high level of net longs, but Bitcoin subsequently dropped by 28.6% to $58,566 by June 30. However, the whales had more success in October 2025 when they last held a similar level of short exposure. Bitcoin peaked at $126,080 on October 6, 2025, closed the month at $109,567, then slid 22.7% to $84,676 by November 22, 2025. So far, their current short position is paying off, as Glassnode noted that they first went net short on October 27 , when Bitcoin closed at $80,801, and Bitcoin has fallen about 6% since. Glassnode tracks only one exchange, leaving gaps in its analysis. A whale might own Bitcoin stored in cold storage, on a centralized exchange, or through an ETF and could short on Hyperliquid to protect their assets without selling, which would still count as a bearish position in Glassnode’s data. Additionally, most Bitcoin transactions occur on exchange order books that don’t interact with the blockchain, which is why significant whale buying in October did not lead to price increases. Hyperliquid represents only a small fraction of the total futures market. For context, on November 7, Binance’s BTCUSDT perpetual contracts accounted for 96,471 BTC (approximately $7.3 billion), while Bybit had 69,555 BTC ($5.28 billion) and OKX had 34,497 BTC ($2.62 billion). Funding rates also provide insight into market sentiment. These rates are the periodic fees that help align perpetual futures prices with the spot price. On November 7, Binance’s funding rate was slightly positive, at 0.0000059, suggesting that the broader market isn’t heavily positioned for a price drop. Thus, the Hyperliquid whales are taking a stance against the rest of the market. Open interest data indicates a directional bias among traders. Glassnode reported that Bitcoin’s open interest rose by about $1 billion during a drop in the U.S. session on November 6, with an additional $500 million the following session, while funding rates rose. This shows that traders were opening new leveraged long positions even as prices declined. If Bitcoin continues to drop, these long positions could face liquidation, an automatic closure of a borrowed position when losses exceed the initial deposit, adding selling pressure in favor of the whales. Moreover, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs reported $1.28 billion in outflows for the week ending November 6, including $430.2 million on November 5 and $411.9 million on November 6. The fund saw inflows on only one of its last five trading days, bringing in $74.6 million on November 4, while total net assets fell from $109.3 billion on October 21 to $95.9 billion. Investors have also been selling at a loss for an unusually long stretch . Based on current indicators, it seems more likely that the whales are making a directional call rather than merely hedging, although only they know their true intentions. At this point, the whales appear to have a stronger stance, especially as ETF investments decline and leveraged longs continue to accumulate beneath them. Their past performance seems to be about even, given the 16.1% rally against them in spring and the 22.7% decline that favored them later in 2025. From April 12 to May 10, Bitcoin surged 16.1%, rising from $70,661 to $82,018 and catching many short traders off guard.
Whales’ long positions also reversed. In May 2026, they reached a high level of net longs, but Bitcoin subsequently dropped by 28.6% to $58,566 by June 30.

However, the whales had more success in October 2025 when they last held a similar level of short exposure. Bitcoin peaked at $126,080 on October 6, 2025, closed the month at $109,567, then slid 22.7% to $84,676 by November 22, 2025. So far, their current short position is paying off, as Glassnode noted that they first went net short on October 27 , when Bitcoin closed at $80,801, and Bitcoin has fallen about 6% since.

Glassnode tracks only one exchange, leaving gaps in its analysis. A whale might own Bitcoin stored in cold storage, on a centralized exchange, or through an ETF and could short on Hyperliquid to protect their assets without selling, which would still count as a bearish position in Glassnode’s data.
Additionally, most Bitcoin transactions occur on exchange order books that don’t interact with the blockchain, which is why significant whale buying in October did not lead to price increases.

Hyperliquid represents only a small fraction of the total futures market. For context, on November 7, Binance’s BTCUSDT perpetual contracts accounted for 96,471 BTC (approximately $7.3 billion), while Bybit had 69,555 BTC ($5.28 billion) and OKX had 34,497 BTC ($2.62 billion).

Funding rates also provide insight into market sentiment. These rates are the periodic fees that help align perpetual futures prices with the spot price. On November 7, Binance’s funding rate was slightly positive, at 0.0000059, suggesting that the broader market isn’t heavily positioned for a price drop. Thus, the Hyperliquid whales are taking a stance against the rest of the market.

Open interest data indicates a directional bias among traders. Glassnode reported that Bitcoin’s open interest rose by about $1 billion during a drop in the U.S. session on November 6, with an additional $500 million the following session, while funding rates rose. This shows that traders were opening new leveraged long positions even as prices declined.

If Bitcoin continues to drop, these long positions could face liquidation, an automatic closure of a borrowed position when losses exceed the initial deposit, adding selling pressure in favor of the whales.

Moreover, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs reported $1.28 billion in outflows for the week ending November 6, including $430.2 million on November 5 and $411.9 million on November 6. The fund saw inflows on only one of its last five trading days, bringing in $74.6 million on November 4, while total net assets fell from $109.3 billion on October 21 to $95.9 billion.

Investors have also been selling at a loss for an unusually long stretch . Based on current indicators, it seems more likely that the whales are making a directional call rather than merely hedging, although only they know their true intentions.

At this point, the whales appear to have a stronger stance, especially as ETF investments decline and leveraged longs continue to accumulate beneath them. Their past performance seems to be about even, given the 16.1% rally against them in spring and the 22.7% decline that favored them later in 2025.
A week of net ETF inflows that surpasses the $1.28 billion that departed in the week ending November 6 could undercut the whales’ short.
